CRISC D3 round 2 (crisc_d3_021 to 050).

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Defining the desired state
questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST basis for the desired state in a risk practitioner's control gap analysis?

options.A: The controls peers use to stay within their own appetite
options.B: The chosen framework's control catalog as written
options.C: The control level needed to keep risk within appetite
options.D: The controls that IT can deliver within this year's budget

questions.key_concept: The desired state in a control gap analysis is the control level needed to bring risk within appetite and meet obligations.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each option would measure the gaps against.
questions.correct_explanation: The desired state should come from what the business has decided it will tolerate: the controls needed to bring each risk within this organization's appetite, along with any legal or contractual requirement. Peer practice is the closest alternative: it is useful context, but peers set their controls against their own risks, objectives and appetite, so copying them can over- or under-protect this organization.

wrong_explanations.A: Peer controls are set to stay within the peers' own appetite and risks, which may differ from this organization's, so copying them can over- or under-protect it.
wrong_explanations.B: A catalog is a menu to tailor from. Taking all of it as the target overspends on risks that matter little here.
wrong_explanations.D: Budget shapes the plan to close gaps, not the target itself. Setting the target at what IT can afford hides the gaps that matter.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a framework catalog as a checklist, and D lets this year's budget set the target in place of the risk.
Final two: C beats A because the target must reflect this organization's appetite; a peer's appetite is input at most, not the limit this business set.
Exam cue: in a gap analysis, the desired state comes from appetite and obligations; frameworks and peers inform it, budgets schedule it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.1 (CSF Profiles: a Current Profile describes outcomes being achieved and a Target Profile the outcomes selected for risk management objectives); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RM-02 (risk appetite and risk tolerance statements are established, communicated and maintained)

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Ordering the gaps
questions.question: A gap analysis at a freight railway lists 14 control gaps, and the CIO wants to close the nine quickest first to show the board progress. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have owners close quick gaps, then plan the rest
options.B: Close the gaps in the order the framework lists them
options.C: Have each control owner set the order for their gaps
options.D: Rank the gaps by the risk each one leaves open

questions.key_concept: Control gaps are ranked by the risk each leaves open, so the largest exposure is funded and fixed first.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the CIO's ordering is designed to show.
questions.correct_explanation: Gaps should be closed in the order of the exposure they leave, so the largest risks to the railway's objectives get resources first; quick fixes can still be scheduled where they fit. Having owners close the quick gaps first is the closest alternative: it shows progress, but the board would hear that things are improving while the gaps that matter most stay open.

wrong_explanations.A: Quick wins show activity, but they may leave the largest exposures untouched while progress looks good.
wrong_explanations.B: A framework's order reflects how the catalog is arranged, not where this organization's risk is greatest.
wrong_explanations.C: Each owner sees only their own gaps, so the order would follow local preference instead of enterprise exposure.

tips: Eliminate: B follows the catalog's layout, and C lets each owner set an order with no view of enterprise exposure.
Final two: D beats A because resources go first to the gaps that leave the most risk open; quick wins can fit around that order.
Exam cue: prioritize remediation by the risk left open, not by ease, catalog order or local preference.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.1 (Organizational Profiles step 4: analyze the gaps between the Current and Target Profiles and develop a prioritized action plan); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-05 (threats, vulnerabilities, likelihoods and impacts are used to understand inherent risk and inform risk response prioritization)

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. One maturity target for all controls
questions.question: To cut costs, a payments processor's IT director proposes one maturity target, level 2 on a 0 to 5 scale, for all IT controls, including card settlement controls. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Adopt level 2 as the common target for IT controls
options.B: Raise the targets for IT controls to the top level
options.C: Set each control's target by the risk it addresses
options.D: Drop maturity targets and rely on control testing

questions.key_concept: Target control maturity is set by the risk each control addresses, agreed with the risk owner, not as one level for every control.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the single target would mean for the highest-risk controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Maturity targets should follow risk: controls protecting card settlement need repeatable, measured practice, while low-risk controls can sit lower. The practitioner proposes targets set with each risk owner by the risk a control addresses, which spends where it matters. Dropping targets for testing is the closest alternative: testing shows a control works today, but maturity shows whether it will keep working.

wrong_explanations.A: One low target saves money on minor controls but under-protects the controls behind the processor's highest risks.
wrong_explanations.B: Top-level maturity everywhere costs far more than lower-risk controls justify; for most of them the cost would exceed the benefit.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing and maturity answer different questions. A control can pass this year's test yet depend on habits that will not last.

tips: Eliminate: A sets one low bar for high and low risks alike, and B pays for top maturity where the risk does not justify it.
Final two: C beats D because testing shows a control works now, while risk-based maturity targets show where it must keep working reliably.
Exam cue: maturity targets are set by risk, neither as high as possible nor as cheap as possible.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 Section 3.2 (CSF Tiers: progression to higher Tiers is encouraged when risks or mandates are greater or when cost-benefit analysis supports it); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 Task 3-2 (Evaluation of Alternatives: effectiveness, feasibility and cost)

CRISC D3 round 2 (crisc_d3_021 to 050). Review fixes 31 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): stem now gives the maturity scale, so 'one low target' in the explanations rests on a stated fact.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Failures found in a sample
questions.question: Testing a sample of 25 days of a water utility's daily backup check, the risk analyst finds no record for 2 days. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Rate the control ineffective and tell its owner
options.B: Replace the two days with two other sampled days
options.C: Report the control as 92% effective to its owner
options.D: Find out why the check was missed on those two days

questions.key_concept: Failures found in a control test sample are investigated for their cause before the tester concludes whether the control can be relied on.
questions.pre_read: Ask what you would need to know before calling the control effective or not.
questions.correct_explanation: A failure in a sample must be understood before the control is judged. The cause shows whether these were one-off lapses with the backups still checked another way, or a breakdown that undermines reliance on the control. Rating it ineffective now is the closest alternative: it may prove right, but concluding before knowing the cause can misstate the control and the risk.

wrong_explanations.A: The two gaps may lead to that rating, but deciding before the cause is known can misstate the control either way.
wrong_explanations.B: Swapping out failed items hides the result. Failures in a sample are evaluated, not replaced.
wrong_explanations.C: A percentage from a small sample says nothing about why the check was missed or whether it can be relied on.

tips: Eliminate: B removes failures from the sample, and C turns two misses into a pass rate without knowing their cause.
Final two: D beats A because the cause decides whether the control can still be relied on; a rating made before knowing it may be wrong.
Exam cue: in control testing, evaluate each failed sample item's cause before concluding on the control.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Reconciliation run by one clerk
questions.question: A distributor's monthly supplier-file reconciliation passed every sampled month, but only one clerk knows how to run it and nothing is written down. Which of the following conclusions is MOST appropriate for the risk practitioner?

options.A: Effective now, but at a low level of maturity
options.B: Ineffective until a written procedure exists
options.C: Mature, with no improvement needed
options.D: Poorly designed and in need of rebuilding

questions.key_concept: Effectiveness shows a control works now; maturity shows it will keep working. A control can be effective yet at low maturity.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the test results show from what the clerk's situation shows.
questions.correct_explanation: The sample shows the reconciliation works today, so it is effective. But it depends on one person with no written procedure, so it would stop if that clerk left or was absent: its maturity is low. The practitioner reports both and proposes documenting and sharing the task. Calling it ineffective is the closest alternative: the gap is about sustainability, not about whether it worked.

wrong_explanations.B: The tests show it worked in every sampled month. Missing documentation threatens whether it keeps working, which is maturity, not current effectiveness.
wrong_explanations.C: Passing tests shows effectiveness, not maturity. Reliance on one undocumented person is a sign of low maturity.
wrong_explanations.D: The design achieved its aim each month. The weakness is how it is sustained, which documentation and cross-training fix without rebuilding it.

tips: Eliminate: C confuses passing tests with maturity, and D calls for a redesign when the design works.
Final two: A beats B because the evidence shows the control works now; dependence on one person threatens how long it will keep working.
Exam cue: effectiveness asks whether a control works now; maturity asks whether it will keep working. Read results for both.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. What the draft plan lacks
questions.question: A risk owner at an insurance broker has agreed a draft action plan that lists each action's owner, budget and due date. Which of the following is MOST important to add to the plan?

options.A: The inherent rating from the first assessment
options.B: The risk level the plan is expected to reach
options.C: A weekly status color for each listed action
options.D: The risk practitioner's approval of the plan

questions.key_concept: A risk action plan states the target risk it should reach, so the owner can judge whether it is enough and later whether it worked.
questions.pre_read: Check the plan for how success will be judged, not only how work is scheduled.
questions.correct_explanation: Owners, budgets and dates show how the work will be done, but not what it must achieve. The target risk, the future residual risk the plan should reach, lets the owner judge whether the plan is enough to meet appetite and later test whether it worked. Weekly status colors are the closest alternative: they track progress, but progress toward an undefined level cannot show success.

wrong_explanations.A: The inherent rating is already in the register. It shows the starting point, not where the plan is meant to take the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Status colors help track actions, but without a target level the plan cannot show whether finishing it is enough.
wrong_explanations.D: The practitioner helps build the plan; the risk owner commits to it. The practitioner's approval adds no authority the owner lacks.

tips: Eliminate: A repeats a starting point already recorded, and D asks the practitioner to approve a plan the risk owner commits to.
Final two: B beats C because a plan needs the level it must reach before progress can mean anything; status colors track activity, not sufficiency.
Exam cue: a treatment plan names owners, actions, resources, dates and the target risk it should reach.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Long plan above appetite
questions.question: A manufacturer's 14-month plan to replace unsupported plant-floor servers leaves the risk above appetite until the work ends. What should the risk practitioner recommend the plan include as MOST important?

options.A: Monthly milestones that reveal schedule slippage early
options.B: The plant manager's acceptance of the risk meanwhile
options.C: Interim controls that reduce exposure during the work
options.D: Quarterly progress reports to the IT steering group

questions.key_concept: When a treatment takes months and risk stays above appetite, the plan includes interim measures that reduce exposure meanwhile.
questions.pre_read: Notice how long the risk stays above appetite before the plan finishes.
questions.correct_explanation: For 14 months the risk stays above appetite, so the plan needs interim measures, such as isolating the old servers and closer monitoring, that lower exposure while the replacement proceeds. Milestones are the closest alternative: they show slippage early and belong in the plan, but they do not reduce the exposure the business carries during those months.

wrong_explanations.A: Milestones belong in the plan and show slippage, but they leave the risk above appetite for the whole 14 months.
wrong_explanations.B: A risk above appetite is not the plant manager's to accept alone; it is treated or elevated to whoever set the appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Progress reports keep IT steering informed, but like milestones they track the work; the exposure stays above appetite for all 14 months.

tips: Eliminate: B has a manager accept a risk above appetite, and D reports progress without lowering the exposure.
Final two: C beats A because interim controls lower the exposure while the work runs; milestones track the work but leave the risk where it is.
Exam cue: a long remediation above appetite needs interim measures, not only a schedule.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Sudden indicator improvement
questions.question: A retailer's KRI for unencrypted laptops fell from 140 to 12 in a month, just after IT moved its data feed to a new device management tool. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Report the improvement to the laptop data-loss risk's owner
options.B: Confirm the new tool covers the same set of laptops
options.C: Ask the risk owner to lower the laptop data-loss rating
options.D: Reset the KRI thresholds to the new baseline

questions.key_concept: Risk data is validated for completeness and consistency before reporting; a sudden metric change after a source change is checked first.
questions.pre_read: Notice what else changed at the same time as the indicator.
questions.correct_explanation: A drop this large right after a data source change is a reason to check the data before using it. If the new tool sees only enrolled laptops, unencrypted ones may simply be missing from the count. The practitioner confirms coverage and definitions match first. Reporting the improvement is the closest alternative: it is the expected next step, but only once the figure is shown to be real.

wrong_explanations.A: Reporting first passes on a figure that may reflect the tool's coverage, leading the owner to relax about a risk that has not changed.
wrong_explanations.C: Asking the owner to re-rate on an unvalidated metric could lower the rating of a risk whose exposure is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.D: Resetting thresholds builds a possible data error into the indicator, so real exposure could stay hidden.

tips: Eliminate: C has the risk owner re-rate the risk on an unchecked figure, and D builds a possible data error into the thresholds.
Final two: B beats A because data is validated before it is reported; a sudden drop after a source change may mean missing laptops, not fixed ones.
Exam cue: a sudden change in a metric, especially after a data source change, is checked against the source before it is reported.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Data missing at reporting time
questions.question: Two of a bus operator's nine depots have not sent this quarter's KRI data, and the risk report goes to the executive committee tomorrow. What is the risk practitioner's BEST approach?

options.A: Fill the two depots' gaps with last quarter's figures
options.B: Delay the report until the two depots send their data
options.C: Leave the two depots out of the report's totals
options.D: Send the report, stating which depots are missing

questions.key_concept: Risk reports state known data limitations, such as missing units, rather than omitting them, estimating silently or delaying all reporting.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the committee needs to read the totals correctly.
questions.correct_explanation: Decision makers need the report on time and need to know its limits. Sending it with the missing depots named lets the committee read the totals correctly and ask for follow-up. Delaying is the closest alternative: complete data is better, but holding the whole report back denies the committee current information on the other seven depots for the sake of two.

wrong_explanations.A: Last quarter's figures may no longer reflect the two depots. Presenting them as current misleads the committee about present exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for complete data delays decisions on the seven depots that did report, when the gap could simply be stated.
wrong_explanations.C: Dropping the depots silently understates the operator's exposure and leaves the committee unaware the totals are incomplete.

tips: Eliminate: A presents stale figures as current, and C silently understates the totals.
Final two: D beats B because a report with its limits stated still supports timely decisions; holding it back costs the committee seven depots' data.
Exam cue: when part of the data is missing, report on time with the limitation stated rather than hiding or guessing.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for an access review control
questions.question: Which of the following should a risk practitioner propose as the BEST key control indicator for a bank's quarterly recertification of user access?

options.A: Number of privileged accounts across the bank
options.B: Share of manager recertifications completed late
options.C: Access requests the help desk closed within target
options.D: Insider fraud cases reported in the past year

questions.key_concept: A key control indicator signals that a specific control is weakening, such as reviews completed late.
questions.pre_read: Decide what each measure tracks: exposure, a control, a process or losses.
questions.correct_explanation: A key control indicator shows when a control is weakening. Late recertifications mean access is not being reviewed on time, a direct sign of this control's health that its owner can act on. Help desk closure time is the closest alternative: it is a performance measure of a related process, showing speed of service, not whether access reviews are being done.

wrong_explanations.A: The number of privileged accounts describes exposure, which suits a KRI. It does not show whether the recertification is working.
wrong_explanations.C: Closure within target is a KPI for service speed. Fast provisioning says nothing about whether access is reviewed.
wrong_explanations.D: Fraud cases are a lagging measure of losses. They appear long after a control failure and cannot show which control failed.

tips: Eliminate: A measures exposure, which is a KRI's job, and D counts losses after the fact.
Final two: B beats C because a KCI tracks this control's health; help desk closure time is a KPI for a different process goal.
Exam cue: KRI for exposure, KCI for a control's health, KPI for process performance; match the metric to the question.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (key control indicator); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: Round 2, 31 Oct 2026: authored from notes 3C3.1 (KRIs, KCIs and KPIs: a KCI is tied to a control and shows failure or weakness, such as overdue reviews; KRIs track exposure and KPIs process goals); original KCI for a bank's quarterly user access recertification scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 round 2 (crisc_d3_021 to 050).

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Reset speed offered as risk evidence
questions.question: A university's IT director tells the risk committee that account-takeover risk is low because 98% of password resets are completed within ten minutes. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Propose a KRI tracking a driver of account takeover
options.B: Ask the service desk to raise its reset target to 99%
options.C: Refer the 98% figure to internal audit to verify
options.D: Record the reset measure as the takeover risk's KRI

questions.key_concept: A KPI measures process performance; risk exposure needs a KRI tied to a driver of the risk scenario.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the 98% figure actually measures.
questions.correct_explanation: Reset speed is a KPI: it measures service performance and says little about takeover exposure, which depends on drivers such as accounts without multifactor sign-in or exposed credentials. The practitioner proposes a KRI tied to such a driver, with thresholds from tolerance. Referring the figure to internal audit is the closest alternative: validation matters, but an accurate measure of the wrong thing still misleads the committee.

wrong_explanations.B: A higher target improves service speed but does not reduce or measure the chance that accounts are taken over.
wrong_explanations.C: Validating data is good practice, but here the problem is the type of measure, not its accuracy.
wrong_explanations.D: Recording a performance measure as a KRI builds the same mistake into the register and future reports.

tips: Eliminate: B improves a performance target that does not measure the risk, and D builds the mix-up into the register.
Final two: A beats C because the measure is the wrong type; checking its accuracy cannot make a KPI warn about takeover risk.
Exam cue: a good KPI does not show a risk is controlled; ask what a measure tracks before accepting it as evidence.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 5.1 (Key CSRM Mechanisms: risk tolerance is translated into security controls, KPIs and KRIs); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: Round 2, 31 Oct 2026: authored from notes 3C3.1 (KRIs, KCIs and KPIs: match the metric to the question; trap, a strong KPI result shows the risk is under control); original university IT director citing password-reset speed as proof of low account-takeover risk scenario written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Human review of AI drafts
questions.question: A hospital requires a doctor to review each discharge summary its AI tool drafts before it goes to the patient. Which of the following BEST indicates that this review control is weakening?

options.A: Summaries the AI tool drafts each working day
options.B: The model's accuracy at its last validation
options.C: Share of drafts approved in under ten seconds
options.D: Patient complaints about discharge summaries

questions.key_concept: A KCI for human review of AI output should show reviewers rubber-stamping, such as very fast approvals, before harm reaches the people affected.
questions.pre_read: Ask how you would know a reviewer had stopped really reviewing.
questions.correct_explanation: A human review reduces risk only if reviewers actually read the drafts. A rising share approved in seconds is an early sign of rubber-stamping, a known risk when people come to trust automated output, so it works as a KCI for the review. Complaints are the closest alternative: they matter, but they arrive after wrong summaries have reached patients, so they warn late.

wrong_explanations.A: Volume shows workload, which may explain rushed reviews, but it does not show whether reviews are being done properly.
wrong_explanations.B: A past validation result describes the model at that time, not the human control now, and it cannot change between validations.
wrong_explanations.D: Complaints are lagging: they appear after wrong summaries reach patients, and many affected patients never complain.

tips: Eliminate: A measures workload rather than review quality, and B describes the model at a past point, not the human control.
Final two: C beats D because fast approvals warn before harm spreads; complaints arrive after wrong summaries have reached patients.
Exam cue: for human review of AI output, watch for signs of rubber-stamping, such as approval time or override rates.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Worsening indicator below red
questions.question: Over four months, an insurer's KCI for production changes deployed without an approved ticket rose from 2% to 9%, still below its 10% red threshold. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Wait until the KCI crosses its red threshold
options.B: Ask the control owner to raise the threshold to 15%
options.C: Review the rising trend with the control owner
options.D: Hand the control owner's approvals to the risk team

questions.key_concept: A worsening KCI trend is raised with the control owner before a threshold breach; the risk function challenges but does not run the control.
questions.pre_read: Look at the direction of the indicator, not only its distance from red.
questions.correct_explanation: A steady rise toward the threshold is a warning in its own right. The practitioner takes the trend to the control owner, who is accountable for change approval, to find the cause and fix it before the limit is breached. Waiting for the red threshold is the closest alternative: thresholds trigger escalation, but trend analysis exists so action can start before a breach.

wrong_explanations.A: Thresholds trigger escalation, but by the time this KCI turns red, more unapproved changes will have reached production.
wrong_explanations.B: Raising the threshold to fit current performance hides the decline and breaks the link between the threshold and tolerance.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk team oversees and challenges controls; taking over the owner's approvals would make it judge its own work and leave the owner's process unfixed.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the limit to fit the decline, and D has the second line run a first-line control.
Final two: C beats A because a worsening trend justifies action before the threshold; the control owner fixes the cause while there is still margin.
Exam cue: read indicators as trends; a steady move toward a threshold goes to the owner before it is breached.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 5.2 (Monitoring Risks: KRIs are observed for trends such as rising likelihood or failing controls); ISACA Glossary (key control indicator)

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. One monitoring cycle for everything
questions.question: A retailer's risk team checks firewall rule changes, critical vulnerability scans and staff background-check records on the same quarterly cycle. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep one quarterly cycle for the three checks
options.B: Align each check with the internal audit cycle
options.C: Move the three checks to daily automated runs
options.D: Set each frequency by risk and rate of change

questions.key_concept: Monitoring frequency is set per item by its risk and rate of change, not one cycle for everything.
questions.pre_read: Ask how fast each of the three items changes.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring frequency should match how fast each item changes and how much risk it carries: firewall rules and critical vulnerabilities change daily, while background-check records change rarely. Setting each frequency on that basis spends effort where exposure moves. Daily automated runs are the closest alternative: automation helps for fast-changing items, but daily checks of static records add cost without reducing risk.

wrong_explanations.A: A single cycle is simple, but it watches fast-changing firewall rules too rarely and static background checks more than needed.
wrong_explanations.B: The audit cycle is an independent assurance schedule. Monitoring that waits for it leaves fast-changing risks unwatched for months.
wrong_explanations.C: Daily automation suits volatile items like firewall rules, but running it on background-check records adds cost without reducing risk.

tips: Eliminate: A applies one rhythm to items that change at very different speeds, and B ties monitoring to the audit calendar.
Final two: D beats C because frequency follows risk and volatility; daily checks of static records add cost but no protection.
Exam cue: continuous monitoring does not mean constant; set each frequency by risk and how fast the item changes.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.2.2 (Establish Monitoring and Assessment Frequencies: control volatility, impact level, known weaknesses, risk tolerance and threat information); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring)

CRISC D3 round 2 (crisc_d3_021 to 050).

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Same cell for three quarters
questions.question: A city council's heat map has shown a supplier-outage risk in the same amber cell for three quarters while its KRI worsened monthly. Which improvement should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Trend arrows fed by each risk's indicators
options.B: More cells to give the heat map finer detail
options.C: An average score for the risks in each cell
options.D: A view limited to the risks in red cells

questions.key_concept: Heat maps show position, not trend; reports add KRI-based trend arrows so a worsening risk is not read as stable.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the heat map shows with what the KRI shows.
questions.correct_explanation: A heat map shows where a risk sits, not where it is heading, so a risk can look stable while its drivers worsen. Trend arrows fed by the KRIs let the council's leaders see direction and act before the risk changes cell. Finer cells are the closest alternative: they show position more precisely, but they still hide direction, which is what was missed here.

wrong_explanations.B: Finer cells sharpen position but still give a snapshot; the worsening trend would stay invisible.
wrong_explanations.C: Heat-map scores are ordinal, so averaging them is not meaningful, and it would blur this risk further.
wrong_explanations.D: Showing only red risks would remove this amber risk from view just as it is worsening.

tips: Eliminate: C does arithmetic on ordinal scores, and D removes the worsening risk from view.
Final two: A beats B because the reader needs direction, not finer position; KRI-fed trend arrows show the movement the cell hides.
Exam cue: a heat map is a snapshot; pair it with trend so a stable position is not read as a stable risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.2.5 (Visualizing Risk Priority: heat maps are a quick-reference guide with limited ability to convey risk information); NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 5.2 (Monitoring Risks: KRIs are observed for trends such as rising likelihood or failing controls)

CRISC D3 round 2 (crisc_d3_021 to 050). questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Audience for a patching report
questions.question: A risk analyst's monthly report on unpatched checkout terminals at a supermarket chain goes to IT operations, but funding the fix needs the retail director's approval. What is the analyst's BEST change to the reporting?

options.A: Send the raw scan results to the retail director
options.B: Copy internal audit on each monthly patching report
options.C: Move the IT operations report to a weekly cycle
options.D: Send it to the retail director with the decision needed

questions.key_concept: Risk reports go to someone with authority to decide on what they show, stating the decision requested.
questions.pre_read: Ask who can approve what the report is asking for.
questions.correct_explanation: A report helps only if it reaches someone who can act on it. Funding the fix is the retail director's decision, so the report should go to the director, in business terms, stating the decision requested. Sending the raw scan results to the director is the closest alternative: it reaches the right person, but raw technical detail without the business impact and the decision requested leaves the director unable to act.

wrong_explanations.A: Raw scan results reach the right person in IT's terms, with no decision stated, so the director cannot see what is being asked or why it matters to the stores.
wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit gives independent assurance; copying it does not get the funding decision made by the person who owns it.
wrong_explanations.C: More frequent reports to the same team repeat the problem faster; the team still cannot approve the funding.

tips: Eliminate: B sends the report to assurance rather than to a decision maker, and C repeats it more often to a team that cannot fund the fix.
Final two: D beats A because the director needs the business impact and the decision requested; raw scan results reach the right person in the wrong terms.
Exam cue: report to the level that can decide, in its terms, with the decision requested.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Rating a distant threat
questions.question: A risk analyst at an energy retailer reads research suggesting quantum computers could one day break the encryption on billing data kept confidential for 15 years. Which rating approach is MOST appropriate for the register?

options.A: A critical rating until the threat is ruled out
options.B: A range of ratings with stated confidence
options.C: A low rating until a working attack is shown
options.D: The rating another firm gave the same threat

questions.key_concept: Emerging risk is rated with ranges and a stated confidence level, then refined as evidence grows, neither ignored nor overstated.
questions.pre_read: Ask how certain anyone can be about this threat today.
questions.correct_explanation: An emerging risk is real enough to record but too uncertain for a single confident score. A range, with the confidence level and assumptions stated and a short review date, tells leaders what is known and lets the rating firm up as evidence grows. A low rating until an attack is shown is the closest alternative: it looks cautious about evidence, but data that must stay confidential for 15 years may be exposed by then.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating it critical without evidence overstates the risk and can pull resources from better-understood risks; emerging risk is reported as uncertain, not certain.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for a working attack treats uncertainty as no risk, yet data encrypted now could be copied today and read later.
wrong_explanations.D: Another firm's rating reflects its own data and exposure, and borrows its assumptions without stating them.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an uncertain risk as certain, and D borrows a rating built on another firm's exposure.
Final two: B beats C because emerging risk is recorded early with its uncertainty stated; waiting for proof leaves long-lived data exposed meanwhile.
Exam cue: rate emerging risk with ranges and stated confidence, neither ignored nor inflated, and refine it as evidence grows.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: uncertainty can be communicated by giving ranges of values rather than single values); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk: compliance, response effectiveness and risk-impacting changes)

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. New AI capability found by scanning
questions.question: Horizon scanning at a parcel carrier finds AI route-planning tools could cut fuel costs 8% but would need customer delivery data shared with vendors. How should the risk practitioner BEST present this to senior management?

options.A: As a threat to block until AI rules are final
options.B: As a tooling choice for the CIO's cost objectives
options.C: As an opportunity with risks weighed against objectives
options.D: As a data-sharing risk for procurement to manage

questions.key_concept: Horizon scanning reports opportunities as well as threats, so leaders weigh a new technology's benefit against its risks.
questions.pre_read: Notice both what the tool offers and what it requires.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk management covers upside as well as downside: the tool supports a business objective, lower cost, while creating data-sharing and vendor risks. Presenting it as an opportunity with its risks lets senior management weigh benefit against exposure and assign an owner. A data-sharing risk for procurement is the closest alternative: the risk is real, but a threat-only framing hides the benefit the decision is about.

wrong_explanations.A: Blocking until rules are final gives up a real benefit on the strength of uncertainty, without weighing the risks against it.
wrong_explanations.B: The CIO can advise on tooling, but the decision affects business objectives and customer data, so it belongs to senior management.
wrong_explanations.D: The data-sharing risk is real, but presenting only the threat leaves out the benefit that management needs to weigh.

tips: Eliminate: A blocks a benefit without weighing it, and B narrows a business decision to an IT tooling choice.
Final two: C beats D because senior management needs the benefit and the risks together; a threat-only view leaves out what is being weighed.
Exam cue: horizon scanning finds opportunities too; present new technology as benefit and risk against objectives, with an owner.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Acceptance after a failed review
questions.question: A retailer's network manager, who owns the firewall rule review, marks the card-data exposure risk acceptable after a failed review; the e-commerce director owns that risk. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Ask internal audit to confirm the acceptance is valid
options.B: Have the network manager add a rationale and expiry date
options.C: Record the acceptance and copy it to the e-commerce director
options.D: Refer the risk decision to the e-commerce director

questions.key_concept: The control owner answers for a control working; only the risk owner, with the right authority, accepts the risk a failing control leaves.
questions.pre_read: Sort the two named people by what each one owns before judging who can make this call.
questions.correct_explanation: The network manager owns a control, so they answer for fixing the failed review, but deciding whether the exposure is acceptable belongs to the e-commerce director as risk owner. The practitioner refers the decision, with the failed review result, to that director. Adding a rationale and expiry date makes the record look formal while leaving the decision with someone who has no authority to make it.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit gives independent assurance; it does not approve risk acceptance, and this acceptance came from the wrong person in the first place.
wrong_explanations.B: A rationale and an expiry date improve the record, but the acceptance would still come from a control owner without authority over the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Recording the acceptance first still lets a control owner make a decision only the risk owner can make; copying the director in afterward is not the director deciding.

tips: Eliminate: A gives a risk decision to internal audit, whose role is assurance, and C records an invalid acceptance, telling the risk owner only after the fact.
Final two: D beats B because a better-documented acceptance is still made by the wrong person; the e-commerce director owns the risk and decides.
Exam cue: a control owner fixes the control; when an option lets them accept the risk it protects, look for the option that returns the decision to the risk owner.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Owner moved after a reorganization
questions.question: After a reorganization, an online furniture retailer's register still names a director who moved to procurement as owner of the customer-portal outage risk. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Revisit the owner at the next annual register review
options.B: Ask senior management to assign the risk to a new owner
options.C: Name the portal's IT manager as the risk's new owner
options.D: Ask the director to choose a successor to take the risk

questions.key_concept: Senior management assigns risk owners, and ownership is revalidated when people or structures change, not left for the annual review.
questions.pre_read: Note what changed for the named director, then ask what a risk owner needs to hold the role.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk owner needs accountability and authority over the affected objective; a director now in procurement has neither for the customer portal. Senior management assigns risk owners, so the practitioner asks it to assign the risk to the manager now accountable for the portal's business outcome. Letting the departing director pick a successor feels like a tidy handover, but it hands an assignment decision to someone who no longer owns the area.

wrong_explanations.A: Ownership is revalidated after reorganizations; leaving a former owner in place for months means nobody with authority decides on the risk meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.C: IT runs the portal's technology, but the outage risk belongs to the business accountable for the portal, and naming an owner without senior management's confirmation gives the assignment no authority.
wrong_explanations.D: A handover sounds orderly, but assigning risk ownership is senior management's call, and the departing director no longer owns the affected area.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for the annual review when ownership should be revalidated after a reorganization, and C gives a business risk to IT, which runs the technology but not the business outcome.
Final two: B beats D because senior management assigns risk owners; a departing owner choosing a successor bypasses the authority that makes the assignment valid.
Exam cue: when people or structures change, revalidate ownership promptly through the level that assigns owners, not through the person leaving.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Control owner retiring
questions.question: The manager who owns a water utility's monthly review of privileged accounts retires next month, and senior management has named a successor. What should the risk practitioner consider MOST important for the handover?

options.A: The risk team covering the review in the gap between owners
options.B: A key control indicator for missed reviews after the change
options.C: A formal handover of the procedure and recent review records
options.D: An exception pausing the review while the successor trains

questions.key_concept: Control ownership moves by formal handover of the procedure and records, so the control keeps running and can still be shown to work.
questions.pre_read: Think about what the successor needs to run the control from day one and show that it ran.
questions.correct_explanation: A control owner answers for the control working and for its evidence. When the owner leaves, ownership transfers formally, with the documented procedure and recent records, so the successor can run the review without a gap and show it ran. An indicator for missed reviews is useful monitoring, but it would only show a gap after one occurred; the handover prevents the gap.

wrong_explanations.A: The second-line risk team oversees and challenges controls; running a first-line review, even for a while, leaves it checking its own work.
wrong_explanations.B: An indicator would show a missed review after it happened; it does not give the successor what they need to run and evidence the review from the first month.
wrong_explanations.D: An exception is for a requirement that cannot be met; a planned handover is no reason to pause a key control over privileged accounts.

tips: Eliminate: A has the second line run a first-line control, and D pauses a key control by exception when nothing stops it from running.
Final two: C beats B because the handover lets the successor run and evidence the review from day one; an indicator only reports a missed review afterward.
Exam cue: when control ownership changes, look for the transfer of procedure and records, not a pause, cover by the risk team, or an after-the-fact alert.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (control owner); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A2.2 (Control Owners and Validating Ownership: when a control owner changes jobs, ownership transfers formally, with a handover of procedures and evidence; validate by evidence, not by the register alone). questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Contract terms before signing
questions.question: Due diligence rated a CRM vendor acceptable for a distributor's customer data, but its standard contract sets no breach-notice time and no audit or assurance rights. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Buy cyber insurance covering breaches at the vendor
options.B: Sign, then request the vendor's assurance report each year
options.C: Have breach-reporting and assurance terms added before signing
options.D: Accept the vendor's standard contract terms as they stand

questions.key_concept: Put breach-reporting and assurance terms in the contract before signing, while leverage is highest; accountability for the data stays with the enterprise.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what each option gives the distributor once the contract is signed and something goes wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Outsourcing moves the work, not accountability for customer data. Without a breach-reporting time the distributor may learn of a breach too late to act or meet its own duties, and without assurance rights it cannot keep checking the vendor. Asking for these terms before signing works because leverage is highest then. A yearly request after signing depends on the vendor's goodwill, since nothing obliges it to provide a report.

wrong_explanations.A: Insurance may repay some breach costs, but it neither tells the distributor about a breach in time nor gives any right to check the vendor.
wrong_explanations.B: Once the contract is signed, the vendor has no duty to provide reports, and the missing breach-reporting time is still missing.
wrong_explanations.D: Passing due diligence shows the vendor is acceptable today; it does not create the notice and assurance rights needed for later monitoring.

tips: Eliminate: A treats insurance as a substitute for contract rights, and D accepts terms that leave no way to hear of breaches or check the vendor later.
Final two: C beats B because terms agreed before signing bind the vendor; a yearly request after signing relies on goodwill and still lacks breach reporting.
Exam cue: what you need from a vendor goes into the contract before signing; after signing, leverage drops while accountability for the data stays with you.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-05 (requirements to address cybersecurity risks in supply chains are established, prioritized and integrated into contracts and other types of agreements with suppliers and other relevant third parties); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 SA-9 (External System Services)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A3.1 (Vendor Due Diligence and Contracts: write security controls, breach notice times, right to audit and assurance into the contract before signing; accountability for the outcome stays with the organization). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a distributor's CRM vendor that passed due diligence but whose standard contract sets no breach-notice time and no audit or assurance rights, written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 round 3 (crisc_d3_051 to 085).

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Access left after a contract ended
questions.question: A parking operator's risk analyst finds a maintenance contractor kept remote access to the payment system five months after its contract ended; IT has since disabled it. What should the analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Start a monthly review of vendor remote-access accounts
options.B: Make access removal a required step in closing a contract
options.C: Ask vendors to confirm unused accounts at contract end
options.D: Cover vendor access duties in contract managers' training

questions.key_concept: Vendor offboarding removes access as a set step when a contract ends, so the cause of leftover access is fixed rather than found later.
questions.pre_read: Ask where in the vendor life cycle this access should have ended, and which option acts at that point.
questions.correct_explanation: The access outlived the contract because nothing in contract closure removed it. Making access removal a required offboarding step fixes that cause at the point the relationship ends. Reviewing vendor accounts monthly would find leftovers sooner, which helps, but it is detective: an account would still stay open for weeks after a contract ended, and finding it depends on the review being done well.

wrong_explanations.A: A monthly review would shorten the window, but it detects leftover access after the fact rather than removing it when the contract ends.
wrong_explanations.C: The vendor's confirmation is its own word, and an account it no longer uses can still be misused by someone else.
wrong_explanations.D: Training helps people remember duties, but without a required step in contract closure, removal still depends on memory.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on the vendor's own word about its accounts, and D leaves removal to memory with no required step at contract end.
Final two: B beats A because a required offboarding step removes access when the contract ends, while a monthly review only finds it later.
Exam cue: for a recurring gap, prefer the control at the point the event happens over a review that catches it afterward.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-10 (cybersecurity supply chain risk management plans include provisions for activities that occur after the conclusion of a partnership or service agreement)

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. AI service outage
questions.question: A vendor's AI service failed for two days, halting a lender's mortgage approvals, and no trained staff remain to check documents by hand. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Higher service credits for each day the service is down
options.B: Weekly sampling of the documents the service has read
options.C: A stricter availability commitment in the vendor contract
options.D: A tested manual process for reading documents in outages

questions.key_concept: A contract can price an AI vendor's failure but cannot keep the business running; a high-risk AI service needs a tested fallback the enterprise controls.
questions.pre_read: Picture the next two-day failure and ask which option would keep approvals moving.
questions.correct_explanation: The failure exposed a dependency with no way around it: when the AI service stops, approvals stop. A tested manual or alternative process lets the lender keep approving loans during an outage, and only the lender can provide it. A stricter availability commitment may reduce how often the vendor fails and adds remedies, but when it does fail, approvals still halt and customers still hold the lender accountable.

wrong_explanations.A: Service credits refund part of the fees after an outage; they do nothing to keep mortgage approvals moving while the service is down.
wrong_explanations.B: Sampling checks the accuracy of what the service reads, a different risk from the outage that halted approvals.
wrong_explanations.C: A stronger commitment adds remedies and may improve uptime, but approvals still stop the next time the service fails.

tips: Eliminate: A refunds fees without keeping the business running, and B checks output accuracy when the risk shown is the service being unavailable.
Final two: D beats C because a contract term cannot keep approvals moving when the vendor fails; a tested fallback the lender controls can.
Exam cue: for a high-risk third-party AI service, look for a contingency the business controls; contracts move cost, not accountability or continuity.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) GOVERN 6.2 (contingency processes are in place to handle failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems deemed to be high-risk); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 3.1 (AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored and risk controls are applied and documented)

CRISC D3 round 3 (crisc_d3_051 to 085).

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Finding nobody will take
questions.question: A finding on shared service accounts at a ticketing firm has had no action owner for five months; IT and HR each say the other should fix it. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Escalate the dispute to the owner of the affected risk
options.B: Assign the finding jointly to the IT and HR managers
options.C: Close the finding and reopen it once an owner is agreed
options.D: Assign the finding to the accounts' system owner in IT

questions.key_concept: Each finding needs one action owner; when teams dispute it, the practitioner escalates to the owner of the affected risk, who names the action owner.
questions.pre_read: Before choosing who fixes it, ask who has the authority to decide who fixes it.
questions.correct_explanation: The finding has stalled because no one with authority has assigned it. The owner of the risk the finding affects is accountable for its treatment, so the practitioner escalates the dispute to that owner, who names one action owner and a date. Assigning it jointly to IT and HR looks like a fair compromise, but shared ownership is how this finding went five months without anyone acting.

wrong_explanations.B: Joint ownership spreads accountability so thin that each team can wait for the other, the same pattern that left the finding untouched.
wrong_explanations.C: Closing an unresolved finding hides a live weakness; findings close on validated fixes, not on disputes about who owns them.
wrong_explanations.D: IT may well do the work, but HR disputes the split, and the practitioner alone has no authority to settle a dispute between departments; the risk owner decides.

tips: Eliminate: C closes a finding that is not fixed, and D has the practitioner settle a dispute between departments without the authority of the owner accountable for the risk.
Final two: A beats B because one accountable owner gets things done; joint ownership is the very gap that let IT and HR each wait for the other.
Exam cue: a stalled finding with no clear owner goes to the owner of the affected risk; the practitioner escalates it to that authority rather than picking a team.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-5 (Plan of Action and Milestones)

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Exemption after a change
questions.question: A parcel firm exempted its handheld scanners from the mobile device standard as they held no personal data; an update now stores recipients' addresses on them. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Wait for the exemption's next scheduled assessment
options.B: Apply the mobile device standard's encryption to the scanners
options.C: Convert the exemption into an exception with an expiry date
options.D: Assess whether the exemption still applies to the scanners

questions.key_concept: An exemption rests on facts about its scope; when those facts change, the practitioner reassesses whether it still applies before anyone changes the response.
questions.pre_read: Note what the exemption was granted for and what the update changed.
questions.correct_explanation: The exemption was granted because the scanners held no personal data, and the update removes that basis. The practitioner first assesses whether the exemption still applies and what risk the scanners now carry, then takes the result to the risk owner. Converting it into a time-limited exception assumes the outcome: the owner might instead apply the standard now, or the assessment might show another control fits better.

wrong_explanations.A: Exemptions are reviewed when their basis changes, not only on schedule; waiting leaves personal data on unprotected devices meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.B: Encryption may be the right fix, but applying it before assessing the change and consulting the owner skips both the analysis and the owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: An exception assumes the scanners must comply later; that is a decision for the risk owner once the changed risk is assessed.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for a scheduled review although the exemption's basis has changed, and B applies a fix before the change is analyzed or the owner consulted.
Final two: D beats C because converting to an exception already decides the outcome; first establish whether the exemption still holds and what risk remains.
Exam cue: when a fact a decision rested on changes, reassess that decision first; words like 'now stores' reopen it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A4.2 (Exceptions and Exemptions: exemptions are reviewed to confirm they still apply; every deviation is risk-assessed and approved by the risk owner). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a parcel firm's handheld scanners, exempted from the mobile device standard because they held no personal data, now storing recipients' addresses after an update, written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 round 3 (crisc_d3_051 to 085). Review fixes 4 Nov 2026 (standards audit and concept review): pre_read no longer leans on the key.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Tool proposed to replace a policy
questions.question: An engineering consultancy's IT director proposes retiring the data handling policy and staff training because the new data-loss prevention tool now blocks unsafe file sharing. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Retire the policy and record the tool as the control
options.B: Replace the training with pop-up warnings from the tool
options.C: Test the tool's blocking before retiring the policy
options.D: Keep the policy and training alongside the tool

questions.key_concept: Technical controls depend on administrative ones: the policy sets what is sensitive and who is accountable, and training covers what the tool cannot see.
questions.pre_read: Ask what tells the tool which files to block, and who answers when it gets one wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Control categories work together. The policy defines what data is sensitive, how it may be shared and who is accountable; the tool's rules are written from it, and training covers handling the tool cannot see, such as printed or spoken data. Testing the tool's blocking first sounds prudent, but even a tool that works perfectly needs the policy and training behind it, so a good test result would not justify retiring them.

wrong_explanations.A: A technical control is not stronger by default; without the policy, the tool's rules have no agreed basis and no one owns the choices they encode.
wrong_explanations.B: Pop-up warnings reach people only at the moment of sharing; they do not teach the handling rules that apply where the tool cannot see.
wrong_explanations.C: Testing confirms the tool blocks what it is set to block, but a passing test does not remove the need for the policy that sets the rules.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a technical control as stronger by default, and B replaces training with warnings that only appear where the tool can see.
Final two: D beats C because the policy is what the tool's rules are built on and training covers what the tool cannot see; even a good test result would not justify retiring them.
Exam cue: a gap in one control category is not filled by strength in another; prefer the option that keeps the control the others depend on.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.PO-01 (policy for managing cybersecurity risks is established based on organizational context, cybersecurity strategy and priorities and is communicated and enforced); ISACA Glossary (policy)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B1.2 (Control Categories by Nature: administrative controls direct behavior and set accountability, and most technical controls depend on them; a gap in one category is not filled by strength in another). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of an engineering consultancy's IT director proposing to retire the data handling policy and staff training because a new data-loss prevention tool blocks unsafe file sharing, written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 round 3 (crisc_d3_051 to 085). questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. One baseline for every system
questions.question: A payments company adopting NIST SP 800-53 plans to apply the SP 800-53B high baseline unchanged to every system, including the staff canteen ordering app. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Select each system's baseline by impact and tailor it
options.B: Apply the high baseline now and remove controls later
options.C: Apply the low baseline company-wide, critical or not
options.D: Adopt CSF 2.0 outcomes instead of a control catalog

questions.key_concept: Each system gets the baseline for its impact level, then tailoring fits it to the system's risk, with each decision and its reason recorded.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the canteen app and the payment systems carry the same risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Each system gets the baseline for its impact level, which is then tailored to its risks: scoping out what does not apply, setting parameters and adding controls where needed, with each decision recorded. That gives the payment systems strong controls without spending the same on a canteen app. Applying the high baseline now and trimming later pays for controls before analyzing them, and removals made afterward tend to lack a recorded risk basis.

wrong_explanations.B: Implementing first and trimming later spends money on controls nobody analyzed, and later removals are hard to justify without a risk-based record.
wrong_explanations.C: The low baseline is cheap but leaves the critical payment systems under-protected; one level for all systems ignores their different risks.
wrong_explanations.D: CSF 2.0 describes outcomes and still needs controls to achieve them; switching frameworks does not answer how much control each system needs.

tips: Eliminate: C sets one low level for systems with very different risks, and D swaps frameworks without deciding how much control each system needs.
Final two: A beats B because tailoring decides by risk before spending; implementing everything and trimming later puts action before analysis.
Exam cue: frameworks are catalogs to choose from; look for tailoring to the organization's risks, with the reasons recorded.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53B Section 2.2 (Selecting Control Baselines: each system's baseline is selected from its impact level, low, moderate or high); NIST SP 800-53B Section 2.4 (Tailoring Control Baselines: align the baseline with organizational risk and record a risk-based justification for each decision)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B1.3 (Control Frameworks and Tailoring: use frameworks as catalogs, not checklists; tailor by scoping out, setting parameters and adding controls, and record why). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a payments company planning to apply the high control baseline unchanged to every system, including a staff canteen ordering app, written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Baseline met, risk still high
questions.question: A ride-hailing firm meets every control in the framework baseline it adopted, yet its driver-payout fraud scenario remains above appetite. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Controls aimed at the payout scenario beyond the baseline
options.B: A stricter framework baseline adopted across the firm
options.C: A lower rating for the scenario to reflect compliance
options.D: Acceptance of the risk by the payout team's manager

questions.key_concept: Meeting a baseline is not the same as having risk within appetite; tailoring adds controls for the risks the baseline does not cover.
questions.pre_read: Separate two questions in the stem: is the firm compliant, and is the risk within appetite?
questions.correct_explanation: A framework baseline addresses common threats, not this firm's specific fraud scenario. With the scenario still above appetite, the response is to supplement the baseline with controls aimed at how payout fraud happens here, chosen with the risk owner. A stricter baseline across the firm adds generic controls to every system at a high cost and may still miss the payout scenario that is above appetite.

wrong_explanations.B: A tougher baseline raises cost across every system while still offering generic controls that may miss how payout fraud works.
wrong_explanations.C: Compliance does not change likelihood or impact; lowering the rating to match a checklist hides a risk that is still above appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: Risk above appetite is treated, or temporarily accepted by the level that set appetite; a team manager cannot accept it.

tips: Eliminate: C lowers a rating for compliance rather than reduced risk, and D lets a team manager accept risk that is above appetite.
Final two: A beats B because the scenario needs targeted controls; a stricter generic baseline costs more everywhere and may still miss it.
Exam cue: compliance with a framework is not risk within appetite; when the two disagree, treat the specific scenario.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53B Section 2.4 (Tailoring Control Baselines: align the baseline with organizational risk and record a risk-based justification for each decision); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 RA-7 (Risk Response)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B1.3 (Control Frameworks and Tailoring: tailor by adding controls for risks the baseline misses; frameworks are catalogs, not proof that risk is within appetite). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a ride-hailing firm that meets every control in its adopted framework baseline while its driver-payout fraud scenario stays above appetite, written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 round 3 (crisc_d3_051 to 085).

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. How much human review
questions.question: Which of the following should BEST determine how much human review a risk practitioner recommends for the outputs of an insurer's AI tools?

options.A: The accuracy rate the vendor reported in testing
options.B: The number of staff free to review the outputs
options.C: The impact of a wrong output in each use
options.D: The size of the model and its training data

questions.key_concept: Human review of AI outputs is scaled to the impact of a wrong output, so high-impact uses get close review and low-impact ones lighter checks.
questions.pre_read: Picture one wrong output in a high-stakes use and one in a trivial use, and ask what should differ.
questions.correct_explanation: Controls are proportionate to risk, and for AI outputs the deciding factor is what a wrong output would do. A wrong answer about a customer's claim needs review before it is sent; a wrong internal summary may need only spot checks. The vendor's reported accuracy matters, but it was measured in the vendor's tests, and even a small error rate can be unacceptable where the impact is high.

wrong_explanations.A: Test accuracy describes the vendor's conditions, not the harm an error would cause here; a low error rate can still be too high for a high-impact use.
wrong_explanations.B: Staff availability shows what is easy to do, not what the risk requires; a gap between the two is a resourcing decision for the owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Model size and training data volume say little about the harm a wrong output would cause in a given use.

tips: Eliminate: B lets staffing set the control level instead of risk, and D looks at model size, which says little about the harm an error causes.
Final two: C beats A because review is set by the impact of an error; a vendor's test accuracy describes its tests, not the harm in your use.
Exam cue: for AI controls, scale input checks, output checks and human review to the impact of a wrong output.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. New approval stalls the work
questions.question: A week after a tram operator's new rule requiring two managers to approve every timetable change went live, trams ran on outdated timetables while approvals waited days. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Suspend the rule while the control owner clears the backlog
options.B: Add more managers to the pool that can approve changes
options.C: Record the delays as an accepted cost of the control
options.D: Rework the approval with its owner to fit change risk

questions.key_concept: A control must fit the process it protects; when it blocks the work, its owner and the practitioner rework it by risk, not drop it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether every timetable change carries the same risk, and what the business needs from the control.
questions.correct_explanation: The control now harms the objective it protects: trams run on wrong timetables. The practitioner works with the control owner to fit the design to risk, such as two approvers for major changes and one for minor edits, so service runs on time and risky changes still get scrutiny. Adding approvers eases the queue, but keeps the same heavy check on every change and adds cost without asking which changes need it.

wrong_explanations.A: Suspending the rule removes protection for every change, including risky ones, and the backlog is a design problem rather than the owner's queue to clear.
wrong_explanations.B: More approvers may speed the queue, but every change still needs two approvals, adding cost where low-risk edits need lighter checks.
wrong_explanations.C: Treating service disruption as a cost of control accepts harm to the business objective without asking whether a better design exists.

tips: Eliminate: A removes the control for risky changes too, and C accepts harm to service as if no better design existed.
Final two: D beats B because the check should match each change's risk; more approvers keep an oversized control on every change.
Exam cue: when a control blocks the business it protects, look for redesign with the control owner, scaled to risk, not removal or more of the same.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Recertification gap finding
questions.question: A risk analyst's gap analysis at a broadcaster finds the quarterly access recertification is well designed but was skipped in two of the last four quarters. What should the analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Ask the control owner to redesign the recertification workflow
options.B: Have the control owner address why reviews were skipped
options.C: Replace the recertification with a stronger automated tool
options.D: Send managers a reminder before each quarterly review

questions.key_concept: A design gap needs a new design; an operating gap needs the control performed, so its owner fixes why it was not done.
questions.pre_read: Decide first whether this is a design gap or an operating gap.
questions.correct_explanation: The design is sound, so this is an operating gap: the control exists but was not performed. The fix is for the control owner to find and address why the reviews were skipped, such as workload, an unclear duty or no follow-up. A reminder before each review is a reasonable step, but it assumes the cause is forgetting; if reviewers lack time or authority, reminders change nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Redesigning a control that is already well designed treats an operating gap as a design gap and leaves the reason for skipping untouched.
wrong_explanations.C: A stronger tool costs more and still fails if the reviews are skipped; the gap is in performing the control, not in its strength.
wrong_explanations.D: Reminders fix forgetfulness only; without knowing why the reviews were skipped, they may not address the actual cause.

tips: Eliminate: A redesigns a control whose design is already sound, and C buys a stronger tool when the problem is that the control was not performed.
Final two: B beats D because the cause is unknown; a reminder treats one possible cause, while finding why reviews were skipped fixes the real one.
Exam cue: tell design gaps from operating gaps; an operating gap is fixed at its cause by the control owner, not by a new design.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Testing 30 controls in two weeks
questions.question: A risk analyst has two weeks to test 30 controls at an insurer, from claims-payment approval limits rated critical to a clean-desk check rated low. Which of the following approaches is BEST?

options.A: Stronger tests for high-rated controls, lighter for the rest
options.B: One inquiry-and-inspection test used across the 30 controls
options.C: Reperformance used as the test for the 30 controls
options.D: Testing of the high-risk controls now and the rest next year

questions.key_concept: Testing depth follows risk: critical controls get the strongest techniques and lower-risk ones lighter tests, so assurance is spent where it matters.
questions.pre_read: Read the time limit and the range of control ratings together before judging any approach.
questions.correct_explanation: The assurance a test must give depends on the risk the control addresses. Critical payment limits warrant strong techniques such as reperformance on a larger sample; a low-rated clean-desk check can rest on inquiry and a short inspection. That covers all 30 controls in two weeks. Testing the high-risk ones now and the rest next year leaves the lower-rated controls untested for a cycle when lighter tests would cover them now.

wrong_explanations.B: A single light test gives weak assurance over the critical payment controls, where a failure would matter most.
wrong_explanations.C: Reperforming every control spends the strongest technique on low-risk checks and is unlikely to fit in two weeks.
wrong_explanations.D: Deferring half the controls leaves them untested this cycle, when lighter, risk-based tests could cover them within the time.

tips: Eliminate: B gives the critical controls the same light test as the low ones, and C spends the costliest technique on every check, including the clean-desk one.
Final two: A beats D because tests scaled to risk cover every control now; deferring the lower ones leaves them unchecked for a cycle.
Exam cue: match the testing technique and depth to the risk the control addresses, with the strongest evidence where failure matters most.
