questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. What a walkthrough shows
questions.question: An online bank's change manager walked the risk analyst through one approved change, from request to deployment. Which of the following conclusions does this walkthrough BEST support?

options.A: Change control worked as intended over the year
options.B: The control's design is in place as described
options.C: Change control is mature enough to rely on
options.D: No unapproved change reached production this year

questions.key_concept: A walkthrough shows a control is designed and in place; operation over a period needs a sample from it, and maturity needs evidence over time.
questions.pre_read: Ask what one traced change can show, and what it cannot show about the rest of the year.
questions.correct_explanation: Tracing one change from request to deployment shows how the control is meant to work and that its steps exist, so it supports a conclusion on design and implementation. It cannot show that the control worked for the rest of the year. Concluding it worked as intended over the year is the runner-up: that is what the manager wants, but it needs a sample the analyst draws from the year's changes.

wrong_explanations.A: One traced change says nothing about the other changes made this year; operating effectiveness needs a sample from the full period.
wrong_explanations.C: Maturity rests on whether the practice is defined, followed and measured over time; one walkthrough cannot show that.
wrong_explanations.D: A walkthrough follows a change that went through the process; it cannot show whether other changes bypassed it.

tips: Eliminate: C claims maturity from a single example, and D draws a conclusion about changes the walkthrough never looked at.
Final two: B beats A because a walkthrough shows design and implementation; a year of operation needs a sample the tester draws.
Exam cue: walkthrough shows design and implementation; a sample over the period shows operation; evidence over time shows maturity.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Buying a tool to raise maturity
questions.question: An airline's IT director plans to lift incident management from maturity level 2 to the agreed level 4 by buying a ticketing tool with built-in dashboards. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Plan each level's steps, starting with defined procedures
options.B: Buy the tool and use its dashboards as the level 4 measures
options.C: Lower the target to level 3 within this year's budget
options.D: Reassess maturity once the tool has run for a year

questions.key_concept: Maturity rises through defined, consistently followed and then measured practice; a tool can support that path but cannot replace its steps.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a process must have in place before its performance can be measured.
questions.correct_explanation: Maturity levels build on each other: a process is defined and documented, followed consistently, then measured and improved. Planning those steps, starting with defined procedures, closes the gap the target set. Using the tool's dashboards as the measures looks like a shortcut, but dashboards over an undefined, inconsistent process measure noise, and the higher rating would not hold up against evidence.

wrong_explanations.B: Dashboards can support measurement, but measuring an undefined, inconsistent process does not reach a higher level; the earlier steps are still missing.
wrong_explanations.C: Targets are set by risk with the owner; cutting the target to fit a budget changes the decision without addressing the risk it reflected.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting a year to reassess spends the money first and finds out later whether maturity improved, with no plan to close the gap.

tips: Eliminate: C changes a risk-based target to fit a budget, and D spends first and checks a year later without a plan for the gap.
Final two: A beats B because measurement needs a defined, consistent process first; a tool's dashboards cannot supply the earlier steps.
Exam cue: maturity is built step by step and rated on evidence; a purchase alone rarely moves a process up a level.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Status reported as green
questions.question: For eight months, the project lead for a manufacturer's 18-month access-control action plan has reported its status as green. What should the risk practitioner request to BEST confirm progress?

options.A: A signed statement from the lead confirming green status
options.B: Records showing each milestone due so far was met
options.C: A revised plan with an earlier final due date
options.D: The project sponsor's own monthly status rating

questions.key_concept: Progress on an action plan is confirmed by evidence at each milestone, not by a status color.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a green status is based on, and what would show it is true.
questions.correct_explanation: A status color is an opinion; milestones break the plan into checkpoints that can be shown met or missed. Records for each milestone due by now confirm real progress and show slippage early, while ten months remain to recover. The sponsor's monthly rating adds a second opinion, which can feel like independent confirmation, but it is still a color with no evidence behind it.

wrong_explanations.A: A signed statement repeats the lead's claim more formally; it adds accountability but no evidence that the milestones were met.
wrong_explanations.C: Moving the end date earlier changes the plan, not the evidence; it does not show whether the work so far is on track.
wrong_explanations.D: A second opinion from the sponsor is still a status rating, not evidence that the planned milestones were delivered.

tips: Eliminate: A formalizes the same claim without evidence, and C changes the plan's end date when the question is whether the work so far is done.
Final two: B beats D because milestone records show what was delivered; the sponsor's rating is another opinion about the color.
Exam cue: validate action plans with evidence at each milestone; a status color alone is a claim, whoever reports it.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plan complete but short of target
questions.question: All actions in a retailer's risk action plan are complete and tested as working; the re-rated risk is within appetite but above the target risk the plan set. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Close the plan and record the risk as within appetite
options.B: Lower the plan's target risk to match the new rating
options.C: Take the shortfall to the risk owner for a decision
options.D: Ask the action owners to add a further control

questions.key_concept: A plan is judged against its own target; if risk ends above it, even within appetite, the risk owner decides whether to accept the gap.
questions.pre_read: Separate whether the actions were done from whether the plan achieved what it promised.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan delivered its actions, but its purpose was to bring the risk to the target the owner set. Within appetite the gap could be accepted, but that is the risk owner's decision, so the practitioner reports the shortfall with the validated rating. Closing the plan because the risk is within appetite is the runner-up: acceptance may be right, but it is the owner's call, not an automatic close.

wrong_explanations.A: Being within appetite makes acceptance possible, but the plan promised a lower target; closing it without the owner's decision skips the person who set that target.
wrong_explanations.B: Moving the target to fit the result reverses the logic; the target was set with the risk owner within appetite, not from what the plan happened to achieve.
wrong_explanations.D: More control may be the answer, but deciding further treatment belongs to the risk owner; action owners carry out the tasks they are given.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the target to fit the result, and D has action owners choose treatment that is the risk owner's call.
Final two: C beats A because the owner set the target; being within appetite makes acceptance possible, but the owner decides whether to accept the gap.
Exam cue: a plan is judged against its own target; when it falls short, even within appetite, the risk owner decides what happens next.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plan agreed in a meeting
questions.question: A city council's risk owner agreed that IT and facilities will fix the data center's cooling risk by year end. Which of the following should the risk practitioner propose adding as MOST important?

options.A: One named person accountable for each action
options.B: Monthly progress reports from IT and facilities
options.C: A note in the register that the risk is treated
options.D: The risk committee as joint owner of the plan

questions.key_concept: A risk action plan names one accountable person for each action; a commitment shared between teams leaves no one to hold to the date.
questions.pre_read: Ask who exactly would be asked if the year-end date slipped.
questions.correct_explanation: A plan agreed between two departments has a date but nobody accountable for each action, so when work slips, IT and facilities can each point to the other. Naming one person for each action, with the risk owner's agreement, makes the plan trackable. Monthly progress reports help monitoring, but reports from two teams with no accountable person describe slippage without anyone answerable for fixing it.

wrong_explanations.B: Progress reports support tracking, but without one accountable person per action, they record slippage that nobody is answerable for.
wrong_explanations.C: Agreeing a plan does not treat the risk; marking it treated before the work is done misstates current risk.
wrong_explanations.D: A committee can oversee the plan, but it cannot be the single accountable owner; shared ownership is the weakness to fix.

tips: Eliminate: C marks the risk treated before any work is done, and D gives ownership to a committee, which oversees but cannot be accountable.
Final two: A beats B because reports only describe progress; one accountable person per action is what makes the date enforceable.
Exam cue: a valid action plan has an owner, a date and resources for each action; shared or committee ownership is the trap.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Same KRI, two methods
questions.question: At a bank, two units report the KRI for overdue critical patches differently: one counts days from the patch's release, the other from its scheduled install date. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Combine both units' figures into one enterprise total
options.B: Agree one definition of when the KRI's count starts
options.C: Report each unit's figure under its own method
options.D: Adopt whichever method shows fewer overdue patches

questions.key_concept: A KRI needs one documented definition, source and formula, so figures from different units mean the same thing before they are compared or combined.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the two units' numbers measure the same thing.
questions.correct_explanation: The two units measure different things: days since release shows exposure to a known flaw, while days since a scheduled date can hide months of delay. The practitioner first gets one documented definition agreed, ideally the one that reflects exposure, so the figures can be compared and combined. Reporting each figure under its own method is transparent, but it leaves leaders comparing numbers that do not mean the same thing.

wrong_explanations.A: Adding figures built on different definitions produces a total that matches neither unit's reality.
wrong_explanations.C: Showing each method is honest, but it leaves leaders comparing two numbers that measure different things.
wrong_explanations.D: Choosing the method that looks better biases the KRI toward reassurance rather than an accurate view of exposure.

tips: Eliminate: A adds numbers built on different definitions, and D picks the definition that flatters the result.
Final two: B beats C because comparable figures need one definition; reporting both methods is open but still not comparable.
Exam cue: before combining or comparing metrics, check that they share one definition, source and formula.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. KRI copied from spreadsheets
questions.question: Each month, an assistant at a property management company builds the KRI for tenant access badges left active after move-out by copying figures from four regional spreadsheets. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A second person rechecking the copied figures each month
options.B: Regional office leads signing their spreadsheets as accurate
options.C: Reporting the KRI each quarter instead of monthly
options.D: Drawing the KRI from lease and badge system records

questions.key_concept: KRI data should come from system sources where possible, with its lineage recorded, rather than from hand-kept spreadsheets copied into reports.
questions.pre_read: Ask where move-out dates and badge deactivations are first recorded.
questions.correct_explanation: Move-out dates and badge deactivations are already recorded in the lease and badge systems, so the KRI can be drawn from them directly, with the source recorded. That removes the hand-kept spreadsheets and the copying, and makes the figure traceable. A second person rechecking the copied figures catches transcription slips, but it still trusts four spreadsheets kept by hand, which may be incomplete or out of date.

wrong_explanations.A: A recheck catches copying slips, but not errors already in the hand-kept spreadsheets, and it adds effort every month.
wrong_explanations.B: A signature adds accountability, but it is the leads' own statement, not evidence that the spreadsheets are complete and correct.
wrong_explanations.C: Reporting less often reduces effort but delays warning, and the quarterly figure still comes from the same hand-kept data.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the leads' own word about their spreadsheets, and C trades early warning for less effort while keeping the same weak data.
Final two: D beats A because system records remove the hand-kept source; a recheck only confirms the copying, not the data.
Exam cue: prefer system-generated data with recorded lineage over hand-kept spreadsheets; checking a weak source does not make it strong.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. One office rates higher
questions.question: Consolidating a car rental firm's registers, the risk analyst finds three regional offices rate a customer-data breach scenario low and one rates it high, with the same controls. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Average the four ratings to set the firm's rating
options.B: Adopt the majority rating of low for the firm
options.C: Find out why one office rates the scenario differently
options.D: Apply the high rating to the scenario in each office

questions.key_concept: When units rate the same risk differently with the same controls, the practitioner finds out why before choosing a combined rating.
questions.pre_read: Ask what could make the same scenario, with the same controls, rate differently in one place.
questions.correct_explanation: The same scenario with the same controls should rate similarly, so the difference is a signal: the high-rating office may face a local threat or weaker practice the others lack, or it may have misapplied the criteria. Finding out why comes before choosing any combined rating. Applying the high rating in each office is cautious, but it could overstate three offices' risk and still miss a local issue the high office has found.

wrong_explanations.A: Averaging ordinal ratings can hide the one office where the risk is high, and it skips asking why the ratings differ.
wrong_explanations.B: A majority vote ignores evidence that one office may face a higher risk than the others.
wrong_explanations.D: Using the highest rating is cautious, but without knowing the cause it may overstate risk at three offices and miss a local problem.

tips: Eliminate: A averages ordinal ratings, which can bury a high-risk unit, and B lets a majority outvote the one office that may see something real.
Final two: C beats D because the cause of the difference decides the right rating; copying the high rating everywhere guesses at it.
Exam cue: when aggregation shows the same risk rated differently, investigate the difference before averaging, voting or taking the worst case.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Cutting a long KRI list
questions.question: A shipping line's risk analyst is cutting the 140 KRIs reported monthly to the risk committee to a usable set. Which of the following should BEST decide which KRIs are kept?

options.A: How early each KRI warns of a top-rated risk
options.B: Whether each KRI breached its risk threshold last year
options.C: How cheaply each KRI's data can be collected
options.D: Whether each KRI's owner reports it on time

questions.key_concept: KRIs are kept for how early they warn of the risks that matter most, not for their collection cost, reporting habits or past breaches.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes a KRI worth a committee's attention each month.
questions.correct_explanation: KRIs earn their place by warning early about the risks that matter most, so the test for keeping one is how early it signals a change in a top-rated risk, before loss occurs. Selecting on last year's breaches looks evidence-based, but it keeps lagging counts that fired after trouble arrived and can drop a leading indicator that has not fired yet, losing the early warning the committee needs.

wrong_explanations.B: Past breaches show where problems arrived; selecting on them favors lagging counts and can drop leading indicators that have not yet fired.
wrong_explanations.C: Cheap data is welcome, but collection cost says nothing about whether the KRI warns of a risk that matters.
wrong_explanations.D: Timely reporting is a data-quality matter; an indicator can arrive on time every month and still track a risk nobody needs to watch.

tips: Eliminate: C picks KRIs by data cost and D by reporting habits; neither says whether a KRI warns of a risk that matters.
Final two: A beats B because a KRI is kept for warning early about a top risk; selecting on past breaches favors lagging counts.
Exam cue: good KRIs are few, tied to top risks, leading and owned; keep them for what they predict, not for cost, habit or history.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators); ISACA Glossary (key risk indicator)

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Ratings move only once a year
questions.question: Over the past year, an insurer made three major system changes and had two serious incidents, yet its risk ratings changed only at the annual review. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Reassess the register quarterly instead of yearly
options.B: Add a KRI tracking open incidents and changes monthly
options.C: Link change and incident processes to reassessment
options.D: Add staff to the risk team for the annual review

questions.key_concept: Material changes, incidents and breaches should trigger reassessment through links to change and incident processes, with scheduled reviews as a backstop.
questions.pre_read: Ask what should have caused the ratings to move between reviews.
questions.correct_explanation: Major changes and serious incidents are triggers: each can shift likelihood or impact the day it happens. Linking change management and incident processes to the risk function makes each trigger start a reassessment, so ratings move when risk moves. Moving to quarterly reviews narrows the gap, but a change made the week after a review still waits up to three months, and the review stays tied to the calendar rather than the event.

wrong_explanations.A: Quarterly reviews narrow the gap, but ratings still wait for the calendar rather than moving when a change or incident happens.
wrong_explanations.B: A KRI shows how many incidents and changes there are, but it re-rates none of the scenarios they affect, so ratings still wait for the annual review.
wrong_explanations.D: More staff make the annual review thorough, but ratings still go a year without reflecting changes and incidents.

tips: Eliminate: B adds an indicator but re-rates nothing, and D strengthens the annual review without shortening the delay.
Final two: C beats A because triggers move ratings when risk moves; a quarterly calendar is still a calendar.
Exam cue: material change, serious incidents and threshold breaches trigger reassessment; look for options tied to the event, not the date.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk: compliance, response effectiveness and risk-impacting changes)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C4.3 (Triggers for Reassessment: link change management and incident processes to the risk function, so a trigger starts a reassessment). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of an insurer whose risk ratings changed only at the annual review despite three major system changes and two serious incidents in the year, written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 round 3 (crisc_d3_051 to 085). Cross-domain fixes 4 Nov 2026: option B (internal audit as a filler distractor) replaced by a monthly KRI on incidents and changes; wrong B and the Eliminate tip updated. Option A now reads 'Reassess the register quarterly instead of yearly', since the old B was the only wrong option with an 'assess' word and the key would otherwise hold it alone. Key unchanged (C).

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Ending scheduled reviews
questions.question: An airport operator now starts a risk reassessment on every major change, incident and threshold breach, and its CIO proposes ending scheduled risk reviews. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: End the scheduled reviews and rely on the triggers
options.B: Replace scheduled reviews with a monthly KRI summary
options.C: Keep scheduled reviews alongside the triggers
options.D: Keep scheduled reviews for the ten highest risks

questions.key_concept: Triggers catch change that someone records; scheduled reviews stay as a backstop for change nobody reports, at a frequency set by risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a trigger depends on to fire, and what happens when that does not occur.
questions.correct_explanation: Triggers fire only when someone records a change, incident or breach; drift, unreported changes and slow shifts in threats pass them by. Scheduled reviews remain the backstop, with frequency set by each risk's rating. Keeping them for the ten highest risks saves effort, but it leaves every other risk without a backstop, even though an unreported change can turn a low-rated risk into a serious one.

wrong_explanations.A: Triggers depend on someone recording the event; without scheduled reviews, unreported change and gradual drift are never picked up.
wrong_explanations.B: A KRI summary shows indicator movement, but risks without KRIs, and changes no indicator tracks, would go unreviewed.
wrong_explanations.D: Limiting reviews to the top ten leaves lower-rated risks with no backstop, though unreported change can raise them.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes triggers catch every change, and B assumes indicators cover every risk.
Final two: C beats D because unreported change can affect any risk; keep a backstop for all of them, with frequency set by rating.
Exam cue: event triggers and scheduled reviews work together; an option that drops either one is the trap.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.2.2 (Establish Monitoring and Assessment Frequencies: event-driven assessments on incidents, new threat information and significant changes, alongside the set frequencies); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C4.3 (Triggers for Reassessment: keep scheduled reviews as a backstop, since not every change is announced). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of an airport operator whose CIO proposes ending scheduled risk reviews now that major changes, incidents and threshold breaches start reassessments, written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. Cross-domain fixes 4 Nov 2026: option B (internal audit as a filler distractor) replaced by a monthly KRI summary in place of scheduled reviews; wrong B and the Eliminate tip updated. questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Asked to fill in a self-assessment
questions.question: A bank's payments division head asks the risk team to complete the division's control self-assessment on its managers' behalf, to save them time. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Run a short workshop where managers rate their controls
options.B: Complete the assessment and have each manager sign it
options.C: Ask internal audit to complete the assessment this year
options.D: Defer the division's assessment to next year's cycle

questions.key_concept: In control self-assessment the risk function designs and facilitates while managers rate their own controls; doing it for them loses the ownership it builds.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose knowledge and ownership a self-assessment is meant to capture.
questions.correct_explanation: Control self-assessment works because the managers who run the controls judge them, which builds first-line ownership. The risk team designs the questions and facilitates, and a short workshop respects the managers' time while keeping the ratings theirs. Completing it for them and collecting signatures looks efficient, but the ratings become the risk team's views, signed by managers who may never have examined their own controls.

wrong_explanations.B: Ratings written by the risk team are second-line opinions under first-line names; the ownership self-assessment exists to build is lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance; completing management's self-assessment would compromise that role and still remove manager ownership.
wrong_explanations.D: Deferring leaves the division's controls unassessed for a year and does not address the managers' time concern.

tips: Eliminate: C has the third line do management's self-assessment, and D leaves the division unassessed without solving the time problem.
Final two: A beats B because the managers must make the ratings; signatures on the risk team's answers keep the form but lose the ownership.
Exam cue: in self-assessment the second line facilitates and challenges; the first line assesses its own controls.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (control risk self-assessment); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C4.2 (Control Self-Assessment and Trend Analysis: the risk function designs the questions and facilitates; managers answer for their own areas). CRISC D3 round 3 (crisc_d3_051 to 085).

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. 600 checks ready to switch on
questions.question: A medical device maker has bought a continuous monitoring platform with 600 ready-made checks, and IT plans to switch them all on next week. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Turn on the 600 checks now and tune out noise later
options.B: Route the alerts to the CISO's team for review
options.C: Enable the checks the vendor rates as highest risk
options.D: Start with checks on controls over the top risks

questions.key_concept: A monitoring strategy decides what to monitor first, how often and who acts, starting with the controls behind the highest risks.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens the week after 600 checks start sending results to people.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring helps only when someone acts on its results. Starting with checks on the controls behind the top risks, each with an owner and response time, builds a strategy tied to risk tolerance and keeps alerts manageable. Turning everything on and tuning later promises full coverage, but floods teams with alerts before anyone knows which matter, so real warnings get lost while tuning catches up.

wrong_explanations.A: Full coverage on day one buries the important alerts in noise; alert fatigue sets in before tuning reaches the checks that matter.
wrong_explanations.B: One team receiving every alert becomes a bottleneck; alerts should reach the owners who can act on each control.
wrong_explanations.C: The vendor's risk rating reflects generic threats, not which controls guard this maker's top risks.

tips: Eliminate: B funnels the alerts to one team instead of the owners who act, and C lets the vendor's risk ratings, not the maker's own risks, decide what to monitor.
Final two: D beats A because a risk-based start keeps alerts actionable; switching everything on and tuning later invites alert fatigue.
Exam cue: monitoring follows a strategy: controls behind the top risks first, an owner for each alert, frequency set by risk.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.1 (Define ISCM Strategy: the strategy is developed in line with organizational risk tolerance and reviewed on trigger criteria as well as a preestablished frequency); NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.2.2 (Establish Monitoring and Assessment Frequencies: control volatility, impact level, known weaknesses, risk tolerance and threat information)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C4.1 (Continuous Monitoring and Automated Alerts: write a monitoring strategy covering what to monitor, how often and who receives the results; set frequency by risk; give every alert an owner). questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. One score from the heat map
questions.question: The board asks a payment firm's risk analyst for one overall IT risk score, computed by averaging the 1 to 25 heat-map scores of its 60 risks. What is the analyst's BEST response?

options.A: Provide the full table of the 60 risk scores
options.B: Offer the profile of risks against appetite and trend
options.C: Weight the average by each risk's impact score
options.D: Average the scores of the risks above appetite

questions.key_concept: Heat-map scores are ordinal, so averaging them misleads; the board gets the risk profile against appetite, with trend.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether a heat-map score of 12 is really twice as bad as a score of 6.
questions.correct_explanation: Heat-map scores rank risks but are not true quantities, so averaging them, weighted or not, produces a number with no clear meaning that can hide a single critical risk. The analyst offers what the board needs to decide: the profile of risks against appetite, with trend. Weighting the average by impact sounds more rigorous, but it adds more arithmetic on ordinal scores and still blends many risks into one figure.

wrong_explanations.A: The full table gives the board detail without the view against appetite it needs; boards want the profile, not every score.
wrong_explanations.C: Weighting adds more arithmetic on ordinal scores; the result still has no clear meaning and still blends risks together.
wrong_explanations.D: Averaging the worst risks still hides which one is furthest above appetite, the fact the board most needs.

tips: Eliminate: A gives the board detail instead of the profile against appetite, and D averages the very risks the board needs to see one by one.
Final two: B beats C because ordinal scores cannot be meaningfully averaged, weighted or not; the board needs the profile against appetite.
Exam cue: do not add, average or weight heat-map scores; report the profile against appetite, with trend, to the board.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.2.5 (Visualizing Risk Priority: heat maps are a quick-reference guide with limited ability to convey risk information); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.2 (Assessment Approaches: semi-quantitative bins and scales have meaning only within the assessment); ISACA Glossary (risk map)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C5.1 (Heat Maps, Scorecards and Dashboards: heat-map scores are ordinal, so cells cannot be added or averaged meaningfully; show trend and thresholds). CRISC D3 round 3 (crisc_d3_051 to 085).

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Bare numbers on a dashboard
questions.question: A telecom's dashboard for its executive committee shows each KRI's current value as a bare number. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend adding as MOST important?

options.A: The underlying records behind each KRI value
options.B: A single overall score combining the KRIs
options.C: Each KRI's thresholds and its recent trend
options.D: Each KRI's value compared with industry averages

questions.key_concept: A KRI value means little alone; thresholds tied to tolerance and the recent trend show whether exposure is acceptable and which way it is moving.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an executive would need to know whether a value of 37 is good or bad.
questions.correct_explanation: A number on its own does not say whether exposure is acceptable or worsening. Thresholds drawn from tolerance show where each KRI sits against the agreed limits, and the recent trend shows direction, so the committee sees what needs a decision. Industry averages add context and tempt, but peers' figures were not set from this telecom's tolerance, so a KRI can beat the average and still breach the company's own limit.

wrong_explanations.A: Underlying records help validate the data, but executives need context to decide, not raw detail.
wrong_explanations.B: Combining unrelated KRIs into one score hides which risk is moving and can mask a single breach.
wrong_explanations.D: Peer averages are not this company's tolerance; a KRI can look better than peers while still beyond the agreed limit.

tips: Eliminate: A gives executives raw detail instead of context, and B blends unrelated indicators into one score that masks which risk is moving.
Final two: C beats D because thresholds come from the company's own tolerance; peer averages say nothing about its limits.
Exam cue: report indicators against their thresholds and trend; a bare value or a peer comparison does not tell leaders when to act.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 5.2 (Monitoring Risks: KRIs are observed for trends such as rising likelihood or failing controls); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.2 (Measurement Reporting: context such as the risk indicated, fit with risk appetite and the decision needed)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3C5.1 (Heat Maps, Scorecards and Dashboards: scorecards and dashboards show indicators against thresholds and trend, not raw counts alone). Round 3, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario of a telecom's executive dashboard showing each KRI's current value as a bare number, written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Same pack for every owner
questions.question: Each quarter, a risk analyst sends all 15 of a manufacturer's risk owners the same 40-page enterprise risk report, and few act on it. What is the analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Add a one-page summary to the front of the report
options.B: Send each owner a report on their own risks and actions
options.C: Ask the CEO to require each owner to read the report
options.D: Send the same 40-page report monthly instead of quarterly

questions.key_concept: Reports are built for the audience's decisions: each risk owner needs their own risks, indicators and actions due, not the enterprise pack.
questions.pre_read: Ask what one risk owner needs to see to know what to do next.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk owners act on their own risks, indicator status, overdue actions and acceptances due for review. A report built around each owner's portfolio puts those in front of them, so what needs action is clear. A one-page summary makes the enterprise report easier to read, but it summarizes the whole enterprise, so each owner still has to hunt through the pages for their own items.

wrong_explanations.A: A summary helps readers of the enterprise view, but it is still not organized around each owner's risks and due actions.
wrong_explanations.C: Pressure from the CEO may get the report read, but owners still have to dig through 40 pages for their own items.
wrong_explanations.D: Sending a report that does not fit its readers more often adds volume without making it more useful.

tips: Eliminate: C pushes owners to read a report that does not fit them, and D sends the same unsuitable report more often.
Final two: B beats A because each owner needs their own risks and actions; a summary still describes the whole enterprise.
Exam cue: match the report to its reader's decisions: boards get the profile against appetite, owners get their risks and actions.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.4 (Analyze Data and Report Findings: recipients, content, format and frequency of reports)

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Committee notes a risk without acting
questions.question: After a risk analyst presents a rising card-fraud risk to an e-commerce firm's executive committee, members note the risk and move to the next item without acting. Which addition would BEST improve the next report?

options.A: The decision needed, with options and their target risk
options.B: The risk's trend against its KRI thresholds over time
options.C: Technical detail of how the fraud attacks are carried out
options.D: A comparison of the firm's fraud losses with its rivals

questions.key_concept: A report that asks for action states the decision requested, the options and what each would leave, so leaders can decide.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the committee already knew and what it did next.
questions.correct_explanation: The committee already knows the risk is rising; nothing in the report asked it for a decision. Stating the decision needed, with the response options and the target risk each would leave, turns the report into something it can act on. Trend against thresholds strengthens the case that action is due, but it repeats what the committee has already heard, that the risk is rising, without saying what to decide.

wrong_explanations.B: Trend against thresholds shows the risk is rising, which the committee already heard; it still does not say what decision is needed.
wrong_explanations.C: Attack detail suits the fraud team; executives need the decision and its options, not how the fraud works.
wrong_explanations.D: Comparing with rivals adds context, but it does not tell the committee what it is being asked to approve.

tips: Eliminate: C gives executives technical detail meant for specialists, and D offers context without saying what to decide.
Final two: A beats B because the committee's gap is the decision, not more evidence that the risk is rising; state the decision and its options.
Exam cue: reports to leaders end with the decision requested and the options, not just the problem.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Hundreds of signals a month
questions.question: A risk analyst's monthly horizon scan for an energy network operator returns about 300 signals from news, vendor alerts, research and regulators. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Screen the signals for relevance to the operator's objectives
options.B: Record each signal in the register as an emerging risk
options.C: Narrow the scan to alerts from government agencies
options.D: Pass the signals to unit heads to check against their objectives

questions.key_concept: Horizon scanning feeds the register only after signals are screened for relevance to the enterprise's objectives and assets.
questions.pre_read: Ask how many of the 300 signals are likely to matter to this business.
questions.correct_explanation: Most signals will not matter to this operator. The analyst first screens them against its objectives, assets and operations, then raises the relevant ones as emerging risks with proposed owners. Passing the signals to unit heads uses their knowledge of their objectives, but sending them hundreds of unfiltered items each month buries the few that matter and pushes the risk function's screening work onto them.

wrong_explanations.B: Recording every signal floods the register with items that have nothing to do with the business and buries the few that do.
wrong_explanations.C: Narrowing the sources misses signals from research, vendors and regulators, where many emerging risks first appear.
wrong_explanations.D: Unit heads know their objectives, but hundreds of unfiltered signals each month bury the relevant ones and shift the screening onto them.

tips: Eliminate: B records every signal as a risk without screening, and C narrows the sources, losing signals from research, vendors and regulators.
Final two: A beats D because the risk function screens first; passing hundreds of unfiltered signals to unit heads buries what matters.
Exam cue: scan widely, then screen against objectives before recording; relevance comes before the register.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. New evidence on a deepfake risk
questions.question: A bank's risk analyst recorded deepfake voice fraud on payment approvals as an emerging risk with a wide rating range; peer losses and control tests now provide solid data. What is the analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Keep it as emerging with a shorter review date
options.B: Close the entry and record the control test results
options.C: Rate it critical from other banks' losses
options.D: Rate it on the usual scale in the main profile

questions.key_concept: An emerging risk moves into the main profile, rated on the usual scale, once evidence is good enough to rate it with confidence.
questions.pre_read: Ask what made the risk 'emerging' in the first place, and whether that is still true.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk is held as emerging while too little is known to rate it normally. Peer losses and the bank's own control tests now provide that evidence, so the analyst rates it on the usual scale and moves it into the main profile, where it is compared with appetite and owned like any other risk. Keeping it emerging with a shorter review date suits real uncertainty, which the new data has now resolved.

wrong_explanations.A: Short reviews suit a risk that is still poorly understood; with solid data available, keeping it emerging delays a normal rating and response.
wrong_explanations.B: A tested control can lower the risk but does not remove it; closing the entry drops a live risk from the register.
wrong_explanations.C: Peer losses are evidence, but the rating should come from the bank's own likelihood, impact and controls, not from alarm.

tips: Eliminate: B removes a risk because one control was tested, and C rates it critical from peer losses rather than the bank's own analysis.
Final two: D beats A because the uncertainty that justified 'emerging' is gone; with solid data, rate it normally in the main profile.
Exam cue: emerging risks are refined as evidence grows and move into the main profile once they can be rated with confidence.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Owner for an AI shopping risk
questions.question: A risk analyst at an online grocer records AI shopping agents that buy for customers as an emerging risk to online sales. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate owner to propose?

options.A: The grocer's chief information officer
options.B: The risk team, as the function that recorded it
options.C: An owner named once the risk can be rated
options.D: The director of the online sales channel

questions.key_concept: An emerging risk gets a business owner while it is still uncertain: the manager whose objectives it affects, not IT or the risk team.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose objectives these agents would help or harm.
questions.correct_explanation: Even while uncertain, an emerging risk needs an owner who will watch it and decide on responses as evidence grows. AI agents buying for customers affect online sales, so the director of that channel owns the risk. Having the risk team that recorded it hold the risk sounds natural, but the practitioner advises and monitors; holding the risk would leave no business decision-maker watching it while it develops.

wrong_explanations.A: The CIO may support the technology work, but the risk is to online sales, a business objective owned by the channel's director.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk team records, analyzes and monitors; recording a risk does not make it the owner, and it leaves no business decision-maker in charge.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting to name an owner until the risk can be rated is the trap; emerging risks need an owner early, with their uncertainty stated.

tips: Eliminate: A gives a business risk to IT because AI is technology, and C delays naming an owner until the risk can be rated.
Final two: D beats B because the practitioner advises and monitors but does not own risk; the channel's director owns the objective at stake.
Exam cue: AI and emerging risks are owned by the business whose objectives they affect, from the day they are recorded.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Loss left after controls
questions.question: After new controls, an event-ticketing platform's breach risk exceeds appetite only on the cost of a large breach, which more controls cannot cut at a sensible price. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Close the ticketing platform to avoid the breach risk
options.B: Accept the remaining risk as it stands
options.C: Insure part of the financial loss from a breach
options.D: Add another layer of controls to the platform

questions.key_concept: Responses combine: once further controls stop being cost-effective, transferring part of the remaining financial impact can bring the risk within appetite.
questions.pre_read: Note which part of the risk is still above appetite, and what more controls would cost.
questions.correct_explanation: The risk is above appetite only on the money a large breach would cost, and more controls are not worth their price. Insurance shares exactly that part, so combining controls with transfer can bring the risk within appetite, while accountability stays with the company. Another control layer is the runner-up: it trims likelihood a little, but it costs more than it saves and barely touches the financial impact that remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Closing the platform gives up the business it exists for; avoidance fits only when the activity is not needed or nothing else brings the risk within appetite.
wrong_explanations.B: A risk still above appetite cannot simply be accepted as it stands; it needs more treatment or a decision from the level that set the appetite.
wrong_explanations.D: More controls would cost more than they save, and they barely reduce the financial impact that keeps the risk above appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A drops a platform the business needs, and B accepts a risk that is still above appetite.
Final two: C beats D because the part above appetite is financial and more controls no longer pay; insurance shares that cost.
Exam cue: responses can be combined; when controls stop paying for themselves, transfer part of the remaining financial impact, knowing accountability stays.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 (Responding to Risk: accept, avoid, mitigate, share or transfer); ISACA Glossary (risk response)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A1.1 (The Four Risk Responses: responses can be combined, reducing likelihood with controls and then insuring part of the financial impact that remains); 3A1.2 (prefer the option that meets appetite at the lowest total cost). questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Little-used payment page
questions.question: A university's old donation page takes 30 card gifts a year, which donors could give on its main platform; securing it to meet appetite would cost $150,000. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retire the old page and its card payments
options.B: Secure the old page to bring the risk within appetite
options.C: Insure against card data losses from the old page
options.D: Have the alumni director accept the risk as it stands

questions.key_concept: Avoidance fits when an activity adds little to objectives and treating it would cost far more than it is worth.
questions.pre_read: Weigh what the old page adds to fundraising against what keeping it would cost.
questions.correct_explanation: Thirty gifts a year that donors could give on the main platform add almost nothing to fundraising, while securing the old page would cost $150,000. Retiring it removes the risk and gives up very little, so avoidance is the proportionate response. Securing the page is the runner-up: it would bring the risk within appetite, but it spends far more than the activity is worth to the university's objectives.

wrong_explanations.B: Securing the page would work, but $150,000 for 30 gifts a year costs far more than keeping the page is worth.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance shares part of the financial loss but leaves the exposure, and the card data, on a page the university barely needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Securing the page to meet appetite would cost $150,000, so the risk is above appetite now and cannot simply be accepted as it stands.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves the exposure in place on a page nobody needs, and D accepts a risk that is above appetite.
Final two: A beats B because the page adds little to objectives and securing it costs far more than it is worth; avoidance removes the risk outright.
Exam cue: avoid when the activity adds little and treatment costs more than it is worth; mitigate when the business needs the activity.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Comparing the options
questions.question: Which of the following BEST helps a risk owner choose among the response options a risk practitioner has identified for a risk above appetite?

options.A: The control the IT team prefers for the risk
options.B: The responses peer firms chose for similar risks
options.C: The risk's inherent rating before controls
options.D: Each alternative's cost and the target risk it leaves

questions.key_concept: The practitioner sets out each response option with its cost and the target risk it would leave; the risk owner chooses.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a decision-maker needs in order to compare options against appetite.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk owner decides by comparing what each option costs with where it would leave the risk against appetite, so the practitioner sets out each option's cost and target risk side by side. Peer firms' choices are the runner-up: they show what others did, but those firms have their own appetite, costs and exposure, so they cannot tell this owner which option fits.

wrong_explanations.A: IT's preferred control is one option, not a comparison; it skips what each option costs and the risk each would leave.
wrong_explanations.B: Peers' choices reflect their own appetite, costs and exposure, so they cannot show which option fits this organization.
wrong_explanations.C: The inherent rating is the same starting point for every option, so it cannot separate one response from another.

tips: Eliminate: A narrows the choice to IT's favorite control, and C gives a rating that is the same whichever option is chosen.
Final two: D beats B because the owner needs this organization's costs and resulting risk; peers chose for their own appetite.
Exam cue: the practitioner lays out options with cost and target risk; the owner picks the one that meets appetite at a fair price.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. One control, several risks
questions.question: A bank's email data-loss prevention control protects risks owned by four business directors, and each director wants their own team to run a copy of the control. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: A copy of the control run by each director's team
options.B: One control owner reporting results to all four
options.C: The CISO as owner of the four directors' risks
options.D: The four directors as joint owners of the control

questions.key_concept: One control can protect several risks: it keeps one accountable control owner, who reports its results to each risk owner relying on it.
questions.pre_read: Separate who owns each risk from who answers for the control that protects them.
questions.correct_explanation: A control can serve several risks. One accountable control owner keeps it consistent, holds its evidence and reports its results to each director, who stays the owner of their own risk. Making the four directors joint owners of the control is the runner-up: it looks inclusive, but shared ownership means no one person answers for the control working or acts when it fails.

wrong_explanations.A: Four copies of one control cost four times as much and drift apart, with no single view of whether email leaks are stopped.
wrong_explanations.C: The CISO may run security, but each director owns the business risk to their own objectives; IT does not take over business risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Joint ownership spreads accountability so thinly that nobody answers for the control working or acts when it fails.

tips: Eliminate: A duplicates one control four times, and C hands the directors' business risks to IT.
Final two: B beats D because a key control needs one accountable owner; joint ownership leaves no one answering for it.
Exam cue: a control may serve many risk owners, but it keeps one control owner who reports to each of them.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Delegating the treatment work
questions.question: A cosmetics retailer's marketing director, who owns a customer-data risk, has asked IT to deliver its treatment plan and wants IT recorded as the risk's owner. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Advise keeping the director as risk owner, IT as action owner
options.B: Record IT as the risk owner while it delivers the plan
options.C: Ask senior management to confirm IT as the risk's owner
options.D: Advise naming the director and IT as joint risk owners

questions.key_concept: Delegating treatment work moves tasks, not accountability: IT can own the actions while the manager whose objectives are at stake keeps the risk.
questions.pre_read: Separate who does the work from who answers for the risk.
questions.correct_explanation: The director can hand the treatment work to IT, but not the accountability: the customer-data risk still threatens marketing's objectives, so the practitioner advises keeping the director as risk owner, with IT as action owner. Asking senior management to confirm IT is the runner-up: senior management does assign owners, but nothing about the risk has changed, and confirming IT would put a business risk with the team doing the work.

wrong_explanations.B: Delivering the plan makes IT responsible for actions, not for the risk; the business objectives at stake are still marketing's.
wrong_explanations.C: Senior management assigns owners, but the risk still threatens marketing's objectives; confirming IT would place a business risk with the team doing the work.
wrong_explanations.D: Joint ownership blurs who decides and who accepts, so neither party is clearly accountable for the risk.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the risk along with the tasks, and D splits accountability between two parties.
Final two: A beats C because handing over work does not move accountability; nothing has changed that needs a new owner confirmed.
Exam cue: action owners do the work; the risk owner keeps the accountability and the decisions.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Due diligence behind schedule
questions.question: An airline wants to start setting up a crew-scheduling SaaS service next week, but due diligence on its handling of crew personal data needs six more weeks. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Load crew data now and finish due diligence later
options.B: Cut due diligence to the vendor's own questionnaire
options.C: Run the setup on test data until the review finishes
options.D: Delay the setup for the six weeks the review needs

questions.key_concept: When the business wants to start before due diligence ends, limit the vendor to test data so work starts without exposing the data under review.
questions.pre_read: Note what the open review covers and what next week's setup involves.
questions.correct_explanation: The open question is how the vendor handles crew personal data, so the exposure comes from loading that data. Setting up on test data, with no crew data loaded, keeps the project moving while the review finishes, without exposing anyone's details. Delaying six weeks is the runner-up: it is safe, but it stops setup work that needs no personal data.

wrong_explanations.A: Loading crew data before due diligence ends exposes it to the very handling the review has not yet checked.
wrong_explanations.B: A vendor's own answers are not evidence for a service that will hold personal data; cutting the review weakens it rather than speeding it safely.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting avoids the exposure, but it holds up setup work that can run on test data without any crew data.

tips: Eliminate: A exposes crew data before the review, and B swaps evidence for the vendor's own claims.
Final two: C beats D because setup on test data keeps the work moving without the exposure; delay is safe but stops work that needs no personal data.
Exam cue: when the business wants to start before assurance finishes, shrink the exposure rather than choosing between rushing and stopping.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Indicator for vendor onboarding
questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST key control indicator for a risk practitioner to propose for a credit union's due diligence on new critical vendors?

options.A: Number of critical vendors reviewed this year
options.B: Average days taken to complete each review
options.C: Number of vendor breaches reported across the sector
options.D: Share of critical vendors contracted before review

questions.key_concept: A KCI shows when a control is failing; for vendor due diligence, contracts signed before the review show the control being bypassed.
questions.pre_read: Ask which measure would show the due diligence control failing to do its job.
questions.correct_explanation: A key control indicator shows weakness in the control itself. Due diligence exists to assess a critical vendor before the contract is signed, so the share of critical vendors contracted before their review shows how often the control is bypassed. Average review time is the runner-up: it measures how efficiently reviews run, a performance measure that can look good while contracts go ahead unreviewed.

wrong_explanations.A: A count of reviews shows activity, not whether any critical vendor was signed without one.
wrong_explanations.B: Review time is a performance measure; reviews can be quick while contracts are still signed before any review is done.
wrong_explanations.C: Sector breaches describe the threat landscape, a risk signal, and say nothing about whether this control works.

tips: Eliminate: A counts activity, and C tracks the sector's breaches rather than this control.
Final two: D beats B because a KCI shows the control failing; review time measures efficiency, not bypass.
Exam cue: for a KCI, ask what the control is meant to stop, then measure how often it happens anyway.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Request to make an exception permanent
questions.question: A city council's finance director wants a three-year-old exception letting the property tax system skip multifactor sign-in made a permanent exemption, as replacement is unfunded. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Grant the permanent exemption the director has asked for
options.B: Advise a renewed exception with a plan to comply
options.C: Have the director re-sign the exception for three years
options.D: Propose removing multifactor sign-in from the standard's scope

questions.key_concept: An exemption fits a requirement that cannot apply; one that can apply after a system change stays an exception with an expiry and a plan.
questions.pre_read: Note why the system skips multifactor sign-in today.
questions.correct_explanation: Multifactor sign-in can apply once the property tax system is replaced, so this is a deviation with an end, not a requirement that can never apply. It stays an exception: the practitioner reassesses its risk and advises renewal with compensating controls, a fresh expiry and a plan to comply, funding included, that the director commits to. Re-signing is the runner-up: it sets an end date but, with no plan, rolls the gap forward.

wrong_explanations.A: An exemption fits a requirement that cannot apply; this one can once the system is replaced, and the practitioner does not grant deviations.
wrong_explanations.C: A new end date without a plan to comply rolls the same gap forward; the exception would expire again with nothing changed.
wrong_explanations.D: Changing the standard to fit one system weakens it for all the others, and the gap on the property tax system remains.

tips: Eliminate: A has the practitioner grant a deviation the facts do not support, and D rewrites the standard around one system.
Final two: B beats C because an exception needs a plan to comply, not just a new date; a rollover without one keeps the gap open.
Exam cue: exemption when a requirement can never apply; exception, with an expiry and a plan, when it cannot apply yet.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Issues kept in three places
questions.question: A manufacturer keeps audit findings in one tool, regulator findings in a spreadsheet and staff-raised issues in email, and nobody can tell which risks have open issues. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: One issue log linking each item to the risk it affects
options.B: One combined list of the open issues, sorted by due date
options.C: A monthly email from each team listing its open items
options.D: A board count of open items by source, age and risk rating

questions.key_concept: Issues from all sources go in one log, each linked to and rated by the risk it affects, so exposure stays visible.
questions.pre_read: Ask what anyone deciding on these issues needs to see about each one.
questions.correct_explanation: Findings matter for the risks they leave exposed. One log that links each issue to the risk it affects, rated by that risk, shows which risks have open issues against them and how serious those are. A combined list sorted by due date is the runner-up: it brings the items together and helps chasing, but it still cannot show which risks they weaken.

wrong_explanations.B: Merging the items in date order makes chasing easier but still says nothing about which risks each one weakens.
wrong_explanations.C: Monthly emails keep the three sources apart and add reading, without linking any item to a risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Counts by rating show volume and severity, not which register risks have open issues against them.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps the sources apart in monthly emails, and D gives the board counts with no link to particular risks.
Final two: A beats B because each issue must be tied to the risk it affects; a date-ordered list gathers items but cannot show exposure.
Exam cue: an issue log earns its keep when each item points to a risk and is rated by it.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Action past the escalation point
questions.question: A port operator's policy sends high-rated findings more than 60 days late to the executive committee, and a risk owner wants one 90 days late left off. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Have the risk owner set a new date for the late fix
options.B: Close the finding and reopen it with a later due date
options.C: Escalate the late finding to the executive committee
options.D: Tell the executive committee once the fix is complete

questions.key_concept: Escalation points set in policy belong to the level that set them; a risk owner cannot opt out of an escalation the policy requires.
questions.pre_read: Note what the policy says and who set it, then weigh the owner's request against it.
questions.correct_explanation: The policy sends high-rated findings more than 60 days late to the executive committee, and this one is 90 days late, so the committee must see it. A risk owner cannot waive an escalation set above them. Telling the committee once the fix is complete is the runner-up: it sounds tidy, but it hides the delay from the people meant to decide whether to step in.

wrong_explanations.A: A new date is useful, but the policy has already moved the item above the owner's level; agreeing a date does not replace escalation.
wrong_explanations.B: Closing and reopening resets the clock and hides how late the action is, which defeats the tracking.
wrong_explanations.D: Reporting only after the fix keeps the delay from the committee while it could still act.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps the item at the owner's level after the policy has moved it up, and B resets the clock so tracking no longer shows the delay.
Final two: C beats D because the policy sets the escalation point; reporting after the fix keeps the committee from acting while it matters.
Exam cue: when a set limit is passed, escalate to the level that set it; an owner cannot waive an escalation above them.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Control types for ransomware
questions.question: A risk practitioner is classifying a water utility's ransomware controls. Which of the following is BEST classified as a corrective control?

options.A: Blocking macros in emailed office documents
options.B: Alerting when many files are encrypted quickly
options.C: Showing a warning banner at each sign-in
options.D: Restoring encrypted systems from offline backups

questions.key_concept: Classify a control by what it does to the event: preventive stops it, deterrent discourages it, detective finds it, corrective restores after it.
questions.pre_read: Ask when each control acts: before, during or after the attack.
questions.correct_explanation: A corrective control limits the damage after an event and restores normal operation, so restoring encrypted systems from offline backups is corrective (some frameworks call this a recovery control). Alerting on rapid file encryption is the runner-up: it acts during the attack, but it detects and reports; it puts nothing back, and it reduces impact only if someone responds in time.

wrong_explanations.A: Blocking macros closes a common way in before the attack starts, which makes it preventive.
wrong_explanations.B: An encryption alert detects the attack in progress; it reports the event but restores nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: A warning banner discourages misuse without stopping it, which makes it a deterrent control.

tips: Eliminate: A acts before the attack, so it is preventive, and C only discourages, so it is a deterrent.
Final two: D beats B because corrective controls restore after the event; an alert detects it and reports.
Exam cue: sort controls by timing and effect: before (prevent, deter), during (detect), after (correct and recover).
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.4 (Risk Mitigation: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective and compensating controls); NIST CSF 2.0 PR.DS-11 (backups of data are created, protected, maintained and tested)

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Automated control setting changed
questions.question: An upgrade reset a distributor's automated credit check to approve orders up to $500,000, not $50,000, unnoticed for three months. Which control should the risk practitioner recommend to BEST prevent a repeat?

options.A: Review of control settings after each system change
options.B: Manual credit control by finance for orders over $50,000
options.C: Recheck of the orders approved in the three months
options.D: Alert to finance when an order exceeds $50,000

questions.key_concept: An automated control repeats a wrong setting on every transaction, so its key settings need review whenever the system changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask what made the control fail, and how many orders one wrong setting affects.
questions.correct_explanation: An automated check applies the same rule to each order, so one wrong setting fails consistently until someone notices. The failure came from an upgrade changing the setting unchecked, so reviewing control settings after each system change stops a repeat. An alert on large orders is the runner-up: it would surface the problem, but only after orders were approved, and it leaves the cause in place.

wrong_explanations.B: Manual review swaps a consistent control for one that varies with people and workload, and leaves the upgrade process unchanged.
wrong_explanations.C: Rechecking past orders repairs this incident's damage; it does nothing to stop the next upgrade changing a setting.
wrong_explanations.D: An alert flags large orders after approval; it detects the effect but leaves unchecked setting changes free to recur.

tips: Eliminate: B gives up consistency for manual review, and C cleans up this incident without stopping the next.
Final two: A beats D because the cause was an unchecked setting change; an alert finds approved orders after the fact.
Exam cue: automated controls fail consistently when misconfigured; protect their settings through change review.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-3 (Configuration Change Control); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CM-4 (Impact Analyses)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B1.2 (Control Categories by Nature: automated controls run the same way every time, but a wrong setting fails every time; new bullet on reviewing automated control settings after system changes). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a distributor's automated credit check reset during an upgrade to approve orders up to $500,000 instead of $50,000 for three months), written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 round 4 (crisc_d3_086 to 115).

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Wrong figures in AI summaries
questions.question: An insurer's AI tool summarizes claim files for adjusters, and some summaries have shown the wrong policy number or claim amount. Which of the following controls should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Training adjusters to spot wrong figures in each summary
options.B: A disclaimer on each summary saying AI wrote it
options.C: Automatic check of the figures against the claim file
options.D: A manager's monthly review of sampled claim summaries

questions.key_concept: Where an AI output states facts that can be checked against source records, validate each output automatically before anyone relies on it.
questions.pre_read: Compare when, and on how many summaries, each control would catch a wrong figure.
questions.correct_explanation: Policy numbers and amounts can be checked against the claim file, so an automatic check catches each wrong figure before an adjuster relies on it, whatever the model gets wrong. A manager's monthly sample is the runner-up: it shows how often errors occur, but it covers a fraction of summaries weeks later, after adjusters have used the wrong figures.

wrong_explanations.A: Training asks busy adjusters to catch each wrong figure by eye, which leaves the check to attention and workload rather than to the source record.
wrong_explanations.B: A disclaimer warns readers without catching any error, so wrong figures still reach decisions.
wrong_explanations.D: A monthly sample measures the error rate after summaries are used and misses most wrong figures.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on adjusters catching errors by eye, and B warns without catching anything.
Final two: C beats D because checkable facts can be validated on each output before use; a monthly sample finds errors after they mattered.
Exam cue: for AI outputs, validate what can be checked against the source before use; sample and monitor the rest.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.4 (the functionality and behavior of the AI system are monitored when in production); NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MANAGE 1.3 (responses to high-priority AI risks are developed, planned and documented, including mitigating, transferring, avoiding or accepting)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B2.1 (Selecting Controls by Root Cause and Cost-Benefit: for AI systems, scale input validation, output checks and human review to the impact of a wrong output; new bullet on checking AI-stated facts against source records). questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Designed without the control owner
questions.question: A hotel group's risk analyst has drafted, alone, a daily reconciliation of guest refunds and plans to hand it to the finance team to run from Monday. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Issue the procedure to finance as a mandatory requirement
options.B: Agree the design with the finance manager as its owner
options.C: Have the risk team run it for its owner for a quarter
options.D: Test the reconciliation on last month's refunds

questions.key_concept: Control design is agreed with the control owner, who will be accountable for running it; the practitioner works with the owner on the design.
questions.pre_read: Note who drafted the reconciliation and who will run it.
questions.correct_explanation: The finance manager will be accountable for the reconciliation working, so the design must be agreed with them before go-live: they know how refunds flow, what is practical, and they will keep its evidence. Testing it on last month's refunds is the runner-up: it checks the logic, but only of the analyst's design, which the person who must own and run it has not yet shaped.

wrong_explanations.A: Mandating a procedure finance never shaped gives it a control on paper that it may not understand or own.
wrong_explanations.C: The risk team running a business control blurs the lines; it can no longer challenge a control it operates.
wrong_explanations.D: A trial checks the analyst's design, but before the owner agrees it, a pass says little about how it will work in finance.

tips: Eliminate: A imposes the control without its owner, and C has the second line run a first-line control.
Final two: B beats D because the owner must shape the design before any trial; testing an unagreed design comes too early.
Exam cue: the practitioner works with control owners on design, not for them; the owner's agreement comes before rollout and testing.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (control owner); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B2.2 (Implementing Controls With Control Owners: the practitioner works with control owners on design and rollout but does not run the control; agree with the control owner what the control does). questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Review that misses unused rules
questions.question: A freight airline's monthly firewall rule review runs on time and checks that each new rule has a ticket, yet 40% of rules serve retired systems. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Retrain reviewers on the current rule checklist
options.B: Review the rules weekly rather than once a month
options.C: Record the review as effective in the register
options.D: Add a check that rules are still needed

questions.key_concept: A design gap means the control as built cannot catch the risk; it needs redesign, not retraining or running more often.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the review failed to run, or ran as built and missed the problem.
questions.correct_explanation: The review runs on time and does what it was built to do, yet it never asks whether old rules are still needed, so rules for retired systems pile up. That is a design gap, closed by adding the missing check. Running the review weekly is the runner-up: it looks like stronger control, but a review that cannot see unused rules misses them weekly instead of monthly.

wrong_explanations.A: Reviewers already follow the checklist; retraining fixes an operating gap, but here the checklist itself lacks the check.
wrong_explanations.B: Running the review more often repeats a check that cannot see unused rules, so the gap stays.
wrong_explanations.C: Running on schedule shows the review operates, not that it is adequate; it misses a risk it was never designed to catch.

tips: Eliminate: A retrains people who already follow the checklist, and C rates the review effective while it misses the risk.
Final two: D beats B because the gap is in the design; running a review that cannot see unused rules more often still misses them.
Exam cue: running on time is not the same as adequate; a control that cannot see the risk as built needs a redesign, not more runs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B2.3 (Control Gap Analysis: separate design gaps, where the control could not work as built, from operating gaps, where it is built right but not performed). Round 4, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a freight airline's firewall rule review that runs on time and checks new rules for tickets while 40% of rules serve retired systems), written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used.
