questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Control internal audit tested recently
questions.question: A risk analyst planning this year's test of a bank's payment-release control learns internal audit tested it two months ago and reported two exceptions. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Read internal audit's results and the two exceptions
options.B: Run the full test with the control owner as planned
options.C: Close the test on internal audit's overall opinion
options.D: Ask the control owner whether the two exceptions are fixed

questions.key_concept: Recent internal audit results on a control are independent evidence; the practitioner starts from them, and their exceptions shape any further testing.
questions.pre_read: Note what has already happened to this control this year.
questions.correct_explanation: Internal audit tested the control two months ago and found two exceptions, so its results are recent, independent evidence. Reading them first shows what failed, whether the causes are known and what any further test should target. Running the planned full test is the runner-up: it produces the analyst's own evidence, but it duplicates recent independent work and ignores what the exceptions already show.

wrong_explanations.B: Running the planned test from scratch with the owner duplicates recent independent work and starts without knowing what the two exceptions were.
wrong_explanations.C: Two exceptions mean audit's opinion cannot simply be carried over; the rating needs what the exceptions show.
wrong_explanations.D: The owner's answer is their own statement; first learn from audit's results what failed and why.

tips: Eliminate: C carries over an opinion despite two exceptions, and D relies on the owner's own word.
Final two: A beats B because recent independent results are the starting point; a full test from scratch duplicates them and ignores what they found.
Exam cue: treat internal audit's recent results as independent evidence; build on them rather than repeating or ignoring them.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Population supplied by the owner
questions.question: To test an online broker's change approval control, the risk analyst will sample from a list of 1,200 production changes that the change manager keeps in a spreadsheet. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Draw a larger sample from the change manager's list
options.B: Have the change manager sign the list as complete
options.C: Check the list against the deployment system's log
options.D: Test the changes the list rates as high risk

questions.key_concept: A sample is only as good as its population; confirm a list the control owner supplies is complete, ideally against system records, before sampling.
questions.pre_read: Note who keeps the list and how it is kept.
questions.correct_explanation: Changes left off the manager's spreadsheet can never be sampled, so any that skipped approval may be missing from the start. Checking the list against the deployment system's log confirms the population is complete before the sample is drawn. A larger sample is the runner-up: it raises confidence about the listed changes, but it cannot reach changes that were never listed.

wrong_explanations.A: A bigger sample from an incomplete list still cannot reach changes that are not on it.
wrong_explanations.B: A signature is the manager's own statement about their own list; it is not evidence that the list is complete.
wrong_explanations.D: Risk-based scoping is sound once the population is trusted; narrowing first leaves the list's completeness untested.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts the owner's word about their own list, and D narrows the test before the list is trusted.
Final two: C beats A because sampling proves nothing about changes missing from the population; a bigger sample of the same list cannot find them.
Exam cue: before sampling, confirm the population is complete from a source the control owner does not keep.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5 Section 2.4.2 (Assessment Methods: examine, interview and test, with depth and coverage); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.4 (Data Quality: a validation process checks the integrity, accuracy and structure of data before any analysis is done)

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plan cost doubles midway
questions.question: Halfway through a freight railway's action plan, its cost estimate has risen from $200,000 to $400,000, while the risk it treats has an expected annual loss of $150,000. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Ask finance to approve the extra $200,000 for the plan
options.B: Update the cost-benefit for the risk owner's decision
options.C: Stop the plan and record the risk as accepted
options.D: Finish the plan, with half the work already paid for

questions.key_concept: When a plan's cost or benefit changes materially, the practitioner updates the cost-benefit and the risk owner decides whether to continue, change or stop.
questions.pre_read: Compare the new cost with the loss the plan avoids, then ask whose decision that trade-off is.
questions.correct_explanation: Doubling the cost changes the case the risk owner approved: the remaining cost against an expected loss of $150,000 a year may still pay back, or a cheaper option may be better. The practitioner updates the cost-benefit and the owner decides whether to continue, change or stop. Asking finance to approve the extra $200,000 is the runner-up: it funds the work, but turns a risk decision into a budget approval made without the owner.

wrong_explanations.A: Finance can fund the plan, but whether its remaining cost is still worth paying against a $150,000 annual loss is the risk owner's decision, not a budget approval.
wrong_explanations.C: Stopping and accepting is a risk decision the practitioner cannot make, and the risk may still need treatment.
wrong_explanations.D: Money already spent is gone whatever is chosen; only the remaining cost against the remaining benefit should decide whether to continue.

tips: Eliminate: C has the practitioner stop the plan and accept the risk, and D lets money already spent decide what to spend next.
Final two: B beats A because whether the remaining cost is still worth paying is the risk owner's call; a finance approval funds it without that decision.
Exam cue: when cost or benefit shifts, rerun the numbers and take the choice back to the risk owner; past spending is not a reason to continue.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 Task 3-2 (Evaluation of Alternatives: effectiveness, feasibility and cost); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-06 (risk responses are chosen, prioritized, planned, tracked and communicated)

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Substitute control proposed
questions.question: Midway through a supermarket chain's action plan to give staff hardware security keys for sign-in, IT proposes app push approvals instead, at a third of the cost. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Estimate the target risk push approvals would leave
options.B: Ask the risk owner to approve the push approvals
options.C: Approve the switch and keep the due date
options.D: Keep the hardware keys that the plan originally set

questions.key_concept: A change to a planned control changes the target risk; estimate what the substitute would leave against appetite before the owner decides.
questions.pre_read: Note what the plan was approved to achieve and what the substitute changes.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan was approved to reach a target risk with hardware keys, which resist phishing. Push approvals cost less but are not phishing-resistant: a fake sign-in page can trigger a real prompt the user approves. So the first step is to estimate the target risk they would leave against appetite. Asking the risk owner first is the runner-up: the decision is theirs, but they would decide on price alone.

wrong_explanations.B: The owner does decide, but without an estimate of the risk the substitute leaves, they would be approving on cost alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Meeting the date says nothing about whether the risk still reaches its target, and the practitioner does not approve plan changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Refusing any change ignores that a cheaper control might still meet appetite; its effect needs estimating first.

tips: Eliminate: C approves on schedule alone and outside the practitioner's role, and D rules out the substitute without looking at its effect.
Final two: A beats B because the owner needs the substitute's target risk to decide; asking first gives them only the price.
Exam cue: when a planned control changes, re-estimate the target risk before anyone approves the change.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Same risk recorded nine ways
questions.question: Consolidating a construction group's unit registers, the risk analyst finds nine units have each recorded a phishing risk, worded differently. Which of the following is the BEST way to show it in the enterprise view?

options.A: Nine separate enterprise entries, as each unit wrote them
options.B: The highest-rated unit entry, standing for the nine
options.C: One enterprise risk, with the nine unit entries closed
options.D: One enterprise risk linked to each unit's entry

questions.key_concept: Merge duplicate unit risks into one representative enterprise risk, keeping a link to each source entry so it stays traceable.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the enterprise view needs, and what each unit still needs to trace.
questions.correct_explanation: Nine wordings of the same risk would clutter the enterprise view and overstate how many distinct risks exist. Merging them into one enterprise risk, linked back to each unit's entry, gives one view while each unit's rating and owner stay traceable. Merging with the unit entries closed is the runner-up: it gives one enterprise view, but closing the sources loses each unit's rating and owner and the trail back to them.

wrong_explanations.A: Nine entries for one risk inflate the risk count and hide that it is a single enterprise-wide exposure.
wrong_explanations.B: Keeping the worst rating looks prudent, but one unit's entry cannot show the exposure across nine units, and the trail to the other eight registers and owners is lost.
wrong_explanations.C: Merging is right, but closing the unit entries cuts the trail: units lose their own ratings and owners, and the enterprise risk can no longer be traced to its sources.

tips: Eliminate: A lists one risk nine times, and B lets one unit's entry stand for all nine, hiding the other eight.
Final two: D beats C because aggregation keeps a link to each source; closing the unit entries loses the trail.
Exam cue: aggregate by merging duplicates into one risk that still traces back to each source register.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. AI-sorted incident data
questions.question: A logistics firm's risk team used an AI tool to sort 300 incident reports into risk categories for the quarterly risk report. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Report the AI's categories with a note on the method
options.B: Ask the vendor for the tool's published accuracy rate
options.C: Check a sample of its categories against the reports
options.D: Ask each unit head to confirm their unit's totals

questions.key_concept: Risk data an AI tool produces is validated like any other source: check a sample against the originals before it is reported.
questions.pre_read: Note where the categories came from and where they are going.
questions.correct_explanation: Categories assigned by an AI tool are data nobody has yet checked. Comparing a sample of its categories with the incident reports shows how accurate the sorting is before the totals reach the report. Reporting its categories with a note on the method is the runner-up: stating limits is good practice, but it passes on figures nobody has validated.

wrong_explanations.A: A note discloses how the figures were made, not whether they are right; validation comes before reporting.
wrong_explanations.B: A vendor's general accuracy figure describes other data, not whether these 300 reports were sorted correctly.
wrong_explanations.D: Unit heads can confirm counts they recognize, not whether each report sits in the right risk category.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on the vendor's general figure rather than these reports, and D asks unit heads about categories they cannot verify.
Final two: C beats A because data is validated before it is reported; a note on the method does not show the figures are right.
Exam cue: validate before you report, whether a person, a spreadsheet or an AI tool produced the figures.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Proposal to raise a breached threshold
questions.question: A telecom chatbot's wrong-answer KRI has sat six weeks above the red threshold approved by its risk owner, the customer director, and the product lead proposes raising it. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Raise the threshold to recent weeks' rate, as proposed
options.B: Refer the breach and the proposal to the director
options.C: Leave the decision to the product lead who runs it
options.D: Report a satisfaction score to the director instead

questions.key_concept: Only whoever approved a KRI threshold, usually the risk owner within senior management's tolerance, can move it; breaches and proposals go to them.
questions.pre_read: Note who approved the threshold, then ask who may change it.
questions.correct_explanation: The customer director owns the risk and approved the red threshold, so only the director, or a level above, can change it; six weeks above red is a breach they must see. The director can have the chatbot fixed, or take a request to carry the risk or change tolerance to the level that set it. Raising the threshold is the runner-up: it silences the alert without the owner who approved the limit.

wrong_explanations.A: Moving the threshold to fit recent results hides the breach and changes a limit the director approved, which only the director or a level above can change.
wrong_explanations.C: The product lead runs the chatbot but did not approve the threshold; a limit the risk owner set is not the product team's to change.
wrong_explanations.D: Satisfaction scores measure performance; reporting one in place of the KRI removes the warning instead of answering it.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves a limit decision with the team that runs the chatbot, and D swaps a risk indicator for a performance score.
Final two: B beats A because a threshold the risk owner approved moves only with the owner, or a level above.
Exam cue: never move a threshold to fit the data; take the breach and any proposed change to whoever set the limit.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.4 (the functionality and behavior of the AI system are monitored when in production); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.4.3 (Risk Owner: risk escalation and elevation)

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for late regulatory filings
questions.question: An asset manager's risk owner for missed regulatory filing deadlines receives a quarterly KRI counting filings submitted late. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as the BEST improvement?

options.A: A KRI on late source data feeds for each filing
options.B: The same count of late filings reported monthly
options.C: A KPI on staff hours spent preparing each filing
options.D: A KRI counting regulator fines paid in the year

questions.key_concept: Late filings are the event itself; a leading KRI tracks a driver, such as late source data, that moves before a deadline is missed.
questions.pre_read: Note what the current KRI counts and when that count changes.
questions.correct_explanation: Counting late filings reports the risk event after it has happened. Late source data feeds are a driver that shows up days before a deadline, while there is still time to act, so they make a leading KRI. Reporting the same count monthly is the runner-up: it arrives sooner, but it still counts filings that are already late.

wrong_explanations.B: Reporting a lagging count more often leaves it lagging; each figure describes deadlines already missed.
wrong_explanations.C: Preparation hours measure effort, a performance measure that need not change before a missed deadline.
wrong_explanations.D: Fines arrive after the miss and after the regulator acts, a later signal than the current KRI.

tips: Eliminate: C measures effort, a KPI, and D counts fines that arrive even later than late filings.
Final two: A beats B because a leading KRI tracks a driver that moves before the event; a lagging count reported more often still lags.
Exam cue: frequency does not make an indicator leading; look for the driver that moves before the loss.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators); ISACA Glossary (key risk indicator)

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Red threshold with no agreed action
questions.question: When an energy retailer's KRI for unpatched billing servers turned red last month, three managers each waited for another to act, and two weeks passed. What should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: A lower red threshold for the patching KRI
options.B: A monthly board report listing red KRIs
options.C: Additional KRIs on the billing servers' patching
options.D: A set response and responder for each level

questions.key_concept: Thresholds work only when the action and the person who takes it are agreed for each level before any breach.
questions.pre_read: Ask what was missing when the red reading arrived.
questions.correct_explanation: The KRI did its job: it turned red. The delay came from not knowing who acts and what they do, so each level needs an agreed response and responder in advance, with escalation for red. A lower red threshold is the runner-up: it would fire sooner, but red should mark the tolerance, and an earlier alarm with no agreed response just starts the same wait sooner.

wrong_explanations.A: A lower red level fires sooner but no longer marks the tolerance; with no agreed response the same wait would simply start earlier.
wrong_explanations.B: Board reporting adds visibility at the top but still names nobody to act when a KRI turns red.
wrong_explanations.C: More indicators add readings that nobody is set to act on; the gap was the response, not the measurement.

tips: Eliminate: B reports red KRIs upward without naming who acts, and C adds measurements when the gap was the response.
Final two: D beats A because an earlier alarm with no agreed action only starts the wait sooner.
Exam cue: thresholds turn metrics into decisions only when each level's action and actor are set before the breach.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 5.1 (Key CSRM Mechanisms: risk tolerance is translated into security controls, KPIs and KRIs); NIST SP 800-137 Section 3.5 (Respond to Findings)

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Accepted risk with no monitoring
questions.question: A courier company's operations director accepted the risk of its legacy routing server failing, on condition its health is watched, but no monitoring was set up. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Remove the risk from the register now it is accepted
options.B: Assess the acceptance again at the next annual review
options.C: Track the server's warning signs with an indicator
options.D: Add a control to cut the server's accepted risk further

questions.key_concept: Accepted risk is still monitored; when an acceptance depends on a condition, the indicator that checks it has to exist.
questions.pre_read: Read the condition attached to the acceptance, and check whether it holds.
questions.correct_explanation: The director accepted the risk on condition that the server's health is watched, so the acceptance rests on monitoring that does not exist. Setting up an indicator for warning signs, such as disk errors or failed restarts, meets the condition and shows if the risk grows. Assessing it again at the annual review is the runner-up: periodic review matters, but a failing server can go down long before the next one.

wrong_explanations.A: Accepted risk stays in the register and is monitored; removing it hides a live risk and the condition attached to it.
wrong_explanations.B: A yearly review leaves the acceptance's condition unmet for months, while the server can fail at any time.
wrong_explanations.D: The director chose to accept, not treat, the risk; what is missing is the monitoring, not another control.

tips: Eliminate: A drops an accepted risk from the register, and D treats a risk the owner chose to accept.
Final two: C beats B because the acceptance depends on ongoing monitoring; a yearly review leaves the condition unmet in between.
Exam cue: acceptance is not the end; watch the accepted risk, especially when the acceptance was conditional.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Acceptance: exposure within risk tolerance is still reported, monitored and managed); NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring)

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Relying on the yearly audit
questions.question: A water utility learns whether its key controls worked only when its external auditors sample them each year. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: The yearly audit of owners' key controls, used as monitoring
options.B: Owner-run KCIs reviewed by the risk team
options.C: The risk team running key controls for their owners
options.D: A mid-year audit sample of the high-risk controls

questions.key_concept: Key controls need ongoing monitoring by their owners, challenged by the risk function; periodic audits give assurance but do not replace monitoring.
questions.pre_read: Ask how soon a failed control would come to light under each option.
questions.correct_explanation: Learning about control failures once a year leaves months of exposure unseen. KCIs that control owners run and the risk team reviews show failures as they happen, keeping the first line accountable and the second line challenging. A mid-year audit sample is the runner-up: it halves the gap, but it is still periodic assurance rather than monitoring, and the owners would still watch nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Audits give periodic assurance on a sample of owners' controls; relying on them as monitoring leaves failures unseen for most of the year.
wrong_explanations.C: If the risk team runs the controls, owners stop owning them and nobody independent can challenge the result.
wrong_explanations.D: A mid-year sample of high-risk controls halves their gap but stays periodic assurance; the owners would still not be monitoring their controls.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a yearly audit as monitoring, and C has the second line take over the owners' controls.
Final two: B beats D because owners monitoring their controls find failures as they happen; a mid-year audit only shortens the gap.
Exam cue: audit is assurance, not monitoring; key controls need owner-run indicators that the risk function challenges.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Figures of different ages
questions.question: A risk analyst's executive dashboard for a payment processor shows some KRI figures from this week and others three months old, with nothing to tell them apart. What is the analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Show the date and source of each figure
options.B: Add a trend arrow beside each KRI's figure
options.C: Add red, amber and green status to each figure
options.D: Show fewer KRIs on each page of the dashboard

questions.key_concept: Each dashboard figure needs its date and source, so readers can tell current data from old and judge how far to rely on it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a reader cannot tell about each number on this dashboard.
questions.correct_explanation: With this week's and three-month-old figures side by side and unmarked, executives cannot tell which numbers describe today, so they may act on an exposure that has since changed. Showing each figure's date and source fixes that. A trend arrow is the runner-up: it adds direction, but a trend drawn from data of unknown age can mislead as much as the figure itself.

wrong_explanations.B: Trend adds direction, but without dates readers cannot tell whether a trend uses current or three-month-old data.
wrong_explanations.C: Status colors worked out from old figures look authoritative while describing a past position.
wrong_explanations.D: Fewer KRIs reduce clutter but leave the remaining figures of unknown age.

tips: Eliminate: C colors figures whose age is unknown, and D trims the page without saying how current anything is.
Final two: A beats B because readers must know how current each figure is before a trend or a status means anything.
Exam cue: each reported figure carries its date and source; without them, readers cannot judge what to rely on.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.2 (Measurement Reporting: context such as the risk indicated, fit with risk appetite and the decision needed); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.1 (Measures Documentation: a standard record of what is measured, the data source, the formula and who handles the data keeps measures traceable)

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Risk profile for audit planning
questions.question: A university's internal audit plans next year's audits from its own systems list, and the plan leaves out three of the risk profile's top five risks. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Propose risk team approval of the internal audit plan
options.B: Have the risk team test controls over the three risks
options.C: Share the risk profile with internal audit for planning
options.D: Rate the three unaudited risks higher in the profile

questions.key_concept: Internal audit sets its own plan, and the risk profile is a key input so audit can give assurance where the top risks are.
questions.pre_read: Note who sets the audit plan and what it is built from.
questions.correct_explanation: Internal audit sets its own plan to stay independent, but a risk-based plan needs to know the top risks. Sharing the risk profile gives audit that input while the planning decisions stay with audit and the audit committee. Having the risk team test controls over the three risks is the runner-up: second-line testing has value, but it is not independent assurance, and it leaves audit's plan blind to the top risks.

wrong_explanations.A: Approving audit's plan would put the second line over the third and undermine the independence that gives audit its value.
wrong_explanations.B: Second-line testing helps, but it is not independent assurance, and audit's plan would still miss the top risks.
wrong_explanations.D: Inflating ratings to steer audit distorts the profile that owners and the board rely on.

tips: Eliminate: A puts the risk team over audit's plan, and D distorts ratings to steer attention.
Final two: C beats B because audit needs the profile to plan independent assurance; second-line testing is not independent.
Exam cue: the risk function informs internal audit's planning with the risk profile; it neither directs audit nor stands in for it.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Reporting emerging risks to the board
questions.question: Which of the following is the BEST way for a risk practitioner to report emerging risks to a board?

options.A: Ranked on the usual scale among the top risks
options.B: Listed once a peer firm has reported a loss
options.C: An appendix of the signals found by horizon scanning
options.D: In their own section, with what is known and not

questions.key_concept: Emerging risks are reported apart from rated risks, with what is known, what is not and what is being done to learn more.
questions.pre_read: Think about how much is known about an emerging risk, and what a board needs from it.
questions.correct_explanation: Emerging risks are not yet understood well enough to rate on the usual scale, so they are reported in their own section, stating what is known, what is not and what is being done to learn more. Ranking them among the top risks is the runner-up: it gets attention, but it presents estimates as measured ratings and mixes them with risks the board can compare reliably.

wrong_explanations.A: Ranking uncertain risks with measured ones presents estimates as ratings the board can compare, which they are not yet.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for a peer's loss is the trap; emerging risks are recorded and reported before they are proven.
wrong_explanations.C: Raw signals bury the board in noise; signals are screened against objectives before anything is reported.

tips: Eliminate: B waits for a loss elsewhere, and C passes unscreened signals to the board.
Final two: D beats A because emerging risks cannot be rated reliably yet; ranking them with measured risks presents estimates as ratings.
Exam cue: emerging risk is reported as uncertain, with its knowns and unknowns, neither ignored nor scored as certain.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Early response to navigation spoofing
questions.question: Horizon scanning shows rising GPS spoofing on a container shipping firm's routes, with unknown effect on its vessels, and the CEO wants a $2,000,000 program at once. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Start the full $2,000,000 program the CEO has asked for
options.B: Take low-cost steps to learn more, with trigger points
options.C: Transfer the spoofing risk through marine insurance
options.D: Hold off acting while no company vessel has been affected

questions.key_concept: Emerging risks get staged responses: learn more cheaply, prepare options and agree triggers for bigger steps as evidence grows.
questions.pre_read: Weigh how much is known about this risk against the size of the response.
questions.correct_explanation: Spoofing is a real but still uncertain risk for this fleet. Low-cost steps, such as checking how crews spot false positions and which routes are exposed, build evidence, and agreed trigger points release more money if the risk grows. The full program is the runner-up: it takes the risk seriously, but it commits $2,000,000 before anyone knows what the fleet needs.

wrong_explanations.A: A large program before the risk is understood may buy the wrong controls; spending should grow with the evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Insurance shares some financial loss but not the safety and delay effects, and cover for a risk nobody has sized yet is hard to price.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for a first incident is the trap; emerging risks are worked on before they materialize.

tips: Eliminate: C leans on insurance for a risk nobody has sized, and D waits for a first incident.
Final two: B beats A because spending on an emerging risk grows with the evidence; a full program first may buy the wrong controls.
Exam cue: for emerging risk, prefer staged steps with triggers over waiting or betting everything at once.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Cover for a risk within appetite
questions.question: A retailer's web-shop outage risk is within appetite even at its worst plausible yearly loss, $150,000; insurance would cost $45,000 a year against a $20,000 expected loss. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the risk owner buy the $45,000 cover
options.B: Add a standby web host to shorten outages
options.C: Have the risk owner accept the risk on record
options.D: Put the uninsured exposure on record for the board

questions.key_concept: Insurance is for financial losses the business cannot absorb; when even the worst plausible loss is within appetite, the owner accepts on record and monitors.
questions.pre_read: Read the loss figures against appetite before weighing any response.
questions.correct_explanation: Even the worst plausible loss, $150,000, sits within appetite, so the retailer can absorb it. Insurance earns its premium when a loss could exceed what the business can bear; here it would cost $45,000 a year to offset an expected $20,000. Buying the cover is the runner-up: it feels prudent, but it pays more than it saves on a risk the owner can accept and monitor.

wrong_explanations.A: Transfer suits financial losses the business cannot absorb; paying $45,000 a year to offset an expected $20,000, when even the worst case is within appetite, costs more than it saves.
wrong_explanations.B: A standby host would mitigate a risk that is already within appetite, adding cost the analysis does not justify.
wrong_explanations.D: The board sets appetite and does not decide individual risks inside it; a risk within appetite is its owner's decision.

tips: Eliminate: B mitigates a risk already within appetite, and D sends a decision inside appetite up to the board.
Final two: C beats A because even the worst plausible loss is within appetite, so there is no loss the business cannot absorb for the cover to take.
Exam cue: insurance is for financial losses the business cannot absorb; within appetite on a sound rating, the owner accepts and monitors.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Owner for a merged enterprise risk
questions.question: A retail group's risk analyst has merged its 14 store brands' entries for refund fraud at store checkouts into one enterprise risk. Which of the following should the analyst propose as its MOST appropriate owner?

options.A: A group executive with authority across the 14 brands
options.B: The 14 brand heads, as joint owners of the risk
options.C: The CIO, whose team runs the checkout systems
options.D: The risk function that built the enterprise entry

questions.key_concept: A risk aggregated across units needs one owner whose authority spans those units; unit heads keep ownership of their own entries.
questions.pre_read: Think about what changed when the entries became one risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Merging the entries creates one enterprise risk that no single brand head can fund or accept for the other 13. Ownership follows authority, so the analyst proposes a group executive over the 14 brands, for senior management to confirm, while each brand head keeps their own entry. Joint ownership by the brand heads is the runner-up: it looks inclusive, but shared owners leave no one accountable for the enterprise decision.

wrong_explanations.B: With 14 joint owners, no single person can decide the enterprise response or accept its residual risk; each head stays owner of their brand's entry.
wrong_explanations.C: The CIO's team runs the checkout systems and may own controls on them, but refund fraud is a business risk to the group's sales and margins.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk function builds, monitors and reports the entry; it does not own business risk or hold authority over the brands.

tips: Eliminate: C hands a business risk to the CIO who runs the systems, and D has the risk function own a risk it monitors.
Final two: A beats B because an enterprise risk needs one owner with authority across the units; joint owners leave no one accountable.
Exam cue: an aggregated risk is owned at the level whose authority spans every unit it covers.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk owner); ISACA Glossary (risk aggregation); NIST CSF 2.0 GV.RR-02 (roles, responsibilities and authorities related to cybersecurity risk management are established, communicated, understood and enforced)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3A2.1 (Assigning Risk Owners; bullet 2 extended: authority must cover every unit the risk spans) with 3C2.2 (merging unit entries into a representative risk). Round 6, 4 Nov 2026: original scenario (a retail group merging 14 store brands' refund-fraud entries into one enterprise risk and proposing its owner), written for KaiSip in our own words; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D3 round 6 (crisc_d3_116 to 128). Neighbours checked: crisc_d3_105 (how to show merged entries; this item asks who owns the result), crisc_d1_052 (two joint accountable roles in a RACI; here the lesson is authority across units), crisc_d3_089 (one control serving four risk owners), crisc_d3_023 (owner by who runs the process), crisc_d2_060 (IT security team named on every entry). Cross-domain fixes 4 Nov 2026 (round 6): explanation says the analyst proposes the owner for senior management to confirm, matching notes 2B3.1 (cross-domain gate observation).

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. AI vendor training on inputs
questions.question: An AI translation vendor may train on a toolmaker's published manuals unless the toolmaker pays $30,000 a year extra; assessed on those terms, the risk is within appetite. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Propose that the business owner fund the no-training tier
options.B: Reassess the risk with the vendor's training terms
options.C: Add a clause shifting misuse risk to the vendor
options.D: Have the business owner accept the risk as rated

questions.key_concept: A vendor finding, AI or not, is rated against appetite; within appetite, the business owner accepts it on record and reviews it at renewal.
questions.pre_read: Check what the vendor would receive and how the risk compares with appetite.
questions.correct_explanation: The manuals are the toolmaker's own and already public, and the risk, assessed on the vendor's terms, is within appetite, so nothing is left to analyze and no treatment is justified. The first step is the business owner's decision: accept on record, with the terms checked again at renewal. Reassessing is the runner-up: it comes first after a change, but nothing has changed since this assessment.

wrong_explanations.A: The tier removes the concern, but $30,000 a year buys little against a risk within appetite on content that is already public.
wrong_explanations.B: Reassessing comes first when something has changed, but nothing has: the risk was assessed on these training terms, so a new assessment repeats work and delays the owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.C: A liability clause shifts some cost after misuse and is hard to enforce; it treats a risk that needs no treatment.

tips: Eliminate: A pays $30,000 a year to treat a risk already within appetite, and C adds a clause that shifts cost only after harm.
Final two: D beats B because the risk was already assessed on these terms; with nothing changed, the owner's decision comes before another assessment.
Exam cue: FIRST does not always mean assess; when a current assessment already covers the facts in the stem and the risk is within appetite, the owner's acceptance comes first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 GV.SC-07 (the risks posed by a supplier, their products and services and other third parties are understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to and monitored); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Acceptance: exposure within risk tolerance is still reported, monitored and managed); ISACA Glossary (risk acceptance)

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Many exceptions, one cause
questions.question: In a year, an insurer's 18 project teams got exceptions to the pre-go-live penetration test standard because the one approved testing firm was booked four months ahead. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have risk owners pre-approve future test exceptions
options.B: Add test capacity, such as a second firm
options.C: Have owners extend the exceptions until slots open
options.D: Keep assessing the risk of each new request

questions.key_concept: Repeated exceptions with one cause signal a root-cause problem; fixing the cause beats approving each deviation well.
questions.pre_read: Read why the exceptions were granted before choosing a response.
questions.correct_explanation: Eighteen exceptions with the same cause show the standard cannot be met as resourced; they are not 18 separate cases. More approved testing capacity, such as a second firm, removes the reason teams deviate, so systems go live tested. Assessing each request carefully is the runner-up: it keeps each deviation controlled, but it leaves the bottleneck in place, and the exceptions keep coming.

wrong_explanations.A: Advance approval saves effort but grants the same deviation before anyone looks at it; systems still go live untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Owners extending the exceptions leaves systems untested for longer and treats the delay as normal rather than fixing it.
wrong_explanations.D: Case-by-case assessment is sound practice, but with one shared cause it controls each deviation without stopping the next.

tips: Eliminate: A and C both keep systems going live untested, one by approving in advance and the other by waiting longer.
Final two: B beats D because a pattern of identical exceptions has one cause; fix it rather than handle each request well.
Exam cue: many exceptions with the same reason point to a root cause; recommend fixing it, not processing more deviations.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-07 (changes and exceptions are managed, assessed for risk impact, recorded and tracked); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-03 (improvements are identified from execution of operational processes, procedures and activities)

Cue pass 5 Nov 2026: C now has owners extend the exceptions, a second owner-naming distractor, so owner options no longer point to the key.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. A catalog to select controls from
questions.question: The risk practitioner wants a detailed catalog of specific security and privacy controls to choose from when treating a set of system risks. Which of the following BEST meets this need?

options.A: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5
options.B: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0
options.C: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1
options.D: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2

questions.key_concept: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 is a catalog of controls to select and tailor; CSF 2.0 lists outcomes and does not prescribe the controls.
questions.pre_read: Recall what each publication is for before matching it to the need.
questions.correct_explanation: SP 800-53 Rev. 5 is NIST's catalog of security and privacy controls, from which organizations select and tailor controls for their risks. CSF 2.0 is the runner-up: it is widely used and links to sources of controls, but it lists outcomes, such as protecting data, and does not prescribe the controls that achieve them.

wrong_explanations.B: CSF 2.0 sets out high-level outcomes and points to other sources for controls; it does not itself prescribe how the outcomes are achieved.
wrong_explanations.C: SP 800-30 Rev. 1 guides how to conduct risk assessments; it helps rate the risks, not choose the controls that treat them.
wrong_explanations.D: SP 800-37 Rev. 2 describes the risk management framework process, with a step to select controls, but the controls come from SP 800-53.

tips: Eliminate: C is a guide to assessing risk, and D is the process that calls for selecting controls, not the controls.
Final two: A beats B because SP 800-53 lists the controls; CSF 2.0 names outcomes and leaves the controls to other sources.
Exam cue: CSF 2.0 says what to achieve, SP 800-53 offers controls to achieve it, and COBIT 2019 sets governance and management objectives.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Section 1.1 (Purpose and Applicability: a comprehensive and flexible catalog of security and privacy controls); NIST CSF 2.0 Section 1 (CSF Overview: the Core is a taxonomy of high-level outcomes and does not prescribe how they are achieved)

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Long outage, rare event
questions.question: An online travel agency's booking-platform outage scenario exceeds appetite because three days offline would lose customers to rivals for good; its likelihood is already rated rare. Which response should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Business interruption insurance for lost bookings
options.B: A second firewall layer in front of the site
options.C: Weekly rather than monthly patching of the servers
options.D: A tested standby site that restores within hours

questions.key_concept: Act on what drives the rating; when money cannot repay the impact, reduce the impact itself rather than an already rare likelihood.
questions.pre_read: Note which part of the rating puts the scenario above appetite.
questions.correct_explanation: The scenario is above appetite because of its impact, customers lost for good during three days offline, not its rare likelihood. A tested standby site acts on that driver by cutting an outage to hours. Insurance is the runner-up: it repays part of the lost bookings, but the customers who leave during three days offline do not come back, and that loss is what puts the scenario above appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Insurance repays some lost revenue, but the site is down for three days and the customers who move to rivals stay lost; transfer suits a loss that is mainly financial.
wrong_explanations.B: A second firewall layer lowers the chance of some attacks, but likelihood is already rare and the three-day impact is unchanged.
wrong_explanations.C: Faster patching removes some causes of failure; with likelihood already rare, the rating stays driven by the outage's length.

tips: Eliminate: B and C both work on likelihood, which is already rare, and leave the three-day impact untouched.
Final two: D beats A because the loss above appetite is customers who leave, which only a shorter outage prevents; insurance repays money, not customers.
Exam cue: find which factor drives a rating above appetite, likelihood or impact, and choose the response that acts on it; insurance fits a loss money can repay.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.3 Task 3-2 (Evaluation of Alternatives: effectiveness, feasibility and cost); NIST IR 8286B-upd1 Section 2.3.4 (Risk Mitigation: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective and compensating controls)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B2.1 (Selecting Controls by Root Cause and Cost-Benefit; bullet 2 extended: favor controls acting on the factor that drives the rating). CRISC D3 round 6 (crisc_d3_116 to 128). Neighbours checked: crisc_d3_086 (insurance keyed when only the financial loss is above appetite and controls cannot cut it; here a control can cut the impact; keep apart), crisc_d3_032 (detection after harm), crisc_d3_009 (root-cause control), CISA d4_162 (backup design for restores), crisc_d2_073 (BIA ranking by outage effect). questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Reconciliation against itself
questions.question: A walkthrough shows a fintech's daily payment reconciliation compares the outgoing file with a copy of itself, not the bank's settlement record; a 30-day sample test comes next. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the control owner for 30 days of records
options.B: Report the design gap to the control owner
options.C: Widen the planned sample to 60 days
options.D: Credit the control if the 30-day sample passes

questions.key_concept: A control that fails on design needs no operating test; the design gap goes to the control owner to fix.
questions.pre_read: Check what the control compares before choosing the next test step.
questions.correct_explanation: Comparing a file with a copy of itself can never find a wrong payment, so the control fails on design, and testing its operation adds nothing. The first step is to report the design gap to the control owner, who redesigns it against the bank's record. Collecting 30 days of records is the runner-up: it looks thorough, but it tests the running of a control that cannot work, which the rating should stop crediting.

wrong_explanations.A: Thirty days of records would show the control ran, not that it can catch errors; operating evidence cannot rescue a broken design.
wrong_explanations.C: A larger sample of a control that compares a file with itself still finds nothing; sample size does not fix a design flaw.
wrong_explanations.D: Every day would match, so crediting the control on the sample would report a control that cannot detect a single error.

tips: Eliminate: C enlarges a test that cannot find errors, and D would credit a control that passes whatever happens.
Final two: B beats A because a design failure ends the test; operating evidence for a broken design proves nothing.
Exam cue: test design first; when the design cannot work, report it rather than sample its operation.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 CA-2 (Control Assessments); NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5 Section 2.4.2 (Assessment Methods: examine, interview and test, with depth and coverage)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 3B3.2 (Design and Operating Effectiveness Testing: test design first; a badly designed control needs no operating test). CRISC D3 round 6 (crisc_d3_116 to 128). Neighbours checked: crisc_d3_066 (what a walkthrough shows), crisc_d3_100 (a review that runs on time but misses retired rules), crisc_d3_064 (well designed but skipped), crisc_d3_036 (two missed days in a sample), CISA d1_214 (walkthrough then sampled records) and CISA d1_192 (untested controls in a residual rating). questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Engineers booked elsewhere
questions.question: A ferry operator's risk owner signed a plan to segment its vessel-control network by June, but the engineers needed are booked on another project until August. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Have the action owner move the due date to August
options.B: Ask the other project to release the engineers
options.C: Raise the staffing conflict with the risk owner
options.D: Track the plan monthly in the risk register

questions.key_concept: A risk action plan needs real resources; when they are missing, the risk owner who committed to the plan resolves the gap.
questions.pre_read: Check whether the plan can still be delivered as signed.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan the owner signed now lacks the people it needs, so its June date cannot be relied on. Resources are part of the plan, and only the risk owner, with the other project's sponsor if needed, can find staff, fund contractors or reset the date with interim measures. Moving the date to August is the runner-up: it looks realistic, but it changes the owner's commitment without the owner.

wrong_explanations.A: An action owner can report that the date will slip, but resetting a committed date, and the exposure it extends, is the risk owner's decision.
wrong_explanations.B: Moving engineers between projects is a resourcing decision for the owners and sponsors involved, not one the practitioner can broker.
wrong_explanations.D: Tracking the plan in the register records a slip that is already certain, instead of resolving the gap while there is time.

tips: Eliminate: B has the practitioner reallocate staff, and D tracks a June date already known to be out of reach.
Final two: C beats A because the risk owner committed the plan's resources and date; changing either is the owner's decision.
Exam cue: a plan without its resources is not a plan; take resource gaps to the risk owner before the dates slip.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Does the KRI warn?
questions.question: A bank's risk committee asks whether its two-year-old KRI for failed sign-in attempts actually warns of account takeovers. Which of the following analyses should the risk analyst use to BEST answer?

options.A: Compare the KRI's level with other banks' figures
options.B: Line up past KRI rises with incident dates
options.C: Reconcile the KRI's data with the sign-in logs
options.D: Poll control owners on the KRI's usefulness

questions.key_concept: A KRI's predictive value is tested against its history: a leading KRI moves before the incidents it is meant to warn of.
questions.pre_read: Pin down exactly what the committee is asking about the KRI.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI warns only if it moves before the event. Checking two years of values against when account takeovers happened shows whether rises in failed sign-ins came first, which is the committee's question. Reconciling the data with the sign-in logs is the runner-up: it confirms the figures are accurate, but an accurate figure can still fail to predict anything.

wrong_explanations.A: Other banks' figures show whether the level is high or low, not whether this KRI moves before takeovers at this bank.
wrong_explanations.C: Reconciling to the logs checks accuracy, which matters, but accurate data says nothing about whether the KRI rises before takeovers.
wrong_explanations.D: Control owners' views show whether the KRI is liked or used, not whether its values have predicted takeovers.

tips: Eliminate: A compares levels with other banks, and D collects opinions; neither tests whether the KRI warns.
Final two: B beats C because the question is predictive power; accurate data can still describe a KRI that never warns.
Exam cue: to test whether a KRI leads, line its history up against past incidents and see which moved first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 4.4 (Evaluating Methods for Supporting Continuous Improvement: leading and lagging indicators); NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 2.1 Table 2 (Data analysis examples: a scatter plot of historical data reveals relationships between two variables)

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Warning and limit levels
questions.question: A bank's digital director owns outage risk under a board tolerance of four hours a year; the risk's KRI goes from green straight to red at four hours. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Ask the board to set the KRI's warning levels
options.B: Have the director move the red level to three hours
options.C: Add a monthly outage count alongside the yearly KRI
options.D: Propose an amber level for the director to approve

questions.key_concept: Amber warns while there is time to act, so it sits below tolerance; red marks the limit itself.
questions.pre_read: Note where each level sits against the board's limit.
questions.correct_explanation: With no amber level, the KRI gives no warning: it moves from green to breach in one step, leaving no time to act. The practitioner proposes an amber level below four hours, and the director, as risk owner, approves it within the board's tolerance. Moving red to three hours is the runner-up: it fires earlier, but red marks the limit, so it would report a breach that has not happened and still give no warning.

wrong_explanations.A: The board set the tolerance; levels inside it are proposed by the practitioner and approved by the risk owner, so the board would be deciding the wrong thing.
wrong_explanations.B: Red marks the tolerance; pulling it to three hours reports a breach before one happens and still leaves no warning step between green and red.
wrong_explanations.C: Another count adds data but no warning point; the yearly KRI would still say nothing until four hours are used up.

tips: Eliminate: A sends warning levels to the board, which set the tolerance, not the thresholds inside it, and C adds a count without adding a warning point.
Final two: D beats B because amber warns while there is time to act and red marks the limit; moving red earlier blurs the two.
Exam cue: green within appetite, amber approaching tolerance, red at the limit; the practitioner proposes the levels and the risk owner approves them.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Measuring the monitoring
questions.question: A utility's continuous control monitoring now raises alerts from 400 automated checks. Which of the following is the BEST indicator for the risk practitioner to show the monitoring process is working?

options.A: Share of alerts resolved within set response times
options.B: Number of automated checks switched on each quarter
options.C: Count of alerts the platform raises each month
options.D: Monitoring platform availability over the quarter

questions.key_concept: Monitoring is working when its alerts are resolved within set response times, not when it raises more alerts or runs more checks.
questions.pre_read: Decide what working should mean for a monitoring process before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring reduces risk only when someone acts on what it finds. The share of alerts resolved within their set response times measures exactly that: whether findings are handled while they still matter. The count of alerts raised is the runner-up: it shows the platform is detecting, but a rising count can just as well mean problems found and left unhandled.

wrong_explanations.B: Switching on more checks measures rollout activity, not whether anyone deals with what the checks find.
wrong_explanations.C: Alert volume shows detection, but many alerts with no response can mean more risk, not less.
wrong_explanations.D: Platform uptime shows the tool is available, not that its findings lead to any action.

tips: Eliminate: B counts checks switched on, and D measures the tool's uptime; neither shows findings are acted on.
Final two: A beats C because monitoring works when alerts are resolved in time; raising them is only half the job.
Exam cue: judge monitoring by the response to its findings, not by how much it watches or reports.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Breach between reports
questions.question: Days after a university's quarterly risk report, the risk analyst confirms unpatched student-records servers have breached the tolerance the executive committee set; the next report is 11 weeks away. What is the analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Report the breach to its owner in the next quarterly report
options.B: Ask the control owner to finish the patching first
options.C: Escalate the breach outside the reporting cycle
options.D: Flag the breach on the live risk dashboard

questions.key_concept: A confirmed tolerance breach goes to the risk owner and the level that set the limit when it happens, not at the next scheduled report.
questions.pre_read: Decide what a confirmed tolerance breach needs before reading the options.
questions.correct_explanation: A confirmed tolerance breach needs a decision from the risk owner and, through the escalation path, the executive committee that set the limit. Waiting 11 weeks for the next report leaves the breach unmanaged, so it is escalated outside the cycle. Flagging it on the live dashboard is the runner-up: it shows the breach at once, but a dashboard waits for someone to look, while escalation asks the people who must decide.

wrong_explanations.A: Holding a confirmed breach for the quarterly report 11 weeks away leaves the risk above tolerance with no decision; scheduled reports do not replace escalation.
wrong_explanations.B: The fix matters, but the control owner's patching does not tell the risk owner or the committee that their limit was breached.
wrong_explanations.D: A dashboard makes the breach visible to anyone who looks, but nobody is asked to decide; a tolerance breach needs an escalation that requests one.

tips: Eliminate: A waits 11 weeks with a breach unreported, and B has the control owner patch first while the risk owner and the committee stay unaware that their limit was breached.
Final two: C beats D because a tolerance breach needs a decision, and escalation asks for one; a dashboard shows the breach only to whoever happens to look.
Exam cue: a confirmed tolerance breach is escalated when it happens; the reporting calendar never delays it.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Signal heard first by staff
questions.question: A water utility's horizon scan of news and alert feeds caught scam texts using its name after a press story; call-center staff had heard of them for months. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Add a second commercial news-monitoring service
options.B: Feed front-line teams' reports into the scan
options.C: Move the horizon scan to a weekly schedule
options.D: Record scam risks once customers report a loss

questions.key_concept: Horizon scanning should draw on front-line teams as well as external feeds, since staff often see an emerging risk first.
questions.pre_read: Note each source that could have picked up the scam texts.
questions.correct_explanation: The signal existed inside the utility for months: call-center staff were hearing about the scam texts. A scan built only on external feeds misses what front-line teams see first, so their reports should feed it. A second news service is the runner-up: it widens the external view, but it would still have waited for the same press story.

wrong_explanations.A: Another news service adds more of the same external sources, which reported the scam only once the press had it.
wrong_explanations.C: Scanning more often does not help when the sources themselves lag; the internal signal would still be missed.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for a reported loss is the trap; emerging risks are recorded and watched before they cause harm.

tips: Eliminate: C repeats the same lagging sources more often, and D waits for a loss before recording the risk.
Final two: B beats A because the missed signal came from inside the utility; more external feeds would still lag.
Exam cue: horizon scanning draws on front-line staff as well as external feeds; insiders often see a new risk first.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-03 (internal and external threats to the organization are identified and recorded); NIST SP 800-39 Section 3.4 (Monitoring Risk: compliance, response effectiveness and risk-impacting changes)

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. New control at plan closure
questions.question: A university's privileged-access vault passed its operating test; its action plan closes as the project team running the monthly checks disbands and IT operations takes them over. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Propose an IT operations manager to own the control
options.B: Write the vault's checks into IT operations' procedures
options.C: Close the plan as scheduled, with the test results filed
options.D: Have internal audit run the vault's monthly checks

questions.key_concept: A control a project delivers needs a named control owner, usually the manager whose team runs it, before the project closes.
questions.pre_read: Note what changes for the vault when the project team leaves.
questions.correct_explanation: Once its builders leave, a control with no owner decays: nobody answers for the checks running, keeps their evidence or reports when they fail. The practitioner proposes the IT operations manager whose team will run them, for the risk owner to confirm, before the plan closes. Writing the checks into procedures is the runner-up: it says what should happen, but a procedure cannot be held to account when a check is skipped.

wrong_explanations.B: A procedure describes the checks, but no one would answer for them running or for acting when they fail.
wrong_explanations.C: A passed test shows the vault works today; closing with no owner leaves nobody to keep the checks running once the team has gone.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit gives independent assurance; running the checks itself would leave nothing independent to audit, and operations would still have no owner.

tips: Eliminate: C closes the plan with nobody to keep the checks running, and D puts internal audit in charge of a control it should assure.
Final two: A beats B because a control needs a person who answers for it; a procedure says what to do but cannot be held to account.
Exam cue: when a project delivers a control, a named control owner takes it over before the project ends.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Rating that counts a planned review
questions.question: An insurer's AI claim-summary errors are rated within appetite only by crediting human review starting in four months; the risk owner proposes accepting them and closing the plan. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the owner accept the risk and close the plan
options.B: Have claims staff start the review next week
options.C: Close the plan and track the review as a project
options.D: Keep the plan open until the review is running

questions.key_concept: Acceptance rests on current risk, counting only controls already working; a rating that credits a planned control shows target risk.
questions.pre_read: Read the owner's proposal and the rating side by side.
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance must rest on current risk, which counts only actions already taken. The within-appetite rating credits human review that has not started, so it is the plan's target, not today's position. Keeping the plan open until the review runs, with the register showing today's level, keeps both the treatment and the rating honest. Accepting as rated is the runner-up: the owner has the authority, but would be accepting a level not yet reached.

wrong_explanations.A: The owner may accept risk within appetite, but this rating credits a review not yet running, so the acceptance would rest on target risk, not current risk.
wrong_explanations.B: When the review starts is the owner's resourcing decision; bringing it forward does not answer a proposal to close the plan now.
wrong_explanations.C: Moving the review to a project log takes it out of the risk plan, so nothing ties the rating to the review actually starting.

tips: Eliminate: B changes the review's start date instead of answering the proposal, and C closes the plan while the rating still depends on it.
Final two: D beats A because acceptance rests on current risk; a rating that credits a review not yet running shows the plan's target.
Exam cue: a within-appetite rating that counts planned controls is a target; keep the plan open until those controls work.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Framework revised
questions.question: A port operator mapped its controls to NIST CSF 1.1 in 2022; CSF 2.0 has since added a Govern Function and moved some 1.1 outcomes. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the 1.1 mapping until the next yearly audit
options.B: Rebuild the operator's controls from CSF 2.0
options.C: Update the control mapping to CSF 2.0's outcomes
options.D: Add new controls to meet the Govern outcomes

questions.key_concept: When a framework is revised, update the mapping of existing controls to the new version to find the real gaps before adding or rebuilding controls.
questions.pre_read: Note what the revision changed and what the operator already has in place.
questions.correct_explanation: CSF 2.0 lists outcomes, not controls, and many of its Govern outcomes, such as roles, policy and supplier oversight, may already be met by the operator's existing practices. Updating the mapping to the revised outcomes shows which are covered and which are real gaps for an action plan. Adding controls for the Govern outcomes is the runner-up: it looks thorough, but it builds controls the operator may already have.

wrong_explanations.A: A mapping to the earlier version hides any gap the revision exposes, and waiting a year for an audit leaves those gaps unseen.
wrong_explanations.B: CSF 2.0 does not prescribe controls, and rebuilding throws away working controls that already meet many of its outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Adding controls skips the mapping; some Govern outcomes are already met, so new controls would duplicate what exists.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps a mapping to the earlier version for a year, and B rebuilds working controls from a framework that prescribes none.
Final two: C beats D because the mapping shows which new outcomes are already met; adding controls first duplicates what exists.
Exam cue: when a framework is revised, update the control mapping to the new version and act on the gaps it shows.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Entry too vague to rate
questions.question: A credit union using AI for loan decisions has an emerging-risk entry reading 'new AI laws may affect us', with an owner and review date. Which addition by the risk analyst is MOST important?

options.A: A single score for the entry on the usual scale
options.B: A scenario of the laws' effect on its objectives
options.C: A list of the AI bills relevant to its objectives
options.D: An IT lead to watch the laws alongside the owner

questions.key_concept: An emerging-risk entry needs a scenario of how the change would affect objectives, so it can be rated, watched and answered.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the entry would need before anyone could rate or watch it.
questions.correct_explanation: An entry saying only that laws may affect the credit union cannot be rated, watched or answered. A scenario sets out what could change, such as rules on explaining AI loan decisions, and how that would affect its objectives, so it can carry a rating range and triggers. A list of relevant bills is the runner-up: useful input, but it does not say what the bills would do.

wrong_explanations.A: A single score claims a precision the entry cannot support; emerging risk is rated with a range and a stated confidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Relevant bills feed the scenario, but a list alone does not say how they would affect lending, so the entry still cannot be rated.
wrong_explanations.D: The entry already has an owner; adding an IT lead splits the watch and treats a business risk as IT's to follow.

tips: Eliminate: A gives a single score the evidence cannot support, and D adds an IT lead to a business risk that already has an owner.
Final two: B beats C because a scenario shows how the change would affect objectives; a list of bills is input to it, not the risk.
Exam cue: record an emerging risk as a scenario tied to objectives, even while its rating is still a wide range.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Counts from regions of different size
questions.question: A telecom's dashboard ranks regions by complaints about its AI chat assistant: North had 300 from 600,000 chats, and South 90 from 30,000. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation for the ranking?

options.A: Rank the regions by how many complaints each had
options.B: Map each region's count onto the 1-to-5 impact scale
options.C: Pool both regions' complaints and chats into one rate
options.D: Compare complaints per 1,000 chats in each region

questions.key_concept: Compare units on rates against a common base, such as complaints per 1,000 chats, because raw counts mostly reflect volume.
questions.pre_read: Note the size of each region's figures before ranking them.
questions.correct_explanation: Raw counts reflect how much each region uses the assistant as much as how well it works. Per 1,000 chats, North has 0.5 complaints and South 3, so the assistant performs worst in South, the reverse of the ranking. Mapping counts onto the impact scale is the runner-up: it looks like normalizing, but it carries the size difference onto the scale, so North still ranks higher.

wrong_explanations.A: North's 300 complaints come from twenty times as many chats, so ranking by count points at the wrong region.
wrong_explanations.B: A common scale aligns different rating methods, not different volumes; North's larger count would still map to the higher score.
wrong_explanations.C: Pooling gives one rate for the assistant but hides the region where it performs worst, which is what the ranking is for.

tips: Eliminate: A ranks raw counts from regions of very different size, and C pools both regions into one rate, which cannot rank them.
Final two: D beats B because a common scale aligns rating methods; only a rate per 1,000 chats removes the volume difference.
Exam cue: before comparing units, turn counts into rates on the same base, such as per 1,000 transactions.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Records made after the fact
questions.question: Testing a hospital's monthly access review, the risk analyst finds all 12 sign-off records were created last week, the day after the test was announced. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Seek system records made when each review ran
options.B: Rate the review ineffective for the past year
options.C: Rely on the sign-off records the owner provided
options.D: Observe the review when it runs next month

questions.key_concept: Records created after a test is announced are not evidence the control ran; seek records made at the time before concluding.
questions.pre_read: Note when the records were made compared with the period they cover.
questions.correct_explanation: Records made after the test was announced show that paperwork exists now, not that the reviews ran each month. Before concluding, the analyst seeks evidence made at the time, such as the review tool's dated logs, access lists sent to managers or removal tickets the reviews raised. Rating the review ineffective is the runner-up: it may be the outcome, but the reviews may have run and been written up late.

wrong_explanations.B: Late paperwork does not prove the reviews never ran; concluding before looking for evidence made at the time could misstate the control.
wrong_explanations.C: A signature on records made last week shows who prepared them, not that each month's review happened when the records say.
wrong_explanations.D: Watching next month's run says nothing about the past 12 months, and people act differently when they know they are observed.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on records made for the test, and D observes a future run that cannot show what happened last year.
Final two: A beats B because the reviews may have run and been written up late; look for evidence from the period before concluding.
Exam cue: inspection is only as good as the records; when they were made after the fact, look for system evidence from the period.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Provider sold to a new owner
questions.question: A water utility's payroll provider was bought by a firm that will move processing abroad next quarter; the yearly vendor review is nine months away. What should the risk practitioner recommend FIRST?

options.A: Hold the reassessment for the yearly vendor review
options.B: Ask the provider for its latest SOC 2 report
options.C: Reassess the provider before the move takes effect
options.D: End the contract before the move abroad

questions.key_concept: A vendor event such as a sale or a move of processing triggers reassessment of the vendor's risk before the change takes effect.
questions.pre_read: Note what has changed about the provider since it was last assessed.
questions.correct_explanation: A new owner and a move abroad change who controls the payroll data, where it sits and which laws reach it, so the earlier due diligence no longer describes the risk. Reassessing before the move gives the business owner time to seek contract changes or plan an exit. The latest SOC 2 report is the runner-up: it is independent evidence, but it covers the provider before the sale, not the new arrangement.

wrong_explanations.A: A sale and a move abroad are triggers for reassessment; nine months of waiting would let processing move before anyone weighs the change.
wrong_explanations.B: The report covers past operations under the old owner and location, so it cannot show the risk of the new arrangement.
wrong_explanations.D: Ending the contract may prove right, but deciding before the change is assessed skips the analysis and the business owner's decision.

tips: Eliminate: A waits nine months for a scheduled review, and D ends the contract before anyone knows whether the change matters.
Final two: C beats B because the report describes the provider before the sale; only a reassessment covers the new owner and location.
Exam cue: after a vendor event such as a sale or a move, earlier due diligence and assurance reports describe the old arrangement; reassess before the change takes effect.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Issues that came back
questions.question: Internal audit finds 7 of 25 control-test issues an airport operator closed last year have recurred; each was closed on its owner's email saying it was fixed. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Reopen the seven issues and have them fixed again
options.B: Require evidence that each fix works before closing
options.C: Have internal audit approve each issue's closure
options.D: Take owners' signed forms as evidence of each fix

questions.key_concept: Close an issue only on evidence that its fix works; owner statements, emailed or signed, let unfixed issues return.
questions.pre_read: Note what each closure rested on.
questions.correct_explanation: Seven of 25 issues came back because closure rested on the owner's word: an email says a fix was made, not that it works. Requiring evidence, such as a retest or a sample, before closing removes the cause of the repeats. Reopening the seven is the runner-up: they do need fixing, but under the same closure rule the next set of issues would come back too.

wrong_explanations.A: The seven need work, but the closure rule that let them through stays the same, so other issues would come back the same way.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit gives independent assurance; approving each closure would put it inside the process it is meant to review.
wrong_explanations.D: A signed form is still the owner's statement; it records who vouches for the fix, not whether the fix works.

tips: Eliminate: C puts internal audit inside the closure process it should assure, and D swaps an email for a signed form, still the owner's word.
Final two: B beats A because the closure rule caused the repeats; reopening the seven treats the symptom and keeps the rule.
Exam cue: an issue closes on evidence that the fix works, not on the owner's statement in any form.
