questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Rise during a change freeze
questions.question: A retailer's KRI for servers missing critical patches has risen three months running to near amber; the IT manager says it does so each holiday change freeze. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Ask the KRI owner to lift the amber level for freeze months
options.B: Raise the rising trend with the patching risk's owner
options.C: Record the IT manager's freeze explanation in the KRI report
options.D: Compare the rise with the same months in past years

questions.key_concept: Trend analysis compares an indicator with the same period in past years, so a seasonal rise is told apart from a real worsening.
questions.pre_read: Note what explanation the stem offers and whether it can be checked.
questions.correct_explanation: Trend analysis reads a series for seasonal patterns as well as direction, so the IT manager's claim is checked against the KRI's history first. A steeper rise than in past freezes is a new worsening; a matching one is a known pattern, still reported with that context, since unpatched servers are real exposure. Raising the trend with the owner is the runner-up; it follows, with that comparison, so the owner hears which it is.

wrong_explanations.A: Thresholds come from tolerance, not from when a rise is expected; exposure during the freeze is still exposure, and only the risk owner approves a threshold change.
wrong_explanations.B: A rise toward amber is worth raising, but the seasonal claim can be checked first, so the owner hears whether the trend is new or the usual pattern.
wrong_explanations.C: Writing the explanation into the report takes the IT manager's word; the KRI's own history can confirm or refute it.

tips: Eliminate: A has the KRI owner bend the threshold to the season when thresholds come from tolerance, and C reports the IT manager's word without checking it.
Final two: D beats B because the seasonal claim can be tested against past years first; raising the trend follows if the rise is new.
Exam cue: before calling a rise a trend, compare it with the same period in past years; seasonal patterns repeat.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Appendix C.3 (Time Series Analysis: shows the level, trend, seasonality or noise within a series of data points); NIST IR 8286C Rev. 1 Section 5.2 (Monitoring Risks: KRIs are observed for trends such as rising likelihood or failing controls)

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Check frequency cut
questions.question: A hospital's pharmacy manager owns the daily check of controlled-drug dispensing and wants it weekly; the clinical services director accepted the drug-diversion risk's residual rating with daily checks. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Leave the check's frequency to the pharmacy manager
options.B: Reassess the diversion risk after the first weekly check
options.C: Refer the change to the clinical services director
options.D: Approve the weekly check while diversion alerts stay low

questions.key_concept: A control owner runs and improves a control, but a change that alters accepted residual risk needs the risk owner's agreement first.
questions.pre_read: Note each person's role and what the acceptance rested on.
questions.correct_explanation: The pharmacy manager owns the check, but the clinical services director accepted the drug-diversion risk's residual rating on the strength of daily checks. Checking weekly could leave more risk than was accepted, so the change goes to the director, with the practitioner's estimate of its effect, before it takes effect. Leaving it to the control owner is the runner-up: they own the control, not the risk it protects.

wrong_explanations.A: The control owner decides how the check runs, but cutting its frequency changes the residual risk the director accepted, which only the director can accept.
wrong_explanations.B: Reassessing after the change means the director learns of any extra risk only once it is already being carried.
wrong_explanations.D: Agreeing to more risk is the risk owner's decision; the practitioner estimates the effect and advises, and fewer alerts may only mean less dispensing is being checked.

tips: Eliminate: B rates the change only after the risk is carried, and D has the practitioner approve a change to accepted risk, which is the risk owner's call.
Final two: C beats A because the check protects a risk the clinical services director accepted at daily frequency; the control owner cannot change that residual risk alone.
Exam cue: a control change that alters accepted residual risk goes to the risk owner before it takes effect.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Losses left out of a rating
questions.question: A hotel group's commercial director will accept a card-fraud risk rated within appetite, but the rating omitted online bookings, 40% of sales, whose losses the payments team records. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Have the director accept as rated, with a review in a year
options.B: Fund the $45,000 fraud-screening upgrade for online bookings
options.C: Note the omitted online losses in the acceptance record
options.D: Re-rate the risk with the payments team's loss records

questions.key_concept: An acceptance rests on its rating; when the rating left out loss data that exists, re-rate before the owner decides.
questions.pre_read: Note what the rating was built on and what has come to light since.
questions.correct_explanation: An acceptance is only as sound as the rating behind it, and this rating left out online bookings, 40% of sales. Their losses are already on record with the payments team, so the rating can be redone before the director, as risk owner, decides; the risk may still be within appetite, or it may not. Noting the gap is the runner-up: it suits data that cannot be had in time, not records another team holds.

wrong_explanations.A: The rating is within appetite only on the data it used; accepting now would rest on a figure that leaves out 40% of sales.
wrong_explanations.B: Spending $45,000 treats a risk whose size is not yet known; the full loss data may show no treatment is needed, or a different one.
wrong_explanations.C: Stating a limitation fits data that cannot be obtained; here the payments team holds the records, so the director can decide on a complete rating.

tips: Eliminate: A accepts on a rating that left out 40% of sales, and B spends $45,000 before the risk's real size is known.
Final two: D beats C because the missing losses are on record and can be added; noting a gap suits data that cannot be had in time.
Exam cue: when a rating proves to have missed data that exists, redo it before anyone accepts or treats the risk.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Values copied from a bank
questions.question: A clinic adopting NIST SP 800-53 copied a bank's parameter values, including 30-day account reviews; its two-person IT team cannot keep pace and signs reviews off unchecked. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Hire a contractor to keep up the 30-day account reviews
options.B: Set each value from the clinic's own risk and staffing
options.C: Move the clinic's account reviews to a 90-day cycle
options.D: Record an exception for the 30-day account review cycle

questions.key_concept: Tailoring a control catalog includes setting each organization-defined parameter value from the organization's own risk and operations.
questions.pre_read: Note where the clinic's control settings came from.
questions.correct_explanation: Assigning values to a catalog's parameters, such as how often accounts are reviewed, is part of tailoring, and each value comes from the organization's own risk and operations. Copied wholesale, the bank's values outran a two-person team, so reviews became sign-offs without checks. A 90-day cycle is the runner-up: it may suit the reviews, but it is one guessed value, and the other copied values stay unchecked.

wrong_explanations.A: A contractor keeps up a value chosen for a bank's risk, not the clinic's, and the other copied values stay unexamined.
wrong_explanations.C: Ninety days may fit, but it is chosen without the clinic's risk, and every other copied value still needs the same review.
wrong_explanations.D: An exception is a temporary deviation from a suitable requirement; here the 30-day value was never set for the clinic's own risk.

tips: Eliminate: A funds a value chosen for a bank's risk, and D treats an unsuitable value as a temporary deviation rather than tailoring it.
Final two: B beats C because every value was copied; changing the review cycle alone leaves the rest unchecked against the clinic's own risk.
Exam cue: tailoring a catalog includes setting each parameter value from the organization's own risk and operations, not another firm's.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Default heat-map colors
questions.question: A retailer's board treats risks scoring over 9 of 25 as above appetite, but its heat map colors scores up to 12 green, the GRC tool's default. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Color bands set from the board's approved appetite
options.B: A note under the map that lists the risks above appetite
options.C: Trend arrows on each risk, fed by its KRI history
options.D: Board approval of the tool's default bands as appetite

questions.key_concept: Heat-map color bands are set from the board's approved appetite and tolerance, not a tool's defaults, so color shows position against appetite.
questions.pre_read: Compare the board's appetite with what the map's colors show.
questions.correct_explanation: A heat map's colors tell the board which risks are acceptable, so its bands must come from the board's own appetite, with tolerance marking the red edge. Here scores of 10 to 12 look acceptable though they are above appetite. A note listing them is the runner-up: it corrects this board pack, but the map would still show them green and mislead the next reader.

wrong_explanations.B: A note corrects one report, but the map's colors still say scores of 10 to 12 are acceptable, so the next reader is misled again.
wrong_explanations.C: Trend arrows show which way a risk is moving, not whether its position is within appetite; the colors would still be wrong.
wrong_explanations.D: Appetite is the board's choice from its objectives and capacity; a software default is no basis for it.

tips: Eliminate: C adds direction when the problem is position against appetite, and D lets a software default set the board's appetite.
Final two: A beats B because the bands themselves misstate appetite; a note fixes one pack while the map keeps showing risks above appetite as green.
Exam cue: heat-map colors must come from the approved appetite and tolerance, or the map tells the board the wrong story.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Ending an interim review
questions.question: A university made an AI tool that flags false expense claims its permanent control; it went live Monday and finance wants to end the interim manual review. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: End the manual review now that the tool is live
options.B: End the manual review once its findings show the tool works
options.C: End the manual review after a quiet month with the tool
options.D: Keep the manual review as a standing second layer of control

questions.key_concept: An interim measure runs until the permanent control is proven on the organization's own data, then ends; go-live alone is not proof.
questions.pre_read: Note what has been shown about the new control so far.
questions.correct_explanation: Go-live shows the AI tool is running, not that it catches the university's false claims. Keeping the manual review until its results prove the tool works compares reviewers' findings with the tool's flags on the same claims; then the interim step ends. Keeping the review for good is the runner-up: it feels safer, but the plan made the tool the permanent control, so after proof both would treat one risk.

wrong_explanations.A: A control that has just gone live is unproven; ending the interim review now leaves false claims uncaught if the tool misses them.
wrong_explanations.C: A quiet month means no one reported a problem, not that the tool caught the false claims; only comparing its flags with reviewers' findings shows that.
wrong_explanations.D: Interim measures cover exposure until the permanent control is proven; keeping both afterward pays twice to treat the same risk.

tips: Eliminate: A treats go-live as proof the tool works, and C takes a quiet month as proof without checking the tool's flags.
Final two: B beats D because the plan made the tool the permanent control; the manual review runs only until its results prove the tool, then ends.
Exam cue: an interim measure stays until the permanent control is shown to work in your own setting, then it can end.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Reviews that find nothing
questions.question: Each six-monthly review of a holiday-rental platform's emerging risk of AI-generated fake listings asks its owner only if anything has changed; the last three answers were no. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Agree with the owner to review the entry each quarter
options.B: Rate the risk on the usual scale in the main profile
options.C: Close the entry until the first AI-made fake listing is found
options.D: Agree with the owner the signs that would show it growing

questions.key_concept: Emerging risks are watched through agreed signs that would show them growing, so each review checks evidence rather than asking if anything changed.
questions.pre_read: Note what each review actually asks the owner.
questions.correct_explanation: The reviews keep finding nothing because they ask only whether anything has changed, with nothing named to check. Agreeing signs that would show the risk growing, such as reported fake listings or cheaper tools for faking photos, gives each review evidence to weigh and tells the owner when to act. A shorter cycle is the runner-up: asking the same open question more often still finds nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Reviewing more often repeats the same open question; with nothing named to check, a three-month review finds nothing new either.
wrong_explanations.B: Nothing new is known, so a usual rating would claim certainty the evidence lacks; an emerging risk joins the main profile once it can be rated with confidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for the first case records the risk only after it has caused harm, which an emerging-risk entry exists to avoid.

tips: Eliminate: B rates the risk with confidence nobody has, and C waits for the first case, losing the early warning the entry is for.
Final two: D beats A because the reviews ask an open question with nothing named to check; asking it more often still finds nothing.
Exam cue: an emerging risk needs named signs to watch, so each review has evidence to check and the owner knows when to act.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Supplier risk terms
questions.question: A risk practitioner is explaining supplier risks to a university's new procurement head. Which of the following BEST describes concentration risk?

options.A: One supplier's controls failing its yearly security review
options.B: A supplier passing customer data on to its subcontractors
options.C: Reliance on a few suppliers whose failure stops many services
options.D: The cost and effort of moving off a supplier's platform

questions.key_concept: Concentration risk is reliance on a few suppliers whose failure would stop many services at once, judged across suppliers rather than one at a time.
questions.pre_read: Note what each option measures before matching it to the term.
questions.correct_explanation: The ISACA Glossary describes concentration risk as reliance on a small number of suppliers, so one supplier's failure can stop every service built on it. It is judged across suppliers, by what depends on each, not one supplier at a time. Lock-in is the runner-up: it also comes from depending on a supplier, but it is the cost of leaving one, not the harm when one fails.

wrong_explanations.A: A failed review is one supplier's control weakness, rated on its own; concentration is about how many services depend on the same few suppliers.
wrong_explanations.B: Onward sharing with subcontractors is a fourth-party data risk; it concerns where data goes, not how many services stop if one supplier fails.
wrong_explanations.D: Lock-in is the cost and effort of leaving a supplier; it can deepen dependence, but it measures the exit, not the services a failure would stop.

tips: Eliminate: A rates one supplier's own controls, and B is about data passing to subcontractors; neither shows how much depends on a few suppliers.
Final two: C beats D because concentration is the harm when a relied-on supplier fails; lock-in is the cost of leaving one.
Exam cue: concentration risk is judged across suppliers by what depends on each; one supplier's score or exit cost does not show it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (concentration risk); NIST SP 800-161 Rev. 1 SR-3(1) (Diverse Supply Base: identify single points of failure and risk among primes and lower-level entities in the supply chain)

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Flaw with a weeks-long fix
questions.question: A housing association rates a tenant-portal flaw, letting tenants see others' rent arrears, above tolerance; the fix takes three weeks, and tenants can check arrears by phone. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Suspend the arrears page until the fix is live
options.B: Have the portal owner monitor arrears views until the fix
options.C: Agree with the owner to accept the risk for three weeks
options.D: Insure against tenants' claims for harm from the exposure

questions.key_concept: Temporary avoidance, such as suspending a feature until its fix is live, suits a risk above tolerance when little benefit is lost.
questions.pre_read: Weigh how long the exposure lasts under each option before choosing.
questions.correct_explanation: The flaw is rated above tolerance and the fix is three weeks away, so the exposure has to stop, not just be watched. Suspending the arrears page avoids the risk for those weeks, and tenants keep the service by phone, so little benefit is lost. Monitoring views is the runner-up: it shows who looked at others' arrears, but only after the data has been seen, so the exposure goes on.

wrong_explanations.B: Monitoring by the portal owner is detective: it records views after tenants' arrears have been seen, so the exposure stays above tolerance for the three weeks.
wrong_explanations.C: A risk above tolerance is beyond what the owner alone can accept; carrying it needs the level that set the limit, and a safer option exists.
wrong_explanations.D: Insurance repays some costs of claims, but tenants' arrears stay visible to others, so the harm and the breach of tolerance continue.

tips: Eliminate: C has the owner accept a risk above tolerance, beyond their authority, and D insures claims while the data stays exposed.
Final two: A beats B because monitoring only shows views after the data is seen; suspending the page stops the exposure, and phone keeps the service.
Exam cue: above tolerance with a slow fix, look for the response that stops the exposure now; avoidance fits when the benefit given up is small.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Exception within its term
questions.question: A school district's exception for an unpatched bus-routing server runs to June, within its approver's authority, and its compensating isolation passes monthly checks; IT wants it escalated. What is the risk analyst's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Escalate the exception to the superintendent for a decision
options.B: Ask the approver to re-sign the exception this month
options.C: Convert the exception into an exemption reviewed yearly
options.D: Review the exception at its scheduled due date

questions.key_concept: An exception within authority, in date and with a working compensating control is reviewed on schedule; escalation needs a trigger.
questions.pre_read: List what the stem says about authority, dates and the compensating control.
questions.correct_explanation: Escalation needs a trigger: a deviation beyond the approver's authority, a failing compensating control, a tolerance breach or a missed date. Here the exception is within authority, in date, and its isolation passes monthly checks, so the scheduled review at its June due date is the right control point. Escalating to the superintendent is the runner-up: it looks cautious, but it moves a decision the approver already holds, with nothing new to decide.

wrong_explanations.A: Nothing exceeds the approver's authority, breaches a limit or fails a check, so escalating moves a decision the approver already holds, with nothing new to decide.
wrong_explanations.B: Re-approval is for changed terms or a renewal; the exception's terms, authority and checks are unchanged, so a new signature adds no assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: An exemption fits a lasting exclusion; this deviation is temporary, ending in June, so an exemption would remove the end date that forces the server to be patched.

tips: Eliminate: B re-signs an exception whose terms have not changed, and C turns a temporary deviation into a lasting exemption, dropping the plan to comply.
Final two: D beats A because escalation needs a trigger, such as authority exceeded or a failing control; the stem gives none, so the agreed review holds.
Exam cue: a deviation within authority, in date and with working controls waits for its scheduled review; escalate when a trigger appears.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Comparing endpoint agents
questions.question: A hospital's comparison of endpoint agents covers detection rates and cost; the preferred agent installs each vendor update on all 6,000 clinical PCs at once. What should the risk analyst recommend adding as MOST important?

options.A: Detection test results for each update from a second lab
options.B: The outage risk if one faulty update reaches every PC
options.C: Clinical staff's views on the agent's effect on PC speed
options.D: License costs for adding PCs in later years

questions.key_concept: Control selection weighs the risks a control brings, such as an update that could stop every device at once, alongside the risk it reduces.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the comparison already covers and what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: Selecting a control means weighing the risks it brings as well as those it reduces. Because this agent pushes each update to all 6,000 clinical PCs at once, one faulty update could halt clinical work across the hospital, and a comparison of detection and cost does not show that. Staff views on PC speed are the runner-up: fit with the work matters, but slowness is a smaller, gradual effect than every PC stopping together.

wrong_explanations.A: Detection is already in the comparison; another lab's results refine a measure the hospital has, while the outage risk from simultaneous updates is still missing.
wrong_explanations.C: Fit with clinical work matters, but slower PCs are a smaller, gradual effect than an update that could stop all 6,000 at once.
wrong_explanations.D: Cost is already compared; later license costs refine that figure but say nothing about what the agent itself could do to clinical work.

tips: Eliminate: A and D add more of what the comparison already covers, detection and cost, rather than a factor it misses.
Final two: B beats C because one faulty update reaching every PC at once could stop clinical work everywhere; slowness is a smaller, gradual effect.
Exam cue: when choosing a control, weigh the risks the control itself brings, such as a single point of failure, alongside the risk it reduces.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Control changed during the year
questions.question: In July, a charity moved grant-payment approvals from paper forms to a workflow, and its board asks the risk analyst whether unapproved grants were paid this year. Which testing BEST supports the analyst's answer?

options.A: Test a sample of payments made since the July change
options.B: Rely on the workflow's go-live test for the whole year
options.C: Sample each method's payments for the months it ran
options.D: Refer the paper-form months to internal audit to test

questions.key_concept: When a control changes during the period under review, each version is tested for the months it ran.
questions.pre_read: Match the period the board asks about with the period each option tests.
questions.correct_explanation: The board's question covers every grant paid this year, and approval was a different control before and after July. Sampling payments approved under each method, for the months it ran, shows whether either let unapproved grants through. Testing only payments since July is the runner-up: it shows how the current workflow works, but it says nothing about grants paid on paper approvals before July.

wrong_explanations.A: This tests only the workflow; grants paid on paper approvals before July stay untested, so the answer cannot cover the year.
wrong_explanations.B: A go-live test shows the workflow was set up correctly on one date; it shows neither later operation nor anything about the paper months.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit sets its own plan, so the paper months may stay untested; the board asked the analyst about every grant paid this year.

tips: Eliminate: B uses a go-live test, which shows set-up on one date and nothing about operation, and D passes the paper months to internal audit, which sets its own plan.
Final two: C beats A because the board asked about the whole year; testing only the workflow leaves grants paid on paper without evidence.
Exam cue: when a control changed during the period in question, test each version for the months it ran.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. Evidence for an automated calculation
questions.question: A toll-road operator's billing system applies frequent-driver discounts automatically each month. Which of the following should the risk analyst rely on MOST as evidence that the discount control is effective?

options.A: Job logs showing each monthly discount run completed
options.B: Discounts the analyst recalculates for sampled accounts
options.C: The billing manager's account of how the discount rules work
options.D: Observation of this month's discount run as it happens

questions.key_concept: Reperformance, recalculating results independently, gives stronger evidence that a calculation control works than records showing it ran.
questions.pre_read: Ask what each piece of evidence actually proves about the discounts.
questions.correct_explanation: Reperformance gives the strongest evidence: recalculating discounts for sampled accounts and comparing them with what the system applied shows directly whether the calculation is right. Job logs are the runner-up: they are system records covering the whole period, but they show only that each run finished, not that the discounts it applied were correct, so a wrong rate would pass every month.

wrong_explanations.A: Logs show each run finished, not whether its discounts were right; a wrong rate would run to completion every month and still look clean.
wrong_explanations.C: An account of the rules is inquiry: it tells the analyst how discounts should work, not whether the system applies them correctly.
wrong_explanations.D: Watching one run shows it happening at that moment, not whether its results were correct or earlier months were.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on inquiry, the weakest evidence on its own, and D observes one run without checking its results.
Final two: B beats A because job logs prove each run finished, not that its discounts were right; recalculating gives an independent result.
Exam cue: for a calculation, the strongest evidence is the tester reaching the result independently; proof that a step ran is not proof it ran correctly.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for data taken by leavers
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk analyst propose as the BEST key risk indicator for staff copying a crop-science company's research data before they leave?

options.A: Large downloads by staff serving their notice period
options.B: Leaver accounts disabled within a day of leaving
options.C: Confirmed cases of data taken by former staff
options.D: Staff who finished data-handling training this year

questions.key_concept: A KRI should track a driver of the named scenario that moves before the loss, not a control or activity measure.
questions.pre_read: Find when the named risk event happens, then check when each measure would move.
questions.correct_explanation: A good KRI tracks a driver of the named scenario and moves before the loss. Unusually large downloads by staff serving notice rise while the data can still be protected, because the copying happens while their accounts are live. Disabling leaver accounts within a day is the runner-up: it is a useful control indicator, but it covers access after people leave, not copying before they go.

wrong_explanations.B: This measures the offboarding control after people leave; most data leaves before they do, while their accounts are still active.
wrong_explanations.C: Confirmed cases count losses that have already happened, so this lagging measure explains a loss rather than warning of one.
wrong_explanations.D: Training completion measures the awareness program's activity; it can stay high while leavers copy data, so it does not track the risk.

tips: Eliminate: C counts confirmed losses after the fact, a lagging measure, and D measures training activity, which need not move with the risk.
Final two: A beats B because the scenario happens before people leave; B tracks an offboarding control that covers access afterward.
Exam cue: the BEST KRI sits on the scenario's own path, before the loss; check when and where the named risk event happens.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Faster grants and more privileges
questions.question: In six months, a broadcaster's KPI for same-day access grants rose from 80% to 97%, and its KRI for accounts with unneeded privileges from 3% to 9%. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Report the access risk as improving, citing the KPI
options.B: Escalate the KRI's rise to the board for its decision
options.C: Have managers remove the unneeded privileges this month
options.D: Check whether faster grants cause the extra privileges

questions.key_concept: A KPI can improve while risk worsens; when they move together, analyze whether the performance push is causing the risk.
questions.pre_read: Compare the direction and timing of the two indicators before choosing an action.
questions.correct_explanation: The two indicators rose over the same months, which suggests the push for same-day grants may be giving people more access than they need. Checking that link first finds the cause, so the fix targets the grant process rather than its output. Removing the privileges now is the runner-up: it lowers today's figure, but if the grant process is the cause, the excess returns with the next requests.

wrong_explanations.A: The KPI measures how fast access is granted, not exposure; the KRI shows the risk rising, so calling it improving misreports the position.
wrong_explanations.B: No threshold breach is reported and the cause is unknown; analysis and the risk owner come before taking the rise to the board.
wrong_explanations.C: A cleanup lowers this month's figure, but if same-day grants are causing the excess, new unneeded privileges keep arriving.

tips: Eliminate: A reports a speed KPI as a risk measure, and B takes an unanalyzed rise with no stated breach straight to the board.
Final two: D beats C because a cleanup treats the symptom; if the same-day push causes the excess, it returns until the grant process changes.
Exam cue: when a KPI improves while a related KRI worsens, check whether the performance push is driving the risk before acting.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Outage at a peer
questions.question: A peer solar-farm operator went offline after its inverter maker pushed a faulty remote update; the risk analyst's firm, with no such event yet, uses the same inverters. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Rate it at the yearly assessment from the firm's own data
options.B: Log the peer's outage as a loss event in the firm's register
options.C: Record it as an emerging risk, citing the peer's outage
options.D: Ask the inverter maker to stop remote updates to its sites

questions.key_concept: A peer's incident on the same technology is valid evidence to record an emerging risk now, without waiting for in-house data.
questions.pre_read: Note what the firm has in common with the peer.
questions.correct_explanation: A peer's outage on the same inverters is relevant outside evidence that this firm is exposed too, so the risk should be recorded now as an emerging risk, with the peer's event as its basis, its uncertainty stated and an owner. Waiting for the yearly assessment and the firm's own data is the runner-up: it sounds rigorous, but it leaves a known exposure unrecorded until the firm suffers the same outage.

wrong_explanations.A: In-house data may arrive only as the firm's own outage; a peer's event on the same inverters is valid evidence now, and the yearly cycle leaves it unrecorded.
wrong_explanations.B: The outage happened at the peer, not here; logging it as this firm's own loss event misstates its loss history rather than recording the exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: This picks a control before the risk is analyzed, and stopping remote updates could also block the security fixes the inverters need.

tips: Eliminate: B files a peer's outage as this firm's own loss event, and D chooses a control first, which could also block needed security fixes.
Final two: C beats A because a peer's outage on the same equipment is valid evidence now; waiting for the firm's own data leaves the risk unrecorded.
Exam cue: outside events, such as a peer's incident or an industry report, are valid triggers to record an emerging risk before it happens to you.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Requests the departments ignore
questions.question: A government agency's register names a junior IT officer as owner of the quarterly contractor-access review, but department heads ignore the officer, leaving 40% of reviews unanswered. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the risk owner remind department heads each quarter
options.B: Name a senior manager over those departments as its owner
options.C: Keep the officer as control owner, with more time to chase replies
options.D: Escalate each unanswered review to the risk committee

questions.key_concept: A control owner needs authority over the people the control depends on; an owner they can ignore leaves the control failing.
questions.pre_read: Ask why the review keeps failing before choosing who should act.
questions.correct_explanation: A control owner answers for the control working, so they need authority over the people it depends on. Department heads ignore a junior officer, so 40% of reviews fail; a senior manager over those departments can hold them to it, while the officer still runs the work. Reminders from the risk owner are the runner-up: they may lift one quarter's replies, but the review still rests with someone the departments can ignore.

wrong_explanations.A: Reminders may lift this quarter's replies, but the review's own owner still lacks authority, so each quarter depends on outside pressure.
wrong_explanations.C: More time gives the officer no authority over department heads; replies still depend on goodwill, and late ones leave contractor access unchecked longer.
wrong_explanations.D: Sending each missed reply to a committee treats every gap as a one-off and floods it; it does not change who answers for the review.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves the review with an owner who has no authority over the departments, and D sends each missed reply to a committee without fixing who owns the review.
Final two: B beats A because reminders lift one quarter's replies; an owner with authority over the departments makes the review work every quarter.
Exam cue: a control owner needs authority over the people the control depends on; when a control fails because its owner is ignored, fix the ownership.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Assurance report at the yearly review
questions.question: A logistics park's gate vendor's full-year SOC 2 Type 2 report shows no exceptions and covers its hosting provider; the park runs the listed user controls. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Send the vendor this year's security questionnaire beside the report
options.B: Commission an on-site audit of the gate vendor's controls
options.C: Repeat the full onboarding due diligence on the vendor
options.D: Rely on the report in this year's review of the vendor

questions.key_concept: An independent report covering the service, its subcontractors and the period, with the customer's user controls running, can be relied on.
questions.pre_read: Check the report's scope, period, subcontractors and user controls before deciding what more is needed.
questions.correct_explanation: The report is independent, tested evidence over a full year, it covers both the service and the host behind it, it shows no exceptions, and the park runs the user controls it depends on. Nothing is left open, so relying on it is sound ongoing monitoring. An on-site audit is the runner-up: it sounds thorough, but it repeats a year of independent testing at the business's cost with no gap to target.

wrong_explanations.A: A self-completed questionnaire is weaker evidence than the independent, tested report already in hand, and it asks again about controls the report has tested.
wrong_explanations.B: A site audit repeats a full year of independent testing with no gap or exception to target, so it adds cost without adding assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Onboarding due diligence suits a new vendor; for a live one, current assurance reports are the ongoing check, and this one leaves nothing open.

tips: Eliminate: A adds the vendor's own answers to tested evidence already in hand, and C repeats onboarding checks on a vendor a current report already covers.
Final two: D beats B because the report covers the service, host and year with no exceptions; a site audit would repeat that testing with no gap to target.
Exam cue: an assurance report counts for what it covers; when scope, period, subcontractors and user controls all check out, rely on it.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Firewall rule set to log
questions.question: A school district rates its finance-system risk crediting a firewall rule as preventive, but the rule only logs student-network traffic to the system for weekly review. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Correct the rating to count the rule as a detective control
options.B: Recommend switching the rule from logging to blocking
options.C: Keep the rating while the logs are reviewed each week
options.D: Leave the rating until the rule's next scheduled control test

questions.key_concept: A control earns credit only for what it does; a firewall rule that only logs traffic detects, so it is not rated as preventive.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the control actually does at the moment the risk event happens.
questions.correct_explanation: The rating credits prevention the rule does not give: it records the traffic, and someone reads the records up to a week later, which is detection. The analyst should first correct the rating to the control's real function, so the risk owner sees the true position against appetite. Switching the rule to blocking is the runner-up: it may well be the fix, but it picks a control before the corrected rating is known.

wrong_explanations.B: Blocking may be the eventual fix, but it chooses a control before the corrected rating is known; the risk owner decides any treatment from that rating.
wrong_explanations.C: A weekly log review finds traffic after it has happened, so it detects; keeping the preventive credit overstates how well the risk is controlled.
wrong_explanations.D: The mismatch is already known; waiting for the next test leaves a wrong rating in place for everyone who relies on it.

tips: Eliminate: C keeps preventive credit for a weekly log review, which detects, and D leaves a known rating error in place until the next test.
Final two: A beats B because the rating must reflect what the rule really does before anyone chooses a fix; blocking may follow once the owner sees it.
Exam cue: classify a control by what it does to the risk event, not by the tool's name; a firewall rule that logs and does not block is detective.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Weld photos a model misreads
questions.question: A car maker's AI model grades weld photos; tests show it passes faulty welds when spatter or poor light blurs a photo. Which of the following controls should the risk analyst recommend as MOST effective?

options.A: Inspector review of a random 2% of graded welds
options.B: Retraining the model on new weld photos every quarter
options.C: A photo-quality check sending blurred photos to inspectors
options.D: A monthly report of weld faults found in later tests

questions.key_concept: An AI input check catches the inputs a model is known to misjudge and sends them to a person before a wrong output is used.
questions.pre_read: Read what the tests found before weighing the controls.
questions.correct_explanation: The model fails on a known kind of input, blurred photos, so the most effective control checks each photo's quality before the grade is trusted and sends blurred ones to an inspector. That catches the cases where faulty welds pass, at the point of use. A random 2% inspector sample is the runner-up: it adds human review, but it reaches few of the blurred photos, so most hidden faults still pass.

wrong_explanations.A: A random sample picks 2% of welds without regard to photo quality, so most blurred photos, where the faults hide, never reach a person.
wrong_explanations.B: A blurred photo lacks the detail to judge a weld; retraining cannot recover it, and faulty welds keep passing in the meantime.
wrong_explanations.D: A monthly report finds faults after the cars have moved on; it measures the problem rather than stopping faulty welds from passing.

tips: Eliminate: B retrains a model on photos that lack the detail to judge, and D reports faults a month later rather than stopping them.
Final two: C beats A because it targets exactly the photos where the model fails; a random sample reaches too few of them.
Exam cue: when an AI model fails on a known kind of input, check inputs before use and route the ones it cannot judge to a person.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Account plan at its end date
questions.question: A rail operator's action plan for signal engineers' named accounts is done: the risk team's operating test passed, and the risk owner signed the re-rated risk at target. What is the risk analyst's BEST action?

options.A: Wait for internal audit's review before closing the plan
options.B: Ask the control owner to repeat the operating test
options.C: Leave the plan open until the risk owner meets next quarter
options.D: Close the plan, citing the test and the risk owner's sign-off

questions.key_concept: An action plan closes once evidence shows the control works and the risk owner signs the re-rated risk at its target.
questions.pre_read: List what closing a plan needs, then check which of those the stem already gives.
questions.correct_explanation: Every closure condition is met: the risk team's operating test showed the named accounts work, and the risk owner signed the re-rated risk at the plan's target, which approves closing it. Closing keeps the register accurate, and the risk moves to routine monitoring. Waiting for internal audit is the runner-up: audit assures on its own plan, but a validated, signed-off action plan does not wait for it.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit reviews on its own plan and cycle; a validated action plan with the owner's sign-off does not need its review to close.
wrong_explanations.B: The control already passed an operating test run by the risk team; repeating it adds no new evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: The risk owner has already signed the re-rated risk; holding the plan for another meeting leaves the register showing finished work as open.

tips: Eliminate: B repeats an operating test that already passed, and C waits for a meeting to approve what the risk owner has already signed.
Final two: D beats A because the target is met, shown by evidence and the owner's sign-off; internal audit's review is not a gate for closing the plan.
Exam cue: keep a plan open until evidence shows the target is met; once it is, with the owner's sign-off, close it and monitor the risk.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Twelve regional outage risks
questions.question: An insurer's risk analyst is rolling 12 regional data-center outage risks into one enterprise line; 11 rate medium, and the region hosting the main claims system rates critical. What is the analyst's BEST approach?

options.A: Show the claims region's outage as its own enterprise risk
options.B: Rate the combined line at the worst region's level
options.C: Have the regional risk owners agree one enterprise rating
options.D: Leave the claims region's risk with its regional owner

questions.key_concept: Aggregation must keep a severe single risk visible; one combined line, averaged or set to the worst rating, misstates where exposure sits.
questions.pre_read: Before combining ratings, check whether one of them stands far apart from the rest.
questions.correct_explanation: One combined line would either hide the critical region inside a middle rating or call all twelve critical. Showing the claims region's outage as its own enterprise risk keeps the severe exposure visible where it sits, while the eleven similar risks roll up together. Rating the whole line at the worst level is the runner-up: it keeps the severity, but it overstates eleven regions and hides which one needs treatment.

wrong_explanations.B: Taking the worst rating keeps the severity but labels eleven medium risks critical and hides which region drives it, so treatment may go to the wrong places.
wrong_explanations.C: Agreeing one enterprise rating blends a critical risk with eleven medium ones; the result hides the severe exposure the enterprise needs to see.
wrong_explanations.D: A critical risk to the main claims system matters to the whole insurer; keeping it at regional level hides it from enterprise decisions.

tips: Eliminate: C blends a critical rating into an agreed middle, and D keeps a critical risk to the main claims system out of the enterprise view.
Final two: A beats B because a separate entry shows where the critical exposure sits; one line at the worst rating overstates eleven regions.
Exam cue: when combining risks, keep a severe single risk visible as its own line; neither averaging nor taking the worst rating shows it.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for an AI screening tool
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk analyst propose as the BEST key risk indicator that a recruitment agency's AI CV-screening tool is unfairly rejecting candidates?

options.A: Upheld discrimination complaints from rejected candidates
options.B: Monthly gap in pass rates between candidate groups
options.C: Screening accuracy reported by the tool's vendor
options.D: Share of CVs screened within an hour of arrival

questions.key_concept: A KRI for unfair AI decisions compares outcomes across groups on the organization's own data; overall accuracy can hide the gap.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the named harm would first show up in the data, then match each measure to it.
questions.correct_explanation: Unfair rejection first shows as a gap between groups' pass rates, so tracking that gap monthly warns while the agency can still correct the tool, before complaints or regulators act. The vendor's reported accuracy is the runner-up: it sounds like the model's own risk measure, but overall accuracy can stay high while one group is rejected far more often, and it reflects the vendor's tests, not the agency's candidates.

wrong_explanations.A: Upheld complaints count harm already done and confirmed months later; this lagging measure explains a loss rather than warning of one.
wrong_explanations.C: Overall accuracy can stay high while one group is rejected far more often, and the vendor's figure comes from its own tests, not these candidates.
wrong_explanations.D: Screening speed is a performance measure for the process; it can look excellent while the tool rejects some groups unfairly.

tips: Eliminate: A counts complaints upheld after the harm, a lagging measure, and D measures screening speed, a KPI that need not move with fairness.
Final two: B beats C because unfair rejection shows as a gap between groups; one overall accuracy figure from the vendor's tests can hide it.
Exam cue: for AI fairness risk, pick an indicator that compares outcomes across groups on your own data, not one overall accuracy figure.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. Indicator shown as a rolling average
questions.question: A mining company's executive dashboard shows its payment-fraud KRI as a 12-month rolling average, green all year, though two single months passed the red threshold. Which change should the risk analyst recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Have the KRI owner shorten the average to the latest quarter
options.B: Let each KRI's owner choose its averaging period
options.C: Plot each month's value against the KRI's thresholds
options.D: Replace the KRI with yearly fraud losses against a threshold

questions.key_concept: Show each period's KRI value against the thresholds set for it; a rolling average can hide single breaches from decision-makers.
questions.pre_read: Note what the executives saw and what they did not see.
questions.correct_explanation: The thresholds apply to each month's value, and a 12-month average dilutes a single bad month until it vanishes, so the executives never saw two red months. Plotting each month against the thresholds shows a breach when it happens, and the average can stay as a trend line. The owner's quarterly average is the runner-up: it reacts faster, but it still blends a red month with two calmer ones.

wrong_explanations.A: A shorter average, whoever sets it, reacts faster but still blends a red month with two others, so a single breach can still show amber or green.
wrong_explanations.B: Letting each owner pick a smoothing period gives inconsistent views and can still hide breaches; the dashboard needs values shown against the thresholds.
wrong_explanations.D: A yearly loss total arrives after the fraud has happened; checking it against a limit swaps an early warning for a lagging count of losses.

tips: Eliminate: B lets each owner pick a smoothing period, which still blends breaches into calmer months, and D swaps an early warning for a yearly loss count.
Final two: C beats A because any average, however short or whoever sets it, blends a red month with calmer ones; each month's value shows a breach when it happens.
Exam cue: compare a KRI with the threshold on the values it was set for; a dashboard that smooths data can hide the breaches it exists to show.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-55v1 Section 3.1.2 (Measurement Reporting: context such as the risk indicated, fit with risk appetite and the decision needed); NIST SP 800-55v1 Appendix C.3 (Time Series Analysis: shows the level, trend, seasonality or noise within a series of data points)
